pages.text: Variance of the Gaussian Random Variable. This page derives the variance of a Gaussian (normal) random variable and proves that the expected squared deviation from the mean equals the parameter σ². Start from the Gaussian integral identity ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) dx = √(2πσ^2) ). This identity represents the normalization property of the Gaussian function and forms the basis of the probability density function of the normal distribution. The probability density function of a Gaussian random variable X with mean μ and variance σ² is ( f_X(x) = 1 / √(2πσ^2) · exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) ). One of the key properties of this distribution is that the variance equals the parameter σ². To prove this, differentiate the Gaussian integral identity with respect to σ²: ( d/dσ^2 ∫_{-∞}^{∞} exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) dx = d/dσ^2 √(2πσ^2) ). Since the integrand is smooth, the derivative can be moved inside the integral: ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} d/dσ^2 [ exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) ] dx = d/dσ^2 √(2πσ^2) ). Apply the chain rule to compute the derivative of the exponential term. Let ( g(σ^2) = -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ). Then ( d/dσ^2 exp(g) = exp(g) · dg/dσ^2 ). The derivative of the exponent becomes ( dg/dσ^2 = (x-μ)^2 / (2(σ^2)^2) ). Therefore ( d/dσ^2 exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) = (x-μ)^2 / (2(σ^2)^2) · exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) ). Substitute this result into the integral to obtain ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} (x-μ)^2 / (2(σ^2)^2) · exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) dx = d/dσ^2 √(2πσ^2) ). Compute the derivative on the right side: ( d/dσ^2 √(2πσ^2) = √(2π) / 2 · (σ^2)^(-1/2) ). Rearranging the equation and introducing the Gaussian density function yields ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} (x-μ)^2 · 1 / √(2πσ^2) · exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) dx = σ^2 ). Recognize that ( 1 / √(2πσ^2) · exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) ) is exactly the Gaussian probability density function f_X(x). Therefore the integral becomes ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} (x-μ)^2 f_X(x) dx ). By the definition of expectation this equals ( E[(X-μ)^2] ). Hence ( E[(X-μ)^2] = σ^2 ). This proves that the variance of a Gaussian random variable equals the parameter σ² that appears in the probability density function, where μ represents the mean and σ² represents the spread of the distribution around the mean.

pages.text: Expectation of a Gaussian Random Variable. This page derives the mean of a Gaussian random variable and proves that the expected value equals the parameter μ. Begin with the Gaussian integral identity ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) dx = √(2πσ^2) ). The integral does not depend on μ because shifting the center of the Gaussian does not change the total area under the curve. Differentiate both sides with respect to μ: ( d/dμ ∫_{-∞}^{∞} exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) dx = d/dμ √(2πσ^2) ). The right side contains no μ, therefore its derivative is zero. Move the derivative inside the integral: ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} d/dμ [ exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) ] dx = 0 ). Apply the chain rule. Let ( g(μ) = -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ). Then ( d/dμ exp(g(μ)) = exp(g(μ)) · dg/dμ ). Compute the derivative of the exponent: ( dg/dμ = (x-μ)/σ^2 ). Therefore ( d/dμ exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) = (x-μ)/σ^2 · exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) ). Substitute this into the integral: ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} (x-μ)/σ^2 · exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) dx = 0 ). Multiply both sides by σ^2: ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} (x-μ) exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) dx = 0 ). Introduce the Gaussian probability density function ( f_X(x) = 1 / √(2πσ^2) · exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) ). This gives ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} (x-μ) f_X(x) dx = 0 ). By definition of expectation ( E[X-μ] = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} (x-μ) f_X(x) dx ). Therefore ( E[X-μ] = 0 ) which implies ( E[X] - μ = 0 ) and hence ( E[X] = μ ). This confirms that μ represents the mean of the Gaussian distribution and also indicates the center of symmetry of the probability density function.

pages.text:
Bayesian Probability Problem with Multiple Boxes. The page introduces a probability problem involving three different boxes containing fruits. The objective is to compute probabilities related to randomly selecting a fruit from one of the boxes. The boxes are labeled r, b, and g. Each box contains apples (A), oranges (O), and limes (L). A box is first chosen randomly according to specified probabilities, and then a fruit is selected randomly from the chosen box. The problem asks two questions: first, the probability of selecting an apple, and second, the probability that the fruit came from box g given that the selected fruit is an orange.

Description of the Boxes. Three boxes are shown. Box r contains three apples, four oranges, and three limes, giving a total of ten fruits. Box b contains one apple and one orange, giving a total of two fruits. Box g contains three apples, three oranges, and four limes, giving a total of ten fruits. The letters inside the circles represent the fruit types: A for apple, O for orange, and L for lime.

Probability of Choosing Each Box. A box is chosen randomly according to the following probabilities: ( P(r) = 0.2 ), ( P(b) = 0.2 ), and ( P(g) = 0.6 ). These values represent the prior probabilities of selecting each box before any fruit is observed.

Part (a): Probability of Selecting an Apple. Let the event A denote the event that the selected fruit is an apple. Since the fruit can come from any one of the three boxes, the total probability of selecting an apple is computed using the law of total probability. The law of total probability states that if a sample space is partitioned into mutually exclusive events, then the probability of another event can be expressed as the sum of conditional probabilities across the partitions.

Thus, the probability of selecting an apple is written as ( P(A) = P(A,r) + P(A,b) + P(A,g) ). Each joint probability can be expressed using conditional probability as ( P(A,r) = P(A|r)P(r) ), ( P(A,b) = P(A|b)P(b) ), and ( P(A,g) = P(A|g)P(g) ). Therefore the total probability becomes ( P(A) = P(A|r)P(r) + P(A|b)P(b) + P(A|g)P(g) ).

Now compute each conditional probability using the fruit composition of each box. In box r there are three apples out of ten fruits, therefore ( P(A|r) = 3/10 ). In box b there is one apple out of two fruits, therefore ( P(A|b) = 1/2 ). In box g there are three apples out of ten fruits, therefore ( P(A|g) = 3/10 ).

Substituting these values together with the box selection probabilities gives ( P(A) = (3/10)(0.2) + (1/2)(0.2) + (3/10)(0.6) ). Compute each term: ( (3/10)(0.2) = 0.06 ), ( (1/2)(0.2) = 0.10 ), and ( (3/10)(0.6) = 0.18 ). Adding these contributions yields ( P(A) = 0.06 + 0.10 + 0.18 = 0.34 ).

Interpretation. The result means that when the box selection and fruit selection processes are both considered, the overall probability of drawing an apple is 0.34. This probability incorporates both the prior probability of choosing each box and the conditional probability of finding an apple within that box.

pages.text: Application of Bayes Theorem in a Fruit Selection Problem. This page continues the probability problem where a fruit is drawn from one of several boxes and the goal is to determine the probability that the fruit came from a particular box given that the observed fruit is an orange. Let the event O represent that the selected fruit is an orange. Let the event L represent that the selected fruit is a lime. Let the event G represent that the fruit was drawn from box g. The goal of this part of the problem is to compute the conditional probability ( P(G | O) ), which represents the probability that the fruit came from box g given that the observed fruit is an orange. To solve this problem we apply Bayes theorem. Bayes theorem provides a mathematical rule that allows us to update the probability of a hypothesis after observing new evidence. The general formula for Bayes theorem is ( P(A | B) = ( P(B | A) P(A) ) / P(B) ). In this expression A represents the hypothesis and B represents the observed evidence. In this problem the hypothesis corresponds to the fruit coming from box g and the observed evidence corresponds to the fruit being an orange. Therefore Bayes theorem becomes ( P(G | O) = ( P(O | G) P(G) ) / P(O) ). Each term in this equation must now be determined using the information given in the previous part of the problem. The prior probability that a randomly selected box is box g is given as ( P(G) = 0.6 ). This value represents the probability of choosing box g before observing any fruit. The next quantity required is ( P(O | G) ), which is the probability of selecting an orange given that the fruit was drawn from box g. From the fruit composition data provided earlier, box g contains 3 oranges out of a total of 10 fruits. Therefore the conditional probability becomes ( P(O | G) = 3/10 ). The denominator of Bayes theorem requires the marginal probability of observing an orange regardless of which box was selected. This probability is computed using the law of total probability. The law of total probability states that if several mutually exclusive events partition the sample space, then the probability of an event can be written as the sum of the conditional probabilities across those events. Therefore ( P(O) = P(O | X) P(X) + P(O | S) P(S) + P(O | G) P(G) ). Here X, S, and G represent the three boxes available for selection. From the problem statement the probabilities of selecting each box are ( P(X) = 0.2 ), ( P(S) = 0.2 ), and ( P(G) = 0.6 ). The probabilities of drawing an orange from each box are determined from the fruit distributions inside each box. From the data the probability of selecting an orange from box X is ( P(O | X) = 4/10 ). The probability of selecting an orange from box S is ( P(O | S) = 1/2 ). The probability of selecting an orange from box G is ( P(O | G) = 3/10 ). Substituting these values into the law of total probability gives ( P(O) = (4/10)(0.2) + (1/2)(0.2) + (3/10)(0.6) ). Compute each term individually. The first term becomes ( (4/10)(0.2) = 0.08 ). The second term becomes ( (1/2)(0.2) = 0.1 ). The third term becomes ( (3/10)(0.6) = 0.18 ). Summing these contributions yields ( P(O) = 0.08 + 0.1 + 0.18 = 0.36 ). Now substitute all values into Bayes theorem. The numerator becomes ( P(O | G) P(G) = (3/10)(0.6) ). This product equals ( 0.18 ). Therefore ( P(G | O) = 0.18 / 0.36 ). Performing the final division gives ( P(G | O) = 0.5 ). This result means that once we observe that the selected fruit is an orange, the probability that it originated from box g becomes 0.5. The interpretation is important. Initially the probability of choosing box g was 0.6, but after observing that the fruit is an orange, the probability that it came from box g decreases to 0.5 because oranges can also come from the other boxes. Bayes theorem updates the prior probability using the evidence provided by the observation of the fruit type.

pages.text: Expectation of a Gaussian Random Variable using Change of Variable Method. This page completes the formal proof that the expected value of a Gaussian random variable equals the parameter μ. Consider a continuous random variable X that follows a normal distribution with mean μ and variance σ², written as ( X ~ N(μ,σ²) ). The probability density function of the Gaussian distribution is given by ( f_X(x) = (1 / √(2πσ²)) exp(-(x-μ)² / (2σ²)) ). The expectation of a continuous random variable is defined as ( E[X] = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} x f_X(x) dx ). Substituting the Gaussian density function into the expectation formula gives ( E[X] = (1 / √(2πσ²)) ∫_{-∞}^{∞} x exp(-(x-μ)² / (2σ²)) dx ). To simplify the integral, a change of variable is introduced to convert the Gaussian expression into the standard normal form. Define the substitution ( t = (x-μ) / (√2 σ) ). This transformation shifts and scales the variable so that the exponential becomes a standard quadratic form. Solving for x gives ( x = √2 σ t + μ ). Differentiating with respect to t gives the differential transformation ( dx = √2 σ dt ). Substituting these expressions into the expectation integral transforms it into ( E[X] = (1 / √(2πσ²)) ∫_{-∞}^{∞} (√2 σ t + μ) exp(-t²) √2 σ dt ). Simplifying the constant terms gives ( E[X] = (√2 σ / √(2πσ²)) ∫_{-∞}^{∞} (√2 σ t + μ) exp(-t²) dt ). The integrand can now be separated into two integrals using linearity of integration: ( E[X] = (√2 σ / √(2πσ²)) [ ∫_{-∞}^{∞} (√2 σ t) exp(-t²) dt + ∫_{-∞}^{∞} μ exp(-t²) dt ] ). Since μ is a constant it can be taken outside the integral. Therefore ( E[X] = (√2 σ / √(2πσ²)) [ √2 σ ∫_{-∞}^{∞} t exp(-t²) dt + μ ∫_{-∞}^{∞} exp(-t²) dt ] ). Consider the first integral ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} t exp(-t²) dt ). The function t exp(-t²) is an odd function because replacing t with -t changes the sign of the function while the integration limits are symmetric. For any odd function integrated over symmetric limits, the integral evaluates to zero. Therefore ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} t exp(-t²) dt = 0 ). Next consider the second integral ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} exp(-t²) dt ). This integral is a well known Gaussian integral which evaluates to √π. Substituting these results into the expression for E[X] leaves only the second term. After simplifying the constants, the final result becomes ( E[X] = μ ). This result proves that for a Gaussian distribution the mean of the distribution is exactly equal to the parameter μ. The parameter μ therefore represents the center of symmetry of the distribution. In a normal distribution the probability mass is symmetrically distributed around μ, which means the average value of the random variable is exactly μ.

pages.text: Uniform Random Variable: Derivation of Mean and Variance. This page derives the expected value and variance of a continuous uniform random variable defined over the interval [a, b]. A uniform random variable represents a distribution in which every value within a fixed interval has equal probability density. The probability density function of a continuous uniform distribution is constant across the interval and zero outside the interval. Therefore the probability density function is defined as ( f_X(x) = 1 / (b-a) ) for ( a ≤ x ≤ b ), and ( f_X(x) = 0 ) otherwise. Graphically this distribution forms a rectangular shape between a and b with constant height ( 1 / (b-a) ). The area under the probability density function must equal 1 because total probability must be equal to one. This can be verified by computing ( ∫_{a}^{b} 1/(b-a) dx = (1/(b-a))(b-a) = 1 ). The next goal is to compute the mean or expected value of the random variable X. The definition of the expected value for a continuous random variable is ( E[X] = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} x f_X(x) dx ). Since the pdf is non-zero only in the interval [a,b], the limits reduce to that interval. Therefore ( E[X] = ∫_{a}^{b} x (1/(b-a)) dx ). The constant term can be taken outside the integral giving ( E[X] = (1/(b-a)) ∫_{a}^{b} x dx ). Now evaluate the integral of x. The antiderivative of x is ( x^2 / 2 ). Therefore ( ∫_{a}^{b} x dx = ( x^2 / 2 )|_{a}^{b} ). Substituting the limits produces ( (b^2 / 2) - (a^2 / 2) ). Factoring gives ( (b^2 - a^2) / 2 ). Substituting back into the expectation formula yields ( E[X] = (1/(b-a)) · ( (b^2 - a^2) / 2 ) ). Recognizing that ( b^2 - a^2 = (b-a)(a+b) ), the term (b-a) cancels with the denominator. This produces the simplified expression ( E[X] = (a+b)/2 ). This result shows that the mean of a uniform distribution is exactly the midpoint of the interval [a,b], which matches the intuitive understanding that the distribution is symmetric across the interval. Next the variance of the random variable is derived. The variance of a random variable is defined as ( Var(X) = E[(X - E[X])^2] ). A commonly used equivalent formula is ( Var(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 ). Therefore we first compute the second moment ( E[X^2] ). The definition of the second moment is ( E[X^2] = ∫_{a}^{b} x^2 f_X(x) dx ). Substituting the uniform pdf gives ( E[X^2] = ∫_{a}^{b} x^2 (1/(b-a)) dx ). Taking the constant outside yields ( E[X^2] = (1/(b-a)) ∫_{a}^{b} x^2 dx ). The integral of ( x^2 ) is ( x^3 / 3 ). Evaluating between limits a and b produces ( (b^3 / 3) - (a^3 / 3) ). Factoring gives ( (b^3 - a^3) / 3 ). Substituting back gives ( E[X^2] = (1/(b-a)) · ( (b^3 - a^3) / 3 ) ). Using the identity ( b^3 - a^3 = (b-a)(b^2 + ab + a^2) ), the term (b-a) cancels again. Therefore ( E[X^2] = (a^2 + ab + b^2) / 3 ). Now compute the variance using ( Var(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 ). Substituting the expressions derived earlier gives ( Var(X) = (a^2 + ab + b^2)/3 - ((a+b)/2)^2 ). Expand the square term: ( ((a+b)/2)^2 = (a^2 + 2ab + b^2)/4 ). Now subtract the two expressions by using a common denominator. Converting both fractions to denominator 12 gives ( Var(X) = (4a^2 + 4ab + 4b^2)/12 - (3a^2 + 6ab + 3b^2)/12 ). Subtracting numerator terms yields ( (a^2 - 2ab + b^2)/12 ). Recognizing the numerator as ( (b-a)^2 ), we obtain the final simplified variance formula ( Var(X) = (b-a)^2 / 12 ). Therefore the uniform random variable defined on the interval [a,b] has mean ( (a+b)/2 ) and variance ( (b-a)^2 / 12 ). These results show that the mean lies at the center of the interval while the variance depends only on the width of the interval.

pages.text:
Variance Identity and Memoryless Property of the Exponential Random Variable. The page presents two important concepts in probability theory. The first concept is a fundamental identity for variance that expresses the variance of a random variable in terms of its second moment and its mean. The second concept is the memoryless property of the exponential random variable, which is a unique property of the exponential distribution and plays a major role in stochastic processes, reliability theory, and queuing systems.

Variance Identity. The variance of a random variable X measures how much the values of X deviate from the mean of the distribution. The variance is defined as the expected squared deviation from the mean. Mathematically this definition is written as ( Var(X) = E[(X - μ_X)^2] ), where μ_X denotes the mean of X, which is ( μ_X = E[X] ). Expanding the squared term gives ( (X - μ_X)^2 = X^2 - 2Xμ_X + μ_X^2 ). Taking expectation on both sides gives ( Var(X) = E[X^2 - 2Xμ_X + μ_X^2] ). Using the linearity property of expectation, which states that the expectation of a sum equals the sum of expectations, we obtain ( Var(X) = E[X^2] - 2μ_X E[X] + μ_X^2 ). Since ( E[X] = μ_X ), substitute this into the expression to obtain ( Var(X) = E[X^2] - 2μ_X^2 + μ_X^2 ). Simplifying the expression gives the well known variance identity ( Var(X) = E[X^2] - μ_X^2 ). This formula is extremely useful in practice because computing the second moment E[X^2] is often easier than directly evaluating E[(X-μ)^2].

Memoryless Property of the Exponential Distribution. The second part of the page discusses the memoryless property of an exponential random variable. Suppose a random variable X follows an exponential distribution with rate parameter α. The cumulative distribution function of the exponential distribution is given by ( F(x) = 1 - e^{-αx} ) for ( x ≥ 0 ). The probability that the variable exceeds a certain value t is therefore ( P(X > t) = 1 - F(t) ). Substituting the expression for F(t) gives ( P(X > t) = e^{-αt} ). This expression is known as the survival function of the exponential distribution.

Memoryless Property Statement. The exponential distribution has the property that the probability of surviving an additional time interval does not depend on how much time has already passed. Formally this is expressed as ( P(X > T + t | X > T) = P(X > t) ). This means that if a system has already survived for time T, the probability that it survives for an additional time t is the same as if the process started fresh at time zero.

Derivation Using Conditional Probability. By definition of conditional probability we write ( P(X > T + t | X > T) = P(X > T + t , X > T) / P(X > T) ). Since the event ( X > T + t ) automatically implies ( X > T ), the joint event simplifies to ( P(X > T + t) ). Therefore the conditional probability becomes ( P(X > T + t | X > T) = P(X > T + t) / P(X > T) ). Using the exponential survival function gives ( P(X > T + t) = e^{-α(T+t)} ) and ( P(X > T) = e^{-αT} ). Substituting these expressions gives ( P(X > T + t | X > T) = e^{-α(T+t)} / e^{-αT} ). Simplifying the exponent yields ( P(X > T + t | X > T) = e^{-αt} ). This expression is exactly equal to ( P(X > t) ). Therefore we obtain ( P(X > T + t | X > T) = P(X > t) ).

Interpretation. This result shows that the exponential distribution has no memory of past events. In reliability theory this means that the probability that a component survives for an additional time period does not depend on how long it has already been operating. This property makes the exponential distribution the continuous time analogue of the geometric distribution in discrete probability.

pages.text: Nonlinear Transformation of Random Variables and Its Implications. This page discusses the relationship between probability density functions when one random variable is obtained as a nonlinear transformation of another random variable. The topic belongs to transformation theory in probability and statistics and is commonly used in statistical signal processing and machine learning. Consider a continuous random variable X with probability density function ( p_X(x) ). Suppose another random variable Y exists with probability density function ( p_Y(y) ). Assume that the two variables are related through a transformation defined as ( X = g(Y) ). In this relationship g(·) represents a nonlinear function. Because the transformation is nonlinear, the probability distribution of Y will not simply be a shifted or scaled version of the distribution of X. Instead the probability density must be adjusted to account for how the transformation stretches or compresses the variable space. The general formula that relates the probability density functions of the two variables is called the change of variables formula for probability densities. If the transformation ( X = g(Y) ) is differentiable and monotonic, the probability density of Y can be written as ( p_Y(y) = p_X(g(y)) | g'(y) | ). This equation shows that the density of Y equals the density of X evaluated at the transformed point multiplied by the absolute value of the derivative of the transformation. The derivative term appears because the transformation may stretch or compress intervals of the variable, which changes how probability mass is distributed. If the transformation expands an interval, the probability density decreases. If the transformation compresses an interval, the probability density increases. The absolute value is used because probability densities must always remain nonnegative. The notes then state the goal of the analysis. The goal is to verify that the locations of the maxima of the two probability density functions are not necessarily directly related through the transformation function. In other words the value of y that maximizes ( p_Y(y) ) is not simply the transformation applied to the value of x that maximizes ( p_X(x) ). This idea is expressed as the statement that the peak of the transformed density does not necessarily occur at ( ŷ = g^{-1}(x̂) ), where x̂ denotes the point that maximizes ( p_X(x) ). To analyze this property we attempt to find the location of the maximum of ( p_Y(y) ). The maximum of a continuous function occurs at a point where its derivative with respect to the variable is zero, provided the second derivative condition is satisfied. Therefore the peak of the distribution ( p_Y(y) ) can be found by solving the equation ( d/dy p_Y(y) = 0 ). Substituting the transformation formula into this derivative condition gives ( d/dy [ p_X(g(y)) | g'(y) | ] = 0 ). This equation determines the value of y where the transformed probability density function achieves its maximum. Because the derivative involves both the original density ( p_X ) and the derivative of the transformation ( g'(y) ), the resulting equation generally becomes nonlinear and complicated. As a result the maximizing value of Y depends not only on the maximizing value of X but also on the rate of change of the transformation function. Therefore the maxima of the two densities are not generally related by a simple transformation. This observation has important implications in statistical inference and machine learning, especially when performing nonlinear transformations of data. For example when transforming variables in probabilistic models or applying nonlinear feature mappings, the location of maximum likelihood or mode values can change in ways that are not directly predictable from the original distribution.

pages.text:
Transformation of Random Variables using a Monotonic Function. This page derives the relationship between the probability density function of a random variable Y obtained by transforming another random variable X through a deterministic function. Suppose X is a continuous random variable with probability density function ( f_X(x) ) and cumulative distribution function ( F_X(x) ). Let Y be defined as a transformation of X through a function ( Y = g^{-1}(X) ) or equivalently ( X = g(Y) ), where the function g(.) is assumed to be monotonic and differentiable so that the transformation is one-to-one. The objective is to determine the probability density function of Y in terms of the density of X and the transformation function.

Start by expressing the cumulative distribution function of Y. By definition the cumulative distribution function is ( F_Y(y) = P(Y < y) ). Since Y is related to X through the transformation ( X = g(Y) ), the event ( Y < y ) can be expressed in terms of X. Specifically we write ( F_Y(y) = P(Y < y) = P(g^{-1}(X) < y) ). If the function g(.) is monotonic increasing, the inequality can be transformed without reversing its direction. Therefore ( P(g^{-1}(X) < y) = P(X < g(y)) ). This allows the probability to be expressed using the cumulative distribution function of X. Hence ( F_Y(y) = P(X < g(y)) ). Since ( F_X(x) = P(X < x) ), we obtain ( F_Y(y) = F_X(g(y)) ). This equation expresses the cumulative distribution function of Y in terms of the cumulative distribution function of X evaluated at the transformed argument g(y).

Next derive the probability density function of Y. The density function is obtained by differentiating the cumulative distribution function with respect to y. Therefore ( f_Y(y) = d/dy F_Y(y) ). Substituting the expression for F_Y(y) gives ( f_Y(y) = d/dy F_X(g(y)) ). Applying the chain rule of differentiation gives ( f_Y(y) = f_X(g(y)) * g'(y) ). Because probability densities must always be non-negative regardless of whether the transformation function is increasing or decreasing, the absolute value of the derivative is taken. This leads to the general transformation formula ( f_Y(y) = f_X(g(y)) |g'(y)| ).

Interpretation of the Transformation Formula. The formula shows that the density of the transformed variable Y depends on two components. The first component is the original density evaluated at the transformed point g(y). The second component is the magnitude of the derivative of the transformation function, which accounts for how the transformation stretches or compresses the probability mass along the real line. If the transformation expands distances, the density decreases accordingly, and if the transformation compresses distances, the density increases to preserve total probability.

Importance of the Result. This transformation rule is one of the most fundamental results in probability theory and statistical signal processing. It allows the probability distribution of complex derived quantities to be computed when they are expressed as functions of other random variables. The rule is widely used in change of variable methods, derivation of distributions such as the chi-square and log-normal distributions, and in probabilistic modeling where variables are transformed through nonlinear functions.

pages.text: Implications of Nonlinear Transformations on the Location of Probability Density Maxima. This page continues the analysis of how nonlinear transformations affect the location of maxima of probability density functions. In the previous derivation the relationship between the densities of two random variables X and Y connected through a nonlinear transformation ( X = g(Y) ) was established as ( p_Y(y) = p_X(g(y)) | g'(y) | ). The goal is to analyze whether the maximum of the transformed density occurs at the transformed location of the maximum of the original density. To determine the peak of the transformed density we examine the derivative of the probability density function with respect to y. The condition for the maximum of the density ( p_Y(y) ) is obtained by setting the derivative equal to zero. Therefore the equation for locating the peak is ( d/dy [ p_X(g(y)) | g'(y) | ] = 0 ). Applying the product rule of differentiation gives a more detailed expression. The derivative of the first term multiplied by the second term plus the first term multiplied by the derivative of the second term leads to the equation ( p_X'(g(y)) ( g'(y) )^2 + p_X(g(y)) | g''(y) | = 0 ). This equation represents the condition that determines the maximizing value of y. The handwritten derivation labels this relation as equation (2). The solution to equation (2) provides the value of y that maximizes the transformed density and is denoted by ( ŷ ). Substituting the maximizing value ( ŷ ) into the equation gives ( p_X'( g(ŷ) ) ( g'(ŷ) )^2 + p_X( g(ŷ) ) | g''(ŷ) | = 0 ). This is shown as equation (3). The equation above is generally nonlinear in terms of the variable ŷ because both the transformation function and its derivatives appear inside the expression. To simplify the notation the transformation of the maximizing point is defined as ( g(ŷ) = x̃ ). Similarly the derivatives of the transformation evaluated at the maximizing point are denoted by ( g'(ŷ) = x̃' ) and ( g''(ŷ) = x̃'' ). Using this notation equation (3) can be rewritten as ( p_X'(x̃) ( x̃' )^2 + p_X(x̃) | x̃'' | = 0 ). This expression is labeled as equation (4). Next recall the condition for the maximum of the original probability density function ( p_X(x) ). The peak of ( p_X(x) ) occurs at the value ( x̂ ) where the derivative of the density with respect to x becomes zero. Therefore the condition for the maximum of the original density is ( d/dx p_X(x) = 0 ). Evaluating this derivative at the maximizing value gives ( p_X'(x̂) = 0 ). This relation is labeled as equation (5). Now compare the conditions for the maxima of the two densities. Equation (4) describes the condition for the maximum of the transformed density while equation (5) describes the condition for the maximum of the original density. These two equations are generally different because equation (4) contains additional terms involving the derivatives of the transformation function. As a result the solutions to the two equations will generally be different. Therefore the maximizing value of x obtained from the transformation of ŷ does not necessarily equal the maximizing value of the original density. In mathematical terms this result is expressed as ( x̂ ≠ x̃ = g(ŷ) ). This shows that the location of the peak of the transformed distribution does not correspond to the transformation applied to the peak of the original distribution. The implication is important in probabilistic modeling and statistical inference. When random variables are transformed through nonlinear functions, the location of the mode of the resulting distribution can shift in ways that depend on both the shape of the original density and the curvature of the transformation function. Consequently nonlinear transformations alter not only the scale of the distribution but also the location of its most probable value.

Relationship Between Maxima under Linear Transformation of Random Variables. This page analyzes the special case where the transformation between two random variables is linear. Previously the general nonlinear transformation relationship between two variables X and Y was considered where ( X = g(Y) ). In this section the transformation function is linear, which significantly simplifies the relationship between the probability densities and their maxima.

Linear Transformation Definition. Consider a transformation defined by ( g(y) = a + by ). This implies that the random variable X is obtained from Y through the linear relation ( X = a + bY ), where a and b are constants. The constant a represents a shift or translation of the variable, while b represents a scaling factor that stretches or compresses the variable.

Properties of the Linear Function. For the function ( g(y) = a + by ), the first derivative with respect to y is constant: ( g'(y) = b ). The second derivative of a linear function is zero: ( g''(y) = 0 ). These derivative properties are used in the earlier derived equation that relates the maxima of the probability density functions of X and Y.

Condition for Maximum of Density Function. A maximum of a density function occurs at the point where the derivative of the density function equals zero. Let ( x̂ ) denote the value of x that maximizes the density ( f_X(x) ). This means ( d/dx f_X(x) = 0 ) at ( x = x̂ ). Similarly, let ( ŷ ) denote the value of y that maximizes the density ( f_Y(y) ). In the earlier derivation involving nonlinear transformations, a relationship was obtained that includes derivatives of the transformation function.

Substitution into the Earlier Equation. Because the transformation here is linear, the second derivative ( g''(y) ) becomes zero. Substituting ( g''(ŷ) = 0 ) into the earlier equation simplifies the condition for maxima. The resulting condition becomes ( f_X'(g(ŷ)) · (g'(ŷ))² = 0 ). Since the derivative of the transformation function is constant ( g'(ŷ) = b ), the expression simplifies further to ( f_X'(g(ŷ)) = 0 ).

Relation to the Maximum of f_X(x). The condition ( f_X'(g(ŷ)) = 0 ) is exactly the same condition used to identify the maximum of the density function ( f_X(x) ). Therefore the argument of the function must equal the maximizing value ( x̂ ). Hence ( x̂ = g(ŷ) ).

Solving for the Maximum of Y. Using the linear transformation ( g(y) = a + by ), the previous equation becomes ( x̂ = a + bŷ ). Solving for ŷ gives the expression ( ŷ = (x̂ - a) / b ). This equation shows that the maximizing point of the transformed random variable Y is directly related to the maximizing point of the original random variable X through the inverse linear transformation.

Interpretation. The result demonstrates that when the transformation between variables is linear, the locations of the maxima of their probability density functions are also linearly related. In other words, if the most probable value of X is known, the most probable value of Y can be obtained simply by applying the inverse linear transformation. This property holds because linear transformations preserve the relative ordering and shape of the probability density function.

Conclusion. The derivation confirms that under a linear transformation ( X = a + bY ), the mode or maximum likelihood location of the probability density transforms linearly. Specifically ( ŷ = (x̂ - a) / b ). This means the maxima of the two distributions are linearly related.

pages.text: Derivation of the Normalizing Constant of the Gaussian Probability Density Function. This page proves that the normalization constant of the Gaussian probability density function is equal to √(2πσ²). The Gaussian or normal distribution is one of the most important distributions in probability theory and statistics. The general form of the Gaussian probability density function for a random variable X with mean μ and variance σ² is given by ( f_X(x) = 1 / √(2πσ^2) · exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) ). The term ( 1 / √(2πσ^2) ) is called the normalization constant. Its role is to ensure that the total probability under the probability density function equals one. For any valid probability density function the condition ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} f_X(x) dx = 1 ) must hold. Therefore the goal of this derivation is to determine the constant that satisfies this condition. To begin the derivation we consider the integral of the exponential part of the Gaussian distribution without the normalization constant. Define the integral ( I = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) dx ). The strategy used to evaluate this integral is to square the integral so that it becomes a double integral. Squaring both sides gives ( I^2 = [ ∫_{-∞}^{∞} exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) dx ] [ ∫_{-∞}^{∞} exp( -(y-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) dy ] ). Because the two integrals are independent variables, they can be combined into a double integral over two dimensions. Therefore ( I^2 = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} ∫_{-∞}^{∞} exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) exp( -(y-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) dx dy ). Combining the exponential terms gives ( I^2 = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} ∫_{-∞}^{∞} exp( -( (x-μ)^2 + (y-μ)^2 ) / (2σ^2) ) dx dy ). For simplicity we perform a change of variables by shifting the origin so that the mean becomes zero. This allows us to write the exponent as ( x^2 + y^2 ). Thus the integral becomes ( I^2 = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} ∫_{-∞}^{∞} exp( -( x^2 + y^2 ) / (2σ^2) ) dx dy ). This integral is easier to evaluate in polar coordinates because the expression ( x^2 + y^2 ) naturally represents the square of the radius in polar coordinates. Therefore we introduce the transformation ( x = r cosθ ) and ( y = r sinθ ). In polar coordinates the relationship ( x^2 + y^2 = r^2 ) holds. The Jacobian of the transformation from Cartesian to polar coordinates is ( dx dy = r dr dθ ). The limits of integration also change accordingly. The angle θ ranges from 0 to 2π because the entire plane is covered. The radial variable r ranges from 0 to ∞ because the domain extends to infinity. Substituting these transformations into the double integral yields ( I^2 = ∫_{0}^{2π} ∫_{0}^{∞} exp( -( r^2 ) / (2σ^2) ) r dr dθ ). Because the integrand separates into independent parts of θ and r, the integral can be separated. Therefore ( I^2 = [ ∫_{0}^{2π} dθ ] [ ∫_{0}^{∞} exp( -( r^2 ) / (2σ^2) ) r dr ] ). The first integral evaluates immediately as ( ∫_{0}^{2π} dθ = 2π ). Thus ( I^2 = 2π ∫_{0}^{∞} exp( -( r^2 ) / (2σ^2) ) r dr ). Next we simplify the radial integral by performing another substitution. Let ( u = r^2 ). Then the differential becomes ( du = 2r dr ). Rearranging gives ( r dr = du / 2 ). Substituting this into the integral produces ( I^2 = 2π ∫_{0}^{∞} exp( -( u ) / (2σ^2) ) (du / 2) ). Simplifying gives ( I^2 = π ∫_{0}^{∞} exp( -( u ) / (2σ^2) ) du ). This expression is now a standard exponential integral. The integral of ( exp( -u / (2σ^2) ) ) with respect to u is ( -2σ^2 exp( -u / (2σ^2) ) ). Evaluating between limits 0 and ∞ gives ( ∫_{0}^{∞} exp( -u / (2σ^2) ) du = 2σ^2 ). Substituting this result back yields ( I^2 = π (2σ^2) ). Therefore ( I^2 = 2πσ^2 ). Taking the square root of both sides gives ( I = √(2πσ^2) ). This result proves that the integral of the Gaussian exponential term equals √(2πσ²). Therefore to normalize the probability density function we must divide by this value. Consequently the normalized Gaussian probability density function becomes ( f_X(x) = 1 / √(2πσ^2) · exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) ). This derivation confirms that √(2πσ²) is the correct normalization constant required to ensure that the total probability under the Gaussian probability density function equals one.

pages.text:
Evaluation of the Gaussian Integral and Determination of the Normalizing Constant. This page completes the derivation of the fundamental Gaussian integral used to determine the normalization constant of the normal distribution. Let the integral be defined as ( I = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} exp(-(x-μ)^2/(2σ^2)) dx ). In the earlier derivation the square of this integral was computed by converting the double integral into polar coordinates. That procedure leads to an expression of the form ( I^2 = π ∫_{0}^{∞} exp(-u/(2σ^2)) du ). The remaining task is to evaluate this integral and obtain the final value of I.

Start with the expression obtained from the previous transformation: ( I^2 = π ∫_{0}^{∞} exp(-u/(2σ^2)) du ). This is a standard exponential integral. Recall the general rule ( ∫ exp(-au) du = -(1/a) exp(-au) ). In this expression the constant ( a = 1/(2σ^2) ). Therefore the integral becomes ( ∫ exp(-u/(2σ^2)) du = -(2σ^2) exp(-u/(2σ^2)) ). Evaluating the definite integral from 0 to ∞ gives ( ∫_{0}^{∞} exp(-u/(2σ^2)) du = [-(2σ^2) exp(-u/(2σ^2))]_{0}^{∞} ). When u → ∞ the exponential term tends to zero because exp(-∞) = 0. When u = 0 the exponential term equals exp(0) = 1. Substituting these limits gives ( ∫_{0}^{∞} exp(-u/(2σ^2)) du = 2σ^2 ). Substituting this result back into the expression for I² gives ( I^2 = π · 2σ^2 ). Simplifying yields ( I^2 = 2πσ^2 ). Taking the square root of both sides gives the final result ( I = √(2πσ^2) ).

Significance of the Result. This result provides the normalization constant required for the Gaussian probability density function. Recall that the probability density function must satisfy the condition ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} f_X(x) dx = 1 ). If we define the Gaussian density as ( f_X(x) = C exp(-(x-μ)^2/(2σ^2)) ), then the constant C must be chosen so that the integral equals one. Using the value of the Gaussian integral obtained above, we determine ( C = 1/√(2πσ^2) ). Therefore the normalized Gaussian probability density function becomes ( f_X(x) = (1/√(2πσ^2)) exp(-(x-μ)^2/(2σ^2)) ).

Interpretation. The factor ( √(2πσ^2) ) appears naturally when integrating the Gaussian exponential function. It represents the total area under the unnormalized Gaussian curve. Dividing the exponential function by this factor ensures that the total probability integrates to one. This normalization is essential for interpreting the function as a probability density.

Importance in Probability and Signal Processing. The Gaussian integral is one of the most important results in probability theory, statistics, and signal processing. It underlies the definition of the normal distribution, which appears in many applications including noise modeling, central limit theorem analysis, statistical estimation, and stochastic signal analysis. The constant ( √(2πσ^2) ) ensures that the Gaussian distribution is properly scaled so that probabilities are valid and meaningful.

pages.text: Derivation Showing that the Variance of a Gaussian Random Variable Equals σ². This page revisits a known property of the Gaussian distribution and provides a derivation that confirms the variance of a Gaussian random variable equals the parameter σ² appearing in the distribution. The derivation begins with the normalization property of the Gaussian probability density function. For a Gaussian random variable X with mean μ and variance σ², the probability density function is given by ( N(x | μ, σ^2) = 1 / √(2πσ^2) · exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) ). Because this is a probability density function, the total probability across the entire real line must equal one. Therefore the normalization condition is ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} N(x | μ, σ^2) dx = 1 ). This equation is labeled as equation (1). The goal is to use this identity to prove that the variance of the random variable equals σ². The strategy used in this derivation is to differentiate equation (1) with respect to the parameter σ². Since the right side of the equation is a constant equal to 1, its derivative with respect to σ² is zero. Therefore differentiating both sides of equation (1) gives ( d/dσ^2 [ ∫_{-∞}^{∞} N(x | μ, σ^2) dx ] = 0 ). Substituting the explicit expression of the Gaussian pdf into the integral yields ( d/dσ^2 [ ∫_{-∞}^{∞} ( 1 / √(2πσ^2) ) exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) dx ] = 0 ). Because the integrand is smooth and differentiable, the derivative with respect to σ² can be moved inside the integral. Thus we obtain ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} d/dσ^2 [ ( 1 / √(2πσ^2) ) exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) ] dx = 0 ). Now apply the product rule of differentiation to the integrand. The first component is the derivative of the normalization factor ( 1 / √(2πσ^2) ). Writing this factor as ( (2πσ^2)^(-1/2) ), its derivative with respect to σ² becomes ( -(1/2) (2π)^(-1/2) (σ^2)^(-3/2) ). This term multiplies the exponential factor inside the integral. The second component arises from differentiating the exponential term ( exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) ). Using the chain rule, the derivative of the exponent with respect to σ² produces a factor involving ( (x-μ)^2 ). Specifically the derivative of the exponent ( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) with respect to σ² yields ( (x-μ)^2 / (2(σ^2)^2) ). Multiplying by the exponential term produces the derivative of the exponential part. Combining both terms and integrating across the real line gives an expression that simplifies to ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} (x-μ)^2 ( 1 / √(2πσ^2) ) exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) dx = σ^2 ). Observe that the expression ( 1 / √(2πσ^2) exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) ) is exactly the Gaussian probability density function. Therefore the integral can be recognized as the expectation of the squared deviation from the mean. In probability theory the variance of a continuous random variable is defined as ( Var(X) = E[(X-μ)^2] ). Using the expectation formula ( E[g(X)] = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} g(x) f_X(x) dx ), we identify that ( ∫_{-∞}^{∞} (x-μ)^2 f_X(x) dx = E[(X-μ)^2] ). Substituting this interpretation into the derived equation gives ( E[(X-μ)^2] = σ^2 ). Since the definition of variance is ( Var(X) = E[(X-μ)^2] ), the final result becomes ( Var(X) = σ^2 ). This derivation confirms that the parameter σ² in the Gaussian distribution directly represents the variance of the random variable. The result also reinforces the interpretation of σ² as a measure of the spread or dispersion of the distribution around its mean μ.

pages.text:
Variance of a Gaussian Random Variable. This page presents the final result of the derivation of the variance of a normal (Gaussian) random variable. The boxed expression shows the important identity ( E[(X - μ)^2] = σ^2 ). This equation states that the expected squared deviation of the random variable X from its mean μ is equal to the variance parameter σ² of the Gaussian distribution. This result confirms that the parameter σ² appearing in the normal distribution is exactly the variance of the distribution.

Definition of Variance. In probability theory the variance of a random variable X is defined as the expected value of the squared difference between the random variable and its mean. Mathematically this is written as ( Var(X) = E[(X - μ)^2] ), where μ = E[X]. The variance measures how spread out the values of the random variable are around the mean. A larger variance means the distribution is more spread out, while a smaller variance means the values are tightly clustered around the mean.

Gaussian Probability Density Function. Suppose X follows a Gaussian distribution with mean μ and variance σ². This is written as ( X ~ N(μ, σ²) ). The probability density function of this distribution is ( f_X(x) = (1 / √(2πσ²)) exp(-(x - μ)^2 / (2σ²)) ). The expectation of any function of X can be computed using the general formula ( E[g(X)] = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} g(x) f_X(x) dx ). Therefore the variance can be computed using ( E[(X - μ)^2] = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} (x - μ)^2 f_X(x) dx ). Substituting the Gaussian density function gives ( E[(X - μ)^2] = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} (x - μ)^2 (1 / √(2πσ²)) exp(-(x - μ)^2 / (2σ²)) dx ).

Evaluation of the Integral. To evaluate this integral a change of variable is usually introduced. Let ( t = (x - μ) / (√2 σ) ). This transformation converts the exponent into the simpler form exp(-t²). Under this transformation we obtain ( x - μ = √2 σ t ) and ( dx = √2 σ dt ). Substituting these relations into the integral transforms it into a standard Gaussian integral involving terms such as ( t^2 exp(-t^2) ). Using properties of even functions and known Gaussian integrals, the integral evaluates to σ².

Final Result. After performing the integration and simplifying the constants, the result becomes ( E[(X - μ)^2] = σ^2 ). This confirms that the parameter σ² in the Gaussian probability density function represents the variance of the distribution. In other words, σ is the standard deviation and σ² is the variance.

Interpretation. The result means that the Gaussian distribution is completely characterized by two parameters: μ and σ². The parameter μ determines the center of the distribution, while σ² determines how widely the distribution spreads around the mean. Because the Gaussian distribution is symmetric around μ, the squared deviations from μ naturally average to σ².

Importance in Signal Processing and Statistics. The Gaussian distribution is widely used to model noise, measurement errors, and many natural phenomena due to the central limit theorem. The identity ( E[(X - μ)^2] = σ^2 ) is fundamental in statistical estimation, signal modeling, filtering theory, and machine learning algorithms where Gaussian assumptions are commonly used.

pages.text: Mode of the Gaussian Distribution. This page derives the mode of the Gaussian (normal) probability distribution. The mode of a probability distribution is defined as the value of the random variable at which the probability density function achieves its maximum value. In mathematical terms the mode is the value that maximizes the probability density function. For a continuous random variable X with probability density function f_X(x), the mode is defined as ( x̂ = arg max_x f_X(x) ). The Gaussian probability density function for a random variable X with mean μ and variance σ² is given by ( f_X(x) = 1 / √(2πσ^2) · exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) ). The objective is to determine the value of x that maximizes this function. Because the Gaussian probability density function is continuous and differentiable, the maximum can be found by computing the derivative of the density function with respect to x and setting it equal to zero. Therefore we begin by applying the condition for a stationary point of a function, which is ( d/dx f_X(x) = 0 ). Substituting the expression for the Gaussian density gives ( d/dx [ (1 / √(2πσ^2)) exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) ] = 0 ). The normalization constant ( 1 / √(2πσ^2) ) does not depend on x, so it can be treated as a constant multiplier during differentiation. Thus the derivative becomes ( (1 / √(2πσ^2)) d/dx [ exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) ] = 0 ). To compute the derivative of the exponential term we apply the chain rule. The derivative of an exponential function exp(g(x)) is exp(g(x)) multiplied by the derivative of the exponent. Let the exponent be defined as ( g(x) = -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ). The derivative of this exponent with respect to x is ( dg/dx = -(2(x-μ)) / (2σ^2) ). Simplifying gives ( dg/dx = -(x-μ) / σ^2 ). Applying the chain rule gives ( d/dx exp(g(x)) = exp(g(x)) · ( -(x-μ) / σ^2 ) ). Substituting this result into the derivative expression yields ( (1 / √(2πσ^2)) exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) · ( -(x-μ) / σ^2 ) = 0 ). The exponential function is always strictly positive, and the normalization constant is also positive. Therefore the only factor that can equal zero is the term ( x - μ ). Thus the stationary point occurs when ( x - μ = 0 ). Solving this equation gives ( x = μ ). Therefore the maximizing value of the Gaussian probability density function is ( x̂ = μ ). This result shows that the mode of the Gaussian distribution is equal to its mean μ. Because the Gaussian distribution is symmetric around the mean, the mean, median, and mode all coincide at the same value. This property is one of the defining characteristics of the normal distribution. Consequently the point μ represents the center of the distribution, the point of maximum probability density, and the balance point of the distribution.

pages.text:
Mode of the Multivariate Gaussian Distribution. This page derives the location of the mode (the point where the probability density function reaches its maximum) for a multivariate Gaussian random variable. The multivariate Gaussian distribution generalizes the one dimensional normal distribution to vectors. Suppose X is a D dimensional random vector written as ( X ∈ ℝ^D ). The probability density function of a multivariate Gaussian distribution is given by ( f_X(x) = 1 / ((2π)^{D/2} |Σ|^{1/2}) · exp( -1/2 (x - μ)^T Σ^{-1} (x - μ) ) ). In this expression μ is the mean vector and Σ is the covariance matrix. The determinant |Σ| appears in the normalization constant and ensures that the total probability integrates to one.

Meaning of the Parameters. The vector μ represents the mean of the multivariate distribution and determines the center of the probability density. The matrix Σ is the covariance matrix which describes how the components of the vector vary and how they are correlated with each other. The matrix Σ must be symmetric and positive definite so that the quadratic form ( (x - μ)^T Σ^{-1} (x - μ) ) is always non negative.

Definition of the Mode. The mode of a probability distribution is defined as the value of x that maximizes the probability density function. Mathematically this is written as ( x̂ = arg max_x f_X(x) ). To find this point we compute the gradient of the density function with respect to x and set it equal to zero. This gives the necessary condition for a maximum.

Gradient Condition. The maximum occurs when ( ∇_x f_X(x) = 0 ). Substituting the multivariate Gaussian density into this condition gives ( ∇_x [ 1 / ((2π)^{D/2} |Σ|^{1/2}) exp( -1/2 (x - μ)^T Σ^{-1} (x - μ) ) ] = 0 ). Because the normalization constant does not depend on x, it can be treated as a constant factor. Therefore the derivative mainly affects the exponential term.

Derivative of the Exponential Term. Using the chain rule for vector derivatives, the gradient of the exponential term becomes proportional to the gradient of the quadratic form ( (x - μ)^T Σ^{-1} (x - μ) ). The derivative of this quadratic form with respect to x is ( 2 Σ^{-1} (x - μ) ). Therefore the gradient of the probability density function becomes proportional to ( Σ^{-1} (x - μ) ). Setting this expression equal to zero gives the condition ( Σ^{-1} (x - μ) = 0 ).

Solving the Equation. Since the covariance matrix Σ is invertible (because it is positive definite), the only solution is obtained by multiplying both sides by Σ. This leads to the equation ( x - μ = 0 ). Therefore the maximizing point becomes ( x̂ = μ ).

Interpretation. The result shows that the maximum value of the multivariate Gaussian density occurs exactly at the mean vector μ. In other words the center of the Gaussian distribution is the point where the probability density is largest. The density decreases as we move away from μ, and the rate of decrease depends on the covariance matrix Σ.

Geometric View. In multiple dimensions the contours of the Gaussian density form ellipsoids centered at μ. The orientation and shape of these ellipsoids are determined by the covariance matrix Σ. Because the quadratic form ( (x - μ)^T Σ^{-1} (x - μ) ) measures the squared Mahalanobis distance from the mean, the density decreases as this distance increases. Thus the smallest value of the quadratic form occurs at x = μ, which corresponds to the maximum of the density.

Final Result. The derivation confirms that for a multivariate Gaussian distribution the mode equals the mean vector. Therefore ( x̂ = μ ). This is consistent with the property of the one dimensional Gaussian distribution where the mean, median, and mode all coincide.

pages.text: Gradient Derivation for the Quadratic Form Appearing in the Multivariate Gaussian Distribution. This page derives the gradient of a quadratic form that appears in the exponent of the multivariate Gaussian probability density function. The expression analyzed is the gradient with respect to the vector variable x of the scalar quantity ( (x - μ)^T Σ^{-1} (x - μ) ). This term is known as a quadratic form and frequently appears in statistical signal processing, machine learning, and multivariate probability theory. The goal is to compute ( ∇_x [ (x - μ)^T Σ^{-1} (x - μ) ] ). This derivative is important because it is used in optimization problems such as maximum likelihood estimation for Gaussian distributions and in deriving the mode of multivariate Gaussian distributions. To begin the derivation the quadratic expression is expanded algebraically. The term ( (x - μ)^T Σ^{-1} (x - μ) ) can be expanded using matrix multiplication properties. Expanding the expression yields ( x^T Σ^{-1} x + μ^T Σ^{-1} μ - x^T Σ^{-1} μ - μ^T Σ^{-1} x ). Each of these four terms is handled separately when computing the gradient with respect to x. Several matrix calculus identities are used during the derivation. The first identity states that for a vector a independent of x, the gradient of the scalar expression ( a^T x ) with respect to x is simply a. Therefore ( ∂/∂x ( a^T x ) = a ). The second identity concerns the derivative of a quadratic form. For a matrix B that does not depend on x, the gradient of ( x^T B x ) with respect to x is ( (B + B^T) x ). This result follows from applying matrix differentiation rules to quadratic forms. These formulas are listed explicitly in the notes as reference identities used during the derivation. Now apply these identities to each term in the expanded quadratic expression. First consider the term ( x^T Σ^{-1} x ). In this expression the matrix B corresponds to ( Σ^{-1} ). Using the quadratic form derivative rule we obtain ( ∇_x ( x^T Σ^{-1} x ) = ( Σ^{-1} + (Σ^{-1})^T ) x ). Next examine the constant term ( μ^T Σ^{-1} μ ). This expression does not depend on x because both μ and Σ are constants with respect to x. Therefore its gradient with respect to x is zero. Thus ( ∇_x ( μ^T Σ^{-1} μ ) = 0 ). Now consider the third term ( x^T Σ^{-1} μ ). This expression has the form ( x^T a ) where ( a = Σ^{-1} μ ). Using the identity ( ∂/∂x ( x^T a ) = a ), the gradient becomes ( ∇_x ( x^T Σ^{-1} μ ) = Σ^{-1} μ ). Finally consider the fourth term ( μ^T Σ^{-1} x ). This expression can be viewed as the transpose of the previous term. Therefore its gradient becomes ( ∇_x ( μ^T Σ^{-1} x ) = ( Σ^{-1} )^T μ ). Combining the gradients of all four terms yields the gradient of the entire quadratic expression. Thus ( ∇_x [ (x - μ)^T Σ^{-1} (x - μ) ] = ( Σ^{-1} + (Σ^{-1})^T ) x - Σ^{-1} μ - (Σ^{-1})^T μ ). For covariance matrices used in multivariate Gaussian distributions an important property applies. Covariance matrices are symmetric matrices. This means ( Σ^T = Σ ). Because the inverse of a symmetric matrix is also symmetric, it follows that ( (Σ^{-1})^T = Σ^{-1} ). Using this property simplifies the expression considerably. Substituting this identity into the gradient expression gives ( ∇_x [ (x - μ)^T Σ^{-1} (x - μ) ] = 2 Σ^{-1} x - 2 Σ^{-1} μ ). Factoring out the common term produces ( ∇_x [ (x - μ)^T Σ^{-1} (x - μ) ] = 2 Σ^{-1} (x - μ) ). This is the final result. The gradient of the quadratic form is therefore proportional to the difference between x and the mean vector μ, scaled by the inverse covariance matrix. This result plays a crucial role in optimization problems involving Gaussian distributions, including finding the maximum likelihood estimate and determining the mode of the multivariate Gaussian distribution.

pages.text:
Final Step in the Derivation of the Mode of the Multivariate Gaussian Distribution. This page shows the final algebraic step that proves that the mode of the multivariate Gaussian distribution occurs at the mean vector. In the previous derivation the gradient of the probability density function of the multivariate Gaussian distribution was taken with respect to the vector variable x and set equal to zero in order to locate the point where the density reaches its maximum.

Recall the Multivariate Gaussian Density. The probability density function of a D dimensional Gaussian random vector X is given by ( f_X(x) = 1 / ((2π)^{D/2} |Σ|^{1/2}) exp( -1/2 (x - μ)^T Σ^{-1} (x - μ) ) ). In this expression μ is the mean vector and Σ is the covariance matrix. The determinant |Σ| appears in the normalization constant and ensures the total probability integrates to one. The quadratic term ( (x - μ)^T Σ^{-1} (x - μ) ) measures the squared Mahalanobis distance between the vector x and the mean μ.

Condition for Maximum of the Density. The location of the maximum value of the density function is found by setting the gradient equal to zero. Therefore we solve ( ∇_x f_X(x) = 0 ). After applying vector differentiation rules and simplifying the expression, the condition obtained in the previous step becomes ( 2 Σ^{-1} x̂ − 2 Σ^{-1} μ = 0 ). Here x̂ denotes the value of x that maximizes the density function.

Algebraic Simplification. The equation ( 2 Σ^{-1} x̂ − 2 Σ^{-1} μ = 0 ) can be simplified by factoring out the constant term and the matrix Σ^{-1}. This gives ( 2 Σ^{-1} (x̂ − μ) = 0 ). Because Σ is a covariance matrix it is positive definite and therefore invertible. Consequently the matrix Σ^{-1} cannot be zero and may be multiplied out of the equation.

Solving for the Maximum Location. Removing the non zero factors from the equation gives ( x̂ − μ = 0 ). Rearranging yields ( x̂ = μ ). This result shows that the point where the multivariate Gaussian probability density function achieves its maximum value is exactly the mean vector μ.

Interpretation. This confirms that the multivariate Gaussian distribution is centered at the mean vector μ and the probability density decreases symmetrically as the vector moves away from this point. Because the covariance matrix Σ only affects the shape and orientation of the distribution but not its center, the peak of the distribution always occurs at μ regardless of the covariance structure.

Geometric Meaning. In multiple dimensions the contours of the Gaussian distribution form ellipsoids centered at μ. The axes and orientation of these ellipsoids are determined by the covariance matrix Σ. The Mahalanobis distance ( (x − μ)^T Σ^{-1} (x − μ) ) measures how far a point lies from the center in terms of the covariance structure. The smallest value of this distance occurs at x = μ, which corresponds to the maximum probability density.

Final Result. The derivation therefore confirms the important property of the multivariate Gaussian distribution that the mode, the mean, and the center of symmetry all coincide. Hence the maximum likelihood point of the distribution is given by ( x̂ = μ ).

pages.text: Maximum Likelihood Estimation of the Mean and Variance of a Gaussian Distribution. This page derives the maximum likelihood estimates of the parameters of a Gaussian distribution when a set of independent and identically distributed observations is given. Consider a dataset consisting of N independent observations drawn from the same Gaussian distribution. Let the dataset be denoted as ( X̄ = { x_1, x_2, ..., x_N } ). The assumption is that each observation x_n is generated from a Gaussian distribution with mean μ and variance σ². Because the observations are independent and identically distributed, the joint probability of observing the entire dataset can be written as the product of the individual probabilities. Therefore the joint probability density function becomes ( P(X̄) = ∏_{n=1}^{N} P(x_n) ). Since each observation follows a Gaussian distribution, this expression becomes ( P(X̄) = ∏_{n=1}^{N} N(x_n | μ, σ^2) ). This expression is called the likelihood function because it represents the probability of the observed data given the parameters μ and σ². Instead of working directly with the likelihood function, it is more convenient to work with the logarithm of the likelihood. Taking the natural logarithm converts the product into a sum and simplifies differentiation. Therefore the log-likelihood function is defined as ( L(X̄) = ln P(X̄) ). Substituting the product form gives ( ln P(X̄) = ln ∏_{n=1}^{N} N(x_n | μ, σ^2) ). Using the logarithm property ( ln ∏ a_i = ∑ ln a_i ), this becomes ( L(X̄) = ∑_{n=1}^{N} ln N(x_n | μ, σ^2) ). Now substitute the Gaussian probability density function ( N(x | μ, σ^2) = 1 / √(2πσ^2) · exp( -(x-μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ) ). Taking the logarithm gives ( ln N(x_n | μ, σ^2) = -1/2 ln(2πσ^2) - (x_n - μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ). Substituting this expression into the log-likelihood gives ( L(X̄) = ∑_{n=1}^{N} [ -1/2 ln(2πσ^2) - (x_n - μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ] ). Because the first term does not depend on n, it can be simplified. Thus the log-likelihood becomes ( L(X̄) = -N/2 ln(2πσ^2) - ∑_{n=1}^{N} (x_n - μ)^2 / (2σ^2) ). The goal of maximum likelihood estimation is to determine the parameter values μ and σ² that maximize this log-likelihood function. Therefore the optimal estimates are defined as ( μ̂ , σ̂^2 = arg max_{μ,σ^2} L(X̄) ). To find the maximizing values we compute the derivatives of the log-likelihood function with respect to the parameters and set them equal to zero. First consider the derivative with respect to μ. Compute ( ∂/∂μ L(X̄) ). The derivative of the first term with respect to μ is zero because it does not depend on μ. The derivative of the second term produces ( ∂/∂μ [ -(1/(2σ^2)) ∑_{n=1}^{N} (x_n - μ)^2 ] ). Applying the chain rule gives ( -(1/(2σ^2)) ∑_{n=1}^{N} 2(x_n - μ)(-1) ). Simplifying yields ( (1/σ^2) ∑_{n=1}^{N} (x_n - μ) ). Setting this derivative equal to zero produces the equation ( ∑_{n=1}^{N} (x_n - μ) = 0 ). Expanding the summation gives ( ∑_{n=1}^{N} x_n - Nμ = 0 ). Solving for μ yields ( μ̂ = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} x_n ). This result shows that the maximum likelihood estimate of the mean of a Gaussian distribution is simply the sample average of the observed data. This derivation is a fundamental result in statistical estimation theory and forms the basis for many algorithms used in statistical signal processing and machine learning.

pages.text:
Maximum Likelihood Estimation of the Mean and Variance of a Gaussian Distribution. This page derives the maximum likelihood estimators for the parameters of a normal distribution using a set of observed samples. Suppose we observe N independent and identically distributed samples denoted by ( x_1, x_2, ..., x_N ) drawn from a Gaussian distribution with unknown mean μ and unknown variance σ². The objective is to estimate the parameters μ and σ² that maximize the likelihood of observing the given data.

Likelihood Function. If the samples are independent, the joint probability density of the observations is the product of the individual Gaussian densities. Therefore the likelihood function is written as ( L(μ,σ²) = ∏_{n=1}^{N} (1 / √(2πσ²)) exp(-(x_n - μ)^2 / (2σ²)) ). To simplify differentiation, the logarithm of the likelihood function is used. This is called the log likelihood and is written as ( ln L(μ,σ²) = -N/2 ln(2πσ²) - (1/(2σ²)) ∑_{n=1}^{N} (x_n - μ)^2 ).

Estimation of the Mean. To obtain the maximum likelihood estimate of μ, differentiate the log likelihood with respect to μ and set the result equal to zero. This gives ( ∂/∂μ ln L = (1/σ²) ∑_{n=1}^{N} (x_n - μ) = 0 ). Rearranging the terms gives ( ∑_{n=1}^{N} x_n - Nμ = 0 ). Solving for μ yields the estimator ( μ̂ = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} x_n ). This result shows that the maximum likelihood estimate of the mean is the sample average of the observations.

Estimation of the Variance. Next the variance parameter is estimated by differentiating the log likelihood with respect to σ² and setting the result equal to zero. Starting with the log likelihood expression, compute ( ∂/∂σ² ln L = ∂/∂σ² [ -N/2 ln(2πσ²) - (1/(2σ²)) ∑_{n=1}^{N} (x_n - μ)^2 ] ). Carrying out the differentiation gives ( -N/(2σ²) + (1/(2σ^4)) ∑_{n=1}^{N} (x_n - μ)^2 = 0 ). Multiplying both sides by (2σ^4) gives ( -Nσ² + ∑_{n=1}^{N} (x_n - μ)^2 = 0 ). Solving for σ² yields ( σ̂² = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} (x_n - μ)^2 ). Substituting the estimate μ̂ for μ gives the final expression ( σ̂² = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} (x_n - μ̂)^2 ).

Interpretation. The results show that the maximum likelihood estimate of the mean is simply the sample mean, while the maximum likelihood estimate of the variance is the average squared deviation of the samples from the estimated mean. These estimators arise naturally from maximizing the likelihood of the observed data under the Gaussian model.

Important Observation. The variance estimator obtained from maximum likelihood uses the factor (1/N) rather than (1/(N-1)). The latter appears in unbiased sample variance estimation, but maximum likelihood estimation focuses only on maximizing probability rather than correcting for estimation bias.

Final Results. The final maximum likelihood estimators are given by ( μ̂ = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} x_n ) and ( σ̂² = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} (x_n - μ̂)^2 ). These formulas are fundamental in statistical signal processing, estimation theory, and machine learning.

pages.text: Expectation of the Product of Gaussian Random Variables and Unbiasedness of the Maximum Likelihood Mean Estimator. This page proves an important expectation identity for Gaussian random variables and then uses it to discuss a property of the maximum likelihood estimator of the mean. Consider a sequence of random variables drawn from a normal distribution. Let the random variable X have mean μ and variance σ^2. Therefore the first two moments of the distribution are given as ( E[X] = μ ) and ( E[X^2] = μ^2 + σ^2 ). These identities follow from the definition of variance, since ( Var(X) = E[X^2] - (E[X])^2 ). Substituting ( Var(X) = σ^2 ) and ( E[X] = μ ) gives ( E[X^2] = μ^2 + σ^2 ). Now consider a sequence of random variables ( x_1, x_2, ..., x_N ) that are independent and identically distributed Gaussian variables with mean μ and variance σ^2. The goal is to compute the expectation of the product ( E[x_n x_m] ). This expectation depends on whether the indices n and m refer to the same observation or to different observations. To express this compactly we introduce the indicator function ( I_nm ), which is defined as the Kronecker delta. The Kronecker delta is defined as ( I_nm = 1 ) when ( n = m ) and ( I_nm = 0 ) when ( n ≠ m ). First consider the case when the indices are equal, meaning ( n = m ). In this situation the expectation becomes ( E[x_n x_n] = E[x_n^2] ). Using the second moment identity derived earlier we obtain ( E[x_n^2] = μ^2 + σ^2 ). Next consider the case when the indices are different, meaning ( n ≠ m ). Because the observations are independent random variables, the expectation of the product factorizes into the product of expectations. Therefore ( E[x_n x_m] = E[x_n] E[x_m] ). Since each variable has mean μ, this becomes ( E[x_n x_m] = μ · μ = μ^2 ). Combining the two cases gives a unified expression for the expectation of the product of two observations. The result can be written as ( E[x_n x_m] = μ^2 + I_nm σ^2 ). This expression captures both cases simultaneously. When ( n = m ), the indicator ( I_nm = 1 ) and the expectation becomes ( μ^2 + σ^2 ). When ( n ≠ m ), the indicator becomes zero and the expectation reduces to ( μ^2 ). This result is useful when computing covariance matrices or analyzing correlations among Gaussian observations. The next part of the page discusses a property of the maximum likelihood estimator of the Gaussian mean. Recall that the maximum likelihood estimator for the mean parameter derived earlier is given by ( μ_ML = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} x_n ). The task is to prove that this estimator is unbiased. An estimator is said to be unbiased if the expected value of the estimator equals the true parameter value. Therefore we must show that ( E[μ_ML] = μ ). Taking the expectation of the estimator gives ( E[μ_ML] = E[ (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} x_n ] ). Because expectation is a linear operator, the constant factor can be taken outside the expectation. Therefore ( E[μ_ML] = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} E[x_n] ). Each observation has expected value μ. Substituting this value yields ( E[μ_ML] = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} μ ). The summation of μ repeated N times equals ( Nμ ). Therefore the expression simplifies to ( E[μ_ML] = (1/N) Nμ ). Finally this reduces to ( E[μ_ML] = μ ). This proves that the maximum likelihood estimator of the Gaussian mean is unbiased. The result is important in statistical estimation theory because it confirms that the sample average provides an accurate estimate of the true mean on average over repeated sampling.

pages.text:
Expectation of Maximum Likelihood Estimators for Mean and Variance of a Gaussian Distribution. This page analyzes the statistical properties of the maximum likelihood estimators derived previously for the Gaussian distribution parameters. In particular it investigates whether the estimators are unbiased by computing their expectations.

Expectation of the Maximum Likelihood Estimate of the Mean. Recall that the maximum likelihood estimator of the mean obtained earlier is ( μ_ML = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} x_n ). To determine whether this estimator is unbiased we compute its expected value. Taking expectation on both sides gives ( E[μ_ML] = E[(1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} x_n] ). Using the linearity of expectation, which allows constants and summations to be taken outside the expectation operator, we obtain ( E[μ_ML] = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} E[x_n] ). Since each sample x_n is drawn from a Gaussian distribution with mean μ, we have ( E[x_n] = μ ). Substituting this into the equation gives ( E[μ_ML] = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} μ ). Because the sum of N identical terms μ is Nμ, we obtain ( E[μ_ML] = (1/N) · Nμ ). Therefore the result simplifies to ( E[μ_ML] = μ ). This shows that the maximum likelihood estimator of the mean is an unbiased estimator.

Expectation of the Maximum Likelihood Estimate of the Variance. Next we examine the estimator of the variance obtained earlier. The maximum likelihood estimate of the variance is ( σ_ML^2 = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} (x_n - μ_ML)^2 ). The goal is to compute the expectation ( E[σ_ML^2] ). Taking expectation gives ( E[σ_ML^2] = E[(1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} (x_n - μ_ML)^2] ). Expanding the squared term produces three components: ( (x_n - μ_ML)^2 = x_n^2 + μ_ML^2 - 2 x_n μ_ML ). Substituting this expansion inside the expectation leads to ( E[σ_ML^2] = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} [ E[x_n^2] + E[μ_ML^2] - 2E(x_n μ_ML) ] ).

Moments of the Gaussian Samples. For a Gaussian random variable with mean μ and variance σ², the second moment is given by ( E[x_n^2] = μ^2 + σ^2 ). Therefore the first term in the summation becomes μ² + σ².

Expectation of the Square of the Sample Mean. The next step is to compute ( E[μ_ML^2] ). Using the definition of the estimator ( μ_ML = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} x_n ), we write ( μ_ML^2 = (1/N^2) (∑_{n=1}^{N} x_n)(∑_{m=1}^{N} x_m) ). Taking expectation gives ( E[μ_ML^2] = (1/N^2) ∑_{n=1}^{N} ∑_{m=1}^{N} E[x_n x_m] ). Because the samples are independent, the cross terms simplify and the result becomes ( E[μ_ML^2] = (1/N^2)(N^2 μ^2 + Nσ^2) ). Simplifying gives ( E[μ_ML^2] = μ^2 + σ^2/N ).

Final Result for the Variance Estimator. Substituting these expressions into the earlier equation and simplifying leads to the final result ( E[σ_ML^2] = ((N-1)/N) σ^2 ). This shows that the maximum likelihood estimator of the variance slightly underestimates the true variance.

Interpretation. The result demonstrates that while the maximum likelihood estimator for the mean is unbiased, the variance estimator obtained using maximum likelihood is biased. The bias arises because the estimator uses the sample mean instead of the true mean when computing squared deviations.

Connection to the Unbiased Variance Estimator. In statistics this bias is corrected by replacing the factor (1/N) with (1/(N-1)). This produces the unbiased sample variance estimator ( s^2 = (1/(N-1)) ∑_{n=1}^{N} (x_n - μ_ML)^2 ). This correction is commonly used in statistical analysis and signal processing applications.

pages.text: Expectation of the Product of an Observation and the Maximum Likelihood Mean and Bias of the Maximum Likelihood Variance Estimator. This page continues the analysis of estimators for a Gaussian distribution. The goal is to compute the expectation of the product of an observation with the maximum likelihood estimator of the mean and then use this result to analyze the bias of the maximum likelihood estimator of the variance. Recall that for a dataset of N independent and identically distributed Gaussian observations ( x_1, x_2, ..., x_N ), the maximum likelihood estimator of the mean is given by ( μ_ML = (1/N) ∑_{m=1}^{N} x_m ). The first step is to compute the expectation ( E[x_n μ_ML] ). Substituting the expression for the estimator gives ( E[x_n μ_ML] = E[ x_n (1/N) ∑_{m=1}^{N} x_m ] ). Because expectation is linear, the constant factor (1/N) can be taken outside the expectation. Therefore ( E[x_n μ_ML] = (1/N) ∑_{m=1}^{N} E[x_n x_m] ). From the result derived earlier, the expectation of the product of two Gaussian observations is ( E[x_n x_m] = μ^2 + δ_nm σ^2 ), where δ_nm is the Kronecker delta. The Kronecker delta equals 1 when n = m and equals 0 when n ≠ m. Substituting this identity into the summation gives ( E[x_n μ_ML] = (1/N) ∑_{m=1}^{N} ( μ^2 + δ_nm σ^2 ) ). The summation can be separated into two parts. The first part sums μ^2 across N terms, giving ( N μ^2 ). The second part sums δ_nm σ^2. Because the Kronecker delta equals 1 only when m = n, the summation contributes exactly one σ^2. Therefore the entire expression becomes ( E[x_n μ_ML] = (1/N) ( N μ^2 + σ^2 ) ). Simplifying the expression yields ( E[x_n μ_ML] = μ^2 + σ^2 / N ). This result is important when analyzing the statistical properties of variance estimators. The next step is to analyze the expectation of the maximum likelihood estimator of the variance. Recall that the maximum likelihood estimator of the variance for a Gaussian distribution is defined as ( σ_ML^2 = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} (x_n - μ_ML)^2 ). To determine whether this estimator is unbiased, we compute its expected value. Expanding the squared term gives ( (x_n - μ_ML)^2 = x_n^2 + μ_ML^2 - 2 x_n μ_ML ). Taking expectations of each term gives ( E[σ_ML^2] = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} [ E[x_n^2] + E[μ_ML^2] - 2 E[x_n μ_ML] ] ). From earlier results we know that ( E[x_n^2] = μ^2 + σ^2 ). The expectation of the squared mean estimator can be expressed using the variance of μ_ML. Because ( Var(μ_ML) = σ^2 / N ), it follows that ( E[μ_ML^2] = μ^2 + σ^2 / N ). We also previously derived that ( E[x_n μ_ML] = μ^2 + σ^2 / N ). Substituting these results into the expectation expression gives ( E[σ_ML^2] = (1/N) ∑_{n=1}^{N} [ (μ^2 + σ^2) + (μ^2 + σ^2/N) - 2(μ^2 + σ^2/N) ] ). Simplifying the terms inside the brackets gives ( σ^2 - σ^2 / N ). Since this value is the same for all N terms in the summation, the final expression becomes ( E[σ_ML^2] = σ^2 (1 - 1/N) ). This can also be written as ( E[σ_ML^2] = (N-1)/N · σ^2 ). This result shows that the maximum likelihood estimator of the variance is biased. Specifically it underestimates the true variance by a factor of ( (N-1)/N ). Because of this bias, an adjusted estimator is commonly used in statistics. The unbiased estimator of the variance replaces the denominator N with (N-1), leading to the sample variance formula ( σ̂^2 = (1/(N-1)) ∑_{n=1}^{N} (x_n - μ_ML)^2 ).
