pages.text:
Decision Theory in Machine Learning Classification Systems. This page illustrates the conceptual pipeline of how decision theory is applied in a classification system within machine learning. The diagram represents the interaction between data, features, models, training, prediction, and evaluation metrics.

Overview. Decision theory provides a mathematical framework for making optimal decisions based on observed data. In classification problems, the goal is to assign an input observation to one of several possible classes by minimizing decision error or expected risk.

Data Input Stage. The process begins with the availability of labeled data. The dataset contains two major components: input features (data) and their corresponding target labels. These labels represent the ground truth categories used for supervised learning.

Cross Validation Strategy. A cross-validation (CV) strategy is applied to split the available dataset into training and testing portions. This ensures that the model generalizes well and avoids overfitting.

Training Data. The portion of the dataset selected for training is used to learn the parameters of the model. During this stage the classification algorithm analyzes the relationship between features and their corresponding labels.

Model Learning. The training process generates a trained model. This model represents a learned decision function that maps input features to predicted labels.

Testing Stage. The testing dataset is passed through the trained model to evaluate its performance. The model predicts labels for unseen testing data.

Prediction Output. The classifier produces predicted labels based on the learned decision boundary. These predicted labels represent the model's decision about which class the input belongs to.

True Labels Comparison. The predicted labels are compared with the true labels from the dataset to evaluate correctness of predictions.

Evaluation Metrics. The results of prediction are summarized using evaluation metrics derived from the confusion matrix. Common evaluation metrics include:
Accuracy (ACC) which measures overall correctness of predictions,
Recall which measures the ability to correctly identify positive cases,
Precision which measures correctness among predicted positives,
F1 Score which balances precision and recall,
AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve) which measures ranking performance of the classifier.

Decision Function Representation. The classification decision can be represented mathematically as a decision function D(x,t). Here x represents the feature vector extracted from the observed data, and t represents the predicted class label.

Observation and Feature Extraction. Observations (Obs) from raw data are first processed through a feature extraction stage. Feature extraction converts raw data into structured numerical representations that can be processed by machine learning models.

Classification Module. The classifier receives the extracted features and uses the trained model to generate predictions. The classifier acts as the decision-making component in the decision theory framework.

Prediction of Labels. Based on the decision rule learned during training, the classifier outputs predicted labels for each input observation.

Role of Decision Theory. Decision theory connects statistical modeling and classification by defining optimal decision rules. These rules minimize classification error or expected loss based on probabilities estimated from data.

Complete Pipeline Summary. Data and labels are collected, cross-validation splits the data, the model is trained using training data, testing evaluates the trained model, predictions are generated by the classifier, and performance metrics assess the quality of the decision-making process.

pages.text: Introduction to Decision Theory and the Classification Problem. Decision theory provides the mathematical foundation for classification in pattern recognition and machine learning. The fundamental problem in classification is to assign an observed data sample to one of several possible classes based on its feature representation. In this formulation the observed input is represented by a feature vector x̄ which contains measurements or attributes describing the data sample. This feature vector is provided as input to a classifier. The classifier processes the feature vector and produces posterior probabilities of the form P(ω_i | x̄). These posterior probabilities represent the probability that the input feature vector x̄ belongs to class ω_i. The set of possible classes is denoted by {ω_1, ω_2, ..., ω_M}, where M represents the total number of classes in the classification problem. Each class corresponds to a particular category or label that the input data may belong to. The goal of the classifier is to determine the most probable class for a given feature vector based on the available statistical information. This framework forms the basis for probabilistic pattern recognition systems. Bayes Decision Theory provides a systematic approach to solving classification problems using probability theory. In the simplest case we consider a two class classification problem where the possible classes are ω_1 and ω_2. The feature vector x̄ is observed and the classifier must decide whether the observation belongs to class ω_1 or class ω_2. In the Bayesian framework certain probabilistic quantities are assumed to be known. First, the prior probabilities P(ω_1) and P(ω_2) represent the probabilities that a randomly selected sample belongs to each class before observing the data. These are called prior probabilities because they reflect prior knowledge about class occurrence. Second, the class conditional probability density functions P(x̄ | ω_i) are assumed to be known. These functions describe the likelihood of observing a particular feature vector given that the sample belongs to class ω_i. In practice these quantities may not always be known exactly. One of the major challenges in decision theory arises when the prior probabilities P(ω_1) and P(ω_2) are unknown. In such situations the solution is to estimate these probabilities using training data. Training data consists of labeled examples from each class and can be used to approximate both prior probabilities and class conditional densities. These estimated probabilities allow the classifier to perform probabilistic decision making even when the true underlying distributions are not fully known.

pages.text:
Parameter Estimation in Decision Theory using Training Data. This page explains how class probabilities and class-conditional probability densities are estimated from a labeled training dataset in a classification problem.

Given Training Dataset. Consider a supervised learning problem where the training dataset is divided into two classes ω1 and ω2. The samples belonging to each class are grouped into sets.

Class Sample Sets. The training samples belonging to class ω1 are represented as S1 = {x̄11, x̄12, x̄13, ..., x̄1N1}. Similarly, the training samples belonging to class ω2 are represented as S2 = {x̄21, x̄22, ..., x̄2N2}. Each vector x̄ij represents a feature vector extracted from an observation.

Class Membership. The samples in S1 belong to class ω1 and the samples in S2 belong to class ω2. These labeled samples provide the basis for estimating statistical properties of each class.

Prior Probability Estimation. The prior probability of each class can be estimated using the relative frequency of samples belonging to that class in the dataset.

Estimated Prior for Class ω1. The probability of class ω1 can be approximated as P(ω1) ≈ N1 / N.

Estimated Prior for Class ω2. The probability of class ω2 can be approximated as P(ω2) ≈ N2 / N.

Total Number of Samples. Here N represents the total number of samples in the dataset and is given by N = N1 + N2.

Unknown Class Conditional Densities. In many real classification problems the class conditional probability densities P(x | ωi) are unknown. These distributions describe how feature vectors are distributed within each class.

Training Data Availability. However, the training data sets S1 and S2 provide sample observations that can be used to estimate these probability distributions.

Assumption of Functional Model. To estimate the class conditional density, a functional model is assumed for the distribution P(x | ωi). This means that the distribution is represented using a parametric function with unknown parameters.

Parametric Representation. The class conditional density can be written as P(x | ωi) = f(x; θi), where θi represents the set of parameters defining the probability distribution for class ωi.

Parameter Estimation. The parameters θi can be estimated using the training samples belonging to class ωi. This estimation process determines the best parameter values that explain the observed training data.

Maximum Likelihood Estimation. One common approach for estimating these parameters is Maximum Likelihood (ML) estimation. ML estimation chooses parameter values that maximize the likelihood of observing the given training data.

Class Conditional Model Construction. Using the estimated parameters, the probability density P(x | ω1) can be constructed from the training set S1. Similarly, the probability density P(x | ω2) can be constructed from the training set S2.

Role in Classification. Once the prior probabilities P(ωi) and the class conditional densities P(x | ωi) are estimated, they can be used within Bayesian decision theory to compute posterior probabilities and perform classification.

pages.text: Bayes Rule and Bayesian Classification for Two Class Problems. In probabilistic classification systems the goal is to determine the posterior probability that an observed feature vector x belongs to a particular class. The classifier receives information from two sources: the prior probability of the class and the likelihood of observing the data given that class. The classifier combines these sources of information to produce the posterior probability P(ω_i | x). The probabilistic relationship between these quantities is given by Bayes Rule. Bayes rule states that the posterior probability of class ω_i given observation x is P(ω_i | x) = P(x | ω_i) P(ω_i) / P(x). In this expression P(x | ω_i) is called the likelihood function. It represents the probability density of observing feature vector x when the sample belongs to class ω_i. The term P(ω_i) represents the prior probability of class ω_i. This reflects the probability of the class before observing the feature vector. The denominator P(x) is called the evidence or marginal likelihood. It ensures that the posterior probabilities are normalized and sum to one across all classes. The evidence can be computed using the law of total probability as P(x) = Σ_{i=1}^{M} P(ω_i) P(x | ω_i). In the two class case where the possible classes are ω_1 and ω_2 this becomes P(x) = P(ω_1)P(x|ω_1) + P(ω_2)P(x|ω_2). Using Bayes rule we compute the posterior probabilities for both classes and assign the observation to the class with the higher posterior probability. This decision strategy is called the Bayes classification rule. For a two class problem the rule states: if P(ω_1 | x) > P(ω_2 | x) then classify the sample x as belonging to class ω_1. Otherwise if P(ω_1 | x) < P(ω_2 | x) then classify x as belonging to class ω_2. Since the denominator P(x) is common for both posterior probabilities it cancels when comparing them. Therefore an equivalent classification rule can be written using only priors and likelihoods. The equivalent rule states that if P(ω_1) P(x | ω_1) > P(ω_2) P(x | ω_2) then x is assigned to class ω_1, otherwise x is assigned to class ω_2. This formulation is commonly used in practical classification algorithms because it avoids explicitly computing the normalization constant.

pages.text:
Equiprobable Case in Bayesian Decision Theory. This page explains a special case of Bayesian classification where both classes have equal prior probability. This situation simplifies the decision rule and helps visualize the probability of classification error.

Equiprobable Case Definition. In the equiprobable case the prior probabilities of both classes are equal. That is P(ω1) = P(ω2) = 1/2. This assumption means that both classes are equally likely before observing any data.

Decision Rule under Equal Priors. When the prior probabilities are equal and the loss functions are symmetric, the Bayesian decision rule simplifies significantly. The classification decision is made by comparing the class conditional densities.

Compact Decision Rule. The decision rule can be written as: decide class ω1 if P(x | ω1) ≥ P(x | ω2), otherwise decide class ω2. Thus the decision boundary occurs at the point where the two probability density functions intersect.

Graphical Interpretation. The diagram illustrates two class conditional probability density functions P(x | ω1) and P(x | ω2). Each distribution represents the likelihood of observing feature value x given a particular class.

Decision Boundary. The intersection point of the two distributions is denoted by x0. This value acts as the decision threshold separating the feature space into two decision regions.

Decision Regions. The feature space is divided into two regions:
R1 which corresponds to the region where samples are classified as class ω1,
R2 which corresponds to the region where samples are classified as class ω2.

Threshold Value. The threshold x0 represents the optimal decision boundary that minimizes classification error when the class priors are equal.

Probability of Classification Error. Because the distributions overlap, some samples may be incorrectly classified. The probability of error Pe represents the probability that the classifier assigns an observation to the wrong class.

Error Expression. The total probability of error is obtained by summing the probabilities of misclassification in each region.

Mathematical Expression for Error. The probability of error can be written as:
Pe = (1/2) ∫_{-∞}^{x0} P(x | ω2) dx + (1/2) ∫_{x0}^{∞} P(x | ω1) dx.

Interpretation of First Term. The first integral represents the probability that a sample from class ω2 falls into region R1 (where the classifier predicts class ω1). This corresponds to the area under P(x | ω2) in region R1.

Interpretation of Second Term. The second integral represents the probability that a sample from class ω1 falls into region R2 (where the classifier predicts class ω2). This corresponds to the area under P(x | ω1) in region R2.

Visualization of Error Regions. In the diagram, the shaded regions represent the misclassification areas where the probability density of one class overlaps with the decision region of the other class.

Importance of Decision Boundary. The optimal threshold x0 minimizes the total probability of classification error. In practice this threshold depends on the shapes and parameters of the class conditional distributions.

Role in Pattern Recognition. This equiprobable case is often used to illustrate the principles of Bayesian decision theory and optimal classification boundaries in pattern recognition systems.

pages.text: Minimizing the Classification Error Probability in Bayesian Decision Theory. In a two class classification problem the goal of a Bayesian classifier is to minimize the probability of classification error. Let the two classes be ω1 and ω2 and let the feature vector be x. The classifier divides the feature space into two decision regions R1 and R2. If the observed feature vector x lies in region R1 then the classifier assigns the sample to class ω1. If the observation lies in region R2 then it is assigned to class ω2. The total probability of classification error is denoted by Pe. This represents the probability that the classifier assigns the observation to the wrong class. The classification error occurs in two situations. The first situation occurs when the true class is ω1 but the classifier assigns the sample to region R2. The second situation occurs when the true class is ω2 but the classifier assigns the sample to region R1. Therefore the probability of classification error can be written as Pe = P(x ∈ R2 , ω1) + P(x ∈ R1 , ω2). Using the definition of conditional probability these joint probabilities can be expanded as Pe = P(x ∈ R2 | ω1) P(ω1) + P(x ∈ R1 | ω2) P(ω2). The conditional probability P(x ∈ R2 | ω1) represents the probability that a sample from class ω1 falls in region R2. Similarly P(x ∈ R1 | ω2) represents the probability that a sample from class ω2 falls in region R1. These terms can be expressed using probability density functions. Therefore the error probability becomes Pe = P(ω1) ∫_{R2} p(x | ω1) dx + P(ω2) ∫_{R1} p(x | ω2) dx. Graphically this corresponds to the overlapping regions of the class conditional densities p(x | ω1) and p(x | ω2). The shaded region in the probability density diagram represents the probability of misclassification. Alternatively the error probability can also be written in terms of joint probability densities. Since p(x, ωi) = p(x | ωi) P(ωi), the expression for error probability becomes Pe = ∫_{R2} p(x, ω1) dx + ∫_{R1} p(x, ω2) dx. Using Bayes rule we can also express the joint probability in terms of posterior probabilities. Because p(x, ωi) = p(ωi | x) p(x), the error probability can be written as Pe = ∫_{R2} p(ω1 | x) p(x) dx + ∫_{R1} p(ω2 | x) p(x) dx. The Bayesian decision rule chooses decision regions in such a way that this probability of error is minimized. In practice the optimal decision boundary occurs where the posterior probabilities of the classes become equal. This principle forms the basis of the minimum error Bayes classifier.

pages.text:
Derivation of the Bayesian Decision Rule using Probability of Error Minimization. This page derives the optimal classification rule in Bayesian decision theory by minimizing the probability of classification error.

Marginal Probability of Class. The marginal probability of class ω1 can be written using the joint probability distribution of the feature variable x and the class label.

Marginal Expression. The marginal probability is expressed as:
P(ω1) = ∫_{-∞}^{∞} P(x, ω1) dx.

Partition of Feature Space. The entire feature space can be divided into two decision regions R1 and R2. Region R1 corresponds to deciding class ω1 and region R2 corresponds to deciding class ω2.

Splitting the Integral. Since R1 and R2 together cover the entire feature space, the marginal probability can be written as:
P(ω1) = ∫_{R1} P(x, ω1) dx + ∫_{R2} P(x, ω1) dx.

Using Conditional Probability. The joint probability P(x, ω1) can be written using conditional probability as:
P(x, ω1) = P(ω1 | x) P(x).

Substituting into the Marginal Expression. Substituting this into the previous equation gives:
P(ω1) = ∫_{R1} P(ω1 | x) P(x) dx + ∫_{R2} P(ω1 | x) P(x) dx.

Error Probability Representation. The probability of classification error Pe is derived by comparing the marginal expression with the misclassification terms. The error occurs when a sample belonging to one class is assigned to the other region.

Error Expression. The probability of error can be written as:
Pe = P(ω1) − ∫_{R1} P(ω1 | x) P(x) dx + ∫_{R1} P(ω2 | x) P(x) dx.

Simplified Error Formula. Rearranging terms leads to:
Pe = P(ω1) − ∫_{R1} [ P(ω1 | x) − P(ω2 | x) ] P(x) dx.

Condition for Minimizing Error. To minimize the probability of error, the integrand term must be positive whenever x lies in region R1.

Optimal Decision Condition. Therefore, the classifier should assign x to class ω1 if:
P(ω1 | x) > P(ω2 | x).

Otherwise Decision Rule. If the inequality is reversed, the sample should be assigned to class ω2.

Bayesian Decision Rule. The final optimal classification rule becomes:
If P(ω1 | x) > P(ω2 | x) then decide x ∈ ω1, otherwise decide x ∈ ω2.

Significance. This rule is known as the Bayes decision rule. It states that the optimal decision is obtained by choosing the class with the maximum posterior probability given the observed data.

Importance in Machine Learning. The Bayes rule forms the theoretical foundation of probabilistic classifiers such as Naive Bayes, Bayesian networks, and many statistical pattern recognition algorithms.

pages.text: Generalization of Bayesian Classification to the Multiclass Case. In many real-world classification problems there are more than two possible classes. Suppose that the set of possible classes is {ω1, ω2, ..., ωM} where M represents the total number of classes. Let x be the observed feature vector representing the input sample. The goal of classification is to determine which class the feature vector most likely belongs to. In Bayesian decision theory the classification rule is based on posterior probabilities. The Bayes rule for multiclass classification states that a sample x should be assigned to class ωi if the posterior probability of that class is greater than the posterior probabilities of all other classes. Mathematically the rule is: if P(ωi | x) > P(ωj | x) for all j ≠ i, then assign x to class ωi. This rule selects the class with the highest posterior probability and therefore is often called the maximum posterior probability rule. One important property of this rule is that it minimizes the probability of classification error. To understand this result we analyze the probability of correct classification. Let Pc denote the probability of making a correct decision. The probability of classification error is then Pe = 1 − Pc. The probability of correct classification can be written as Pc = Σ_i P(x ∈ Ri , ωi), where Ri represents the decision region corresponding to class ωi. This expression represents the probability that the observation x lies in the decision region Ri and that the true class of the observation is ωi. Using joint probability densities this expression can be written as Pc = Σ_i ∫_{Ri} p(x , ωi) dx. Using Bayes rule the joint probability density can be expressed as p(x , ωi) = p(x) P(ωi | x). Substituting this into the previous expression gives Pc = Σ_i ∫_{Ri} p(x) P(ωi | x) dx. Alternatively the expression can also be written using conditional densities as Pc = Σ_i P(ωi) ∫_{Ri} p(x | ωi) dx. These equivalent expressions show that the probability of correct classification depends on how the decision regions Ri are defined. The Bayes decision rule defines the decision regions in such a way that the posterior probability of the chosen class is always the largest. As a result the probability of correct classification Pc becomes maximum, which equivalently means that the probability of classification error Pe is minimized. This establishes that the Bayes classifier provides the optimal decision rule in terms of minimum classification error.

pages.text:
Bayesian Decision Rule and Maximization of Correct Classification Probability. This page explains how Bayesian decision theory minimizes classification error by maximizing the probability of correct classification. It also illustrates the concept using multiple class-conditional probability density functions.

Multiple Class Conditional Distributions. The diagram shows several probability density functions such as P(x|ω1), P(x|ω2), P(x|ω3), and so on. Each curve represents the probability distribution of feature variable x for a specific class ωi.

Decision Regions. The feature space along the x-axis is divided into several decision regions R1, R2, R3, R4 and so on. Each region corresponds to the class that the classifier assigns to any observation x lying within that region.

Interpretation of Regions. If x lies in region R1 the classifier decides class ω1. If x lies in region R2 the classifier decides class ω2. Similarly, regions R3 and R4 correspond to classes ω3 and ω4 respectively.

Overlap of Distributions. Because the class conditional densities overlap, there are regions where observations from different classes can appear. This overlap is the fundamental cause of classification error in pattern recognition systems.

Probability of Correct Classification. Let Pc denote the probability that the classifier correctly assigns the class label. The goal of the classifier is to maximize Pc.

Relation Between Error and Correct Classification. The probability of error Pe and probability of correct classification Pc are related as:
Pe = 1 − Pc.
Therefore minimizing Pe is equivalent to maximizing Pc.

Expression for Correct Classification Probability. The probability of correct classification can be written as:
Pc = Σi ∫_{Ri} P(ωi | x) P(x) dx.

Interpretation of the Formula. This expression represents the total probability that the classifier assigns the correct class in each decision region Ri. For every region Ri the classifier predicts class ωi.

Maximization Condition. For Pc to be maximized, the integrand inside each region Ri must be maximized.

Simplification Using Posterior Probability. Since P(x) is the same for all classes at a given observation x, the maximization depends only on the posterior probability P(ωi | x).

Optimal Decision Rule. Therefore in each region Ri the classifier should choose the class whose posterior probability is maximum.

Bayesian Classification Rule. The optimal decision rule becomes: assign observation x to class ωi if P(ωi | x) is the largest among all class posterior probabilities.

Implication. This rule ensures that the probability of correct classification Pc is maximized and the probability of error Pe is minimized.

Conclusion. Hence the Bayes decision rule provides the optimal classifier under the assumption that the class posterior probabilities are known. It forms the theoretical basis for probabilistic classification methods in machine learning and pattern recognition.

pages.text: Risk Functions and the Limitations of Minimizing Classification Error Probability. In Bayesian decision theory the probability of classification error Pe is often used as the objective for designing classifiers. However an important issue arises when considering whether Pe is the most appropriate criterion for all decision problems. The classification error probability assigns equal importance to all types of errors. In many real-world applications this assumption is not realistic because different misclassification errors may have different consequences. For example consider a medical diagnosis problem involving tumor classification. The two possible classes may be malignant and benign tumors. Suppose the classifier predicts that a tumor is benign when in reality it is malignant. This error is extremely serious because it may prevent the patient from receiving necessary treatment. On the other hand predicting malignant when the tumor is actually benign may still be undesirable but is usually less dangerous. Therefore the two types of errors do not have equal importance. Let e1 represent the error where a malignant tumor is incorrectly classified as benign. Let e2 represent the error where a benign tumor is incorrectly classified as malignant. In this case error e1 is more serious than error e2. Because of such situations it is useful to assign different weights or penalties to different types of classification errors. This leads to the concept of a risk function. The risk function incorporates the costs associated with different decisions and therefore provides a more flexible decision criterion. A modified risk expression can be defined as r = λ12 P(ω1) ∫_{R2} p(x | ω1) dx + λ21 P(ω2) ∫_{R1} p(x | ω2) dx. In this expression λ12 represents the loss incurred when an observation from class ω1 is incorrectly assigned to class ω2. Similarly λ21 represents the loss incurred when an observation from class ω2 is incorrectly assigned to class ω1. The integrals represent the probabilities of making these respective classification errors. When the loss parameters λ12 and λ21 are both equal to one the risk function reduces to the classification error probability Pe. Therefore the probability of error can be viewed as a special case of the more general risk function. In applications such as medical diagnosis it is often reasonable to choose λ12 greater than λ21 because misclassifying a malignant tumor as benign has more severe consequences than the reverse error. This framework allows classifiers to incorporate domain specific priorities and make decisions that minimize expected loss rather than simply minimizing the number of errors.

pages.text:
Error and Loss in Multi-Class Decision Theory. This page explains how classification errors are handled in multi-class decision problems and introduces the concept of the loss matrix used in Bayesian decision theory.

Influence of Loss Terms. The note states that when one loss term is larger than another, for example λ12 > λ21, the contribution of certain misclassification events becomes more important. In such a case the term P(ω1) ∫_{R2} P(x|ω1) dx has greater influence on the overall risk. This means that misclassifying samples from class ω1 into region R2 becomes more costly.

Feature Space Representation. The diagram shows a two-dimensional feature space divided into several regions labeled R1, R2, and R3. Each region represents a decision region where the classifier assigns observations to a specific class.

Decision Regions. Points in the feature space correspond to observed samples. Depending on where a sample lies relative to the decision boundaries, it is assigned to one of the decision regions.

Visualization of Errors. In the diagram, some points belonging to one class appear in a region assigned to another class. These points represent classification errors in the feature space.

Multi-Class Classification Problem. Consider a classification problem with M different classes. The feature space is partitioned into M decision regions Rj where j = 1, 2, ..., M.

Decision Regions Definition. Each region Rj corresponds to deciding that the observation belongs to class ωj.

Condition for Classification Error. A classification error occurs when a sample actually belonging to class ωk falls into a decision region Rj where j ≠ k. In other words, the classifier assigns the wrong class label.

Example of Error. For example, a sample that truly belongs to class ω1 might fall into decision region R2. In this case the classifier incorrectly assigns the sample to class ω2.

Loss Associated with Errors. To quantify the impact of such errors, a loss term λki is assigned to each possible misclassification. This value represents the penalty incurred when the true class is ωk but the classifier decides class ωi.

Loss Matrix Representation. All loss values are organized in a loss matrix. The matrix contains elements λij representing the loss incurred when the true class is ωi but the predicted class is ωj.

General Form of Loss Matrix.
[ λ11  λ12  ... ]
[ λ21  λ22  ... ]
[ ...  ...  ... ]
[ λM1  λM2  ... λMM ]

Interpretation of Loss Matrix. Each element λij defines the cost of deciding class j when the actual class is i.

Zero Loss for Correct Classification. Typically the diagonal elements of the loss matrix are set to zero. That is λkk = 0, meaning no loss occurs when the classification is correct.

Loss for Misclassification. Off-diagonal elements λki for k ≠ i represent the loss associated with misclassification.

Role in Bayesian Decision Theory. The loss matrix allows the classifier to incorporate different costs for different types of errors. This leads to a decision rule that minimizes the expected risk rather than simply minimizing the probability of error.

Importance in Practical Systems. In many real-world problems different errors have different consequences. For example misclassifying a serious disease as healthy may be far more costly than the reverse. The loss matrix enables decision systems to account for such asymmetric risks.

pages.text: Risk Associated with a Decision and the Average Risk in Bayesian Decision Theory. In Bayesian decision theory the objective is to minimize the expected risk associated with classification decisions. Consider a classification problem with M possible classes denoted by {ω1, ω2, ..., ωM}. Let R_i represent the decision region corresponding to class ω_i. If the feature vector x lies in region R_i then the classifier assigns the observation to class ω_i. The risk associated with deciding class ω_k when the true class may be different is defined using loss parameters. The conditional risk associated with class ω_k is defined as γ_k = Σ_{i=1}^{M} λ_{ki} ∫_{R_i} p(x | ω_k) dx. In this expression λ_{ki} represents the loss incurred when the true class is ω_k but the classifier assigns the observation to class ω_i. The integral term ∫_{R_i} p(x | ω_k) dx represents the probability that a sample from class ω_k falls in decision region R_i. Therefore this quantity corresponds to the probability that a sample belonging to class ω_k is classified into class ω_i. This region under the likelihood function represents the probability of misclassification for that class decision. In many formulations the loss for correct classification is assumed to be zero, meaning λ_{kk} = 0. After defining the conditional risk for each class the next step is to compute the average risk over all possible classes. The average risk r is obtained by weighting each conditional risk by the prior probability of the corresponding class. Therefore the average risk is defined as r = Σ_{k=1}^{M} γ_k P(ω_k). Substituting the expression for γ_k into this formula gives r = Σ_{k=1}^{M} P(ω_k) Σ_{i=1}^{M} λ_{ki} ∫_{R_i} p(x | ω_k) dx. Rearranging the order of summation and integration allows the expression to be written as r = Σ_{i=1}^{M} ∫_{R_i} [ Σ_{k=1}^{M} λ_{ki} p(x | ω_k) P(ω_k) ] dx. This formulation shows that the average risk is obtained by integrating a weighted combination of class conditional probabilities over each decision region. The goal of Bayesian decision theory is to choose decision regions R_i that minimize this average risk r. The optimization problem therefore becomes selecting decision regions such that the expected loss is minimized. In practice the risk is minimized when the integrand inside each region is minimized. This leads to the Bayesian minimum risk decision rule which generalizes the minimum error classifier to situations where different classification errors have different costs.

pages.text:
Bayesian Decision Rule with Loss Function and Risk Minimization. This page derives the optimal decision rule in a multi-class classification problem when a loss matrix is incorporated. The objective is to minimize the expected risk rather than only minimizing classification error.

Non-Negativity of Loss Terms. Since the loss values λki are assumed to be non-negative, and probabilities P(ωk) and P(x|ωk) are also non-negative, the expression involving their product remains non-negative.

Expected Loss in Decision Region. For a decision region Ri, the expected loss contributed by samples falling in that region can be written as:
∫_{Ri} Σ_{k=1}^{M} λki P(x|ωk) P(ωk) dx.

Minimization Condition. This quantity will be minimized if and only if the summation term inside the integral is minimized for each observation x.

Interpretation of the Summation. The term
Σ_{k=1}^{M} λki P(x|ωk) P(ωk)
represents the conditional risk associated with deciding class ωi when the observation is x.

Definition of Conditional Risk. Let li denote the conditional risk associated with choosing class ωi. It is defined as:
li = Σ_{k} λki P(x|ωk) P(ωk).

Optimal Decision Regions. The decision regions Ri should be chosen such that the conditional risk li is smaller than the risks associated with all other classes.

Mathematical Condition. In other words, for a sample x to belong to region Ri the following condition must hold:
li < lj for all j ≠ i.

Decision Rule. Therefore the decision rule becomes:
Assign x to region Ri if
li = Σ_{k} λki P(x|ωk) P(ωk)
< lj = Σ_{k} λkj P(x|ωk) P(ωk)
for all j ≠ i.

Interpretation of the Rule. This means that the classifier selects the class that produces the minimum expected loss given the observed feature vector x.

Relation to Bayesian Decision Theory. This rule generalizes the Bayes decision rule. Instead of simply maximizing posterior probability, the classifier chooses the class that minimizes expected risk.

Special Case. If all misclassification losses are equal and correct classification loss is zero, then minimizing expected risk reduces to maximizing posterior probability.

Importance in Real Applications. In practical systems different types of errors may have different consequences. Using a loss matrix allows the classifier to incorporate these different costs and make more informed decisions.

pages.text: Likelihood Ratio Test for Two-Class Bayesian Decision Problem. In Bayesian decision theory the classification decision can also be expressed in terms of the likelihood ratio test when dealing with a two-class classification problem. Consider two classes denoted by ω1 and ω2. The Bayesian decision rule is based on minimizing the expected risk associated with each possible decision. For a general M-class problem the conditional risk associated with deciding class ω_i is defined as l_i = Σ_{k=1}^{M} λ_{ki} p(x | ω_k) P(ω_k), where λ_{ki} represents the loss incurred when the true class is ω_k but the classifier decides class ω_i. The term p(x | ω_k) represents the likelihood of observing feature vector x given class ω_k and P(ω_k) is the prior probability of class ω_k. For the special case of two classes the number of classes becomes M = 2. Therefore the conditional risk expressions simplify. The risk associated with deciding class ω1 becomes l_1 = λ_{11} p(x | ω_1) P(ω_1) + λ_{21} p(x | ω_2) P(ω_2). Similarly the risk associated with deciding class ω2 becomes l_2 = λ_{12} p(x | ω_1) P(ω_1) + λ_{22} p(x | ω_2) P(ω_2). According to the Bayesian minimum risk decision rule the classifier assigns the observation x to class ω1 if the risk associated with choosing ω1 is less than the risk associated with choosing ω2. Therefore the decision rule becomes: decide ω1 if l_1 < l_2, otherwise decide ω2. Substituting the expressions for l_1 and l_2 leads to the inequality λ_{11} p(x | ω_1) P(ω_1) + λ_{21} p(x | ω_2) P(ω_2) < λ_{12} p(x | ω_1) P(ω_1) + λ_{22} p(x | ω_2) P(ω_2). Rearranging this inequality gives (λ_{21} − λ_{22}) p(x | ω_2) P(ω_2) < (λ_{12} − λ_{11}) p(x | ω_1) P(ω_1). This expression forms the basis of the likelihood ratio test. The likelihood ratio p(x | ω_1) / p(x | ω_2) is compared against a threshold that depends on the prior probabilities and the loss parameters. The threshold incorporates the cost of different types of classification errors. A common assumption in decision theory is that the loss associated with incorrect decisions is larger than the loss for correct decisions. This means λ_{ki} > λ_{kk}. Under such assumptions the decision boundary can be interpreted as a comparison between the likelihood ratio and a constant threshold derived from the loss function and prior probabilities. The likelihood ratio test therefore provides an equivalent formulation of the Bayesian minimum risk classifier for the two-class case and forms the theoretical foundation for many statistical pattern recognition methods.

pages.text:
Likelihood Ratio Test in Bayesian Decision Theory. This page derives the likelihood ratio test used for binary classification problems and shows how it depends on prior probabilities and loss terms.

Rewriting the Decision Rule. The Bayesian decision rule can be rewritten in terms of the ratio of class conditional probabilities. The comparison becomes:

P(x | ω1) / P(x | ω2) > P(ω2)(λ21 − λ22) / [ P(ω1)(λ12 − λ11) ].

Likelihood Ratio Definition. The quantity

Λ(x) = P(x | ω1) / P(x | ω2)

is called the likelihood ratio. It compares how likely the observation x is under class ω1 versus class ω2.

Likelihood Ratio Test. The decision rule can therefore be written using the likelihood ratio test:

Decide class ω1 if

Λ(x) > P(ω2)(λ21 − λ22) / [ P(ω1)(λ12 − λ11) ].

Otherwise decide class ω2.

Interpretation of the Threshold. The term on the right side of the inequality is the decision threshold. It depends on the class prior probabilities and the loss values associated with misclassification.

Decision Rule Representation. The decision rule can be written as:

x ∈ ω1 if

P(x|ω1) / P(x|ω2) > threshold.

Otherwise x ∈ ω2.

Special Case 1. If correct classifications incur no loss, then λ11 = λ22 = 0. The decision rule becomes:

P(x|ω1) / P(x|ω2) > P(ω2)λ21 / [ P(ω1)λ12 ].

This shows that the decision threshold depends only on prior probabilities and misclassification losses.

Special Case 2. If the loss for correct decisions is zero and the class prior probabilities are equal (P(ω1) = P(ω2)), then the decision rule simplifies further to:

P(x|ω1) / P(x|ω2) > λ21 / λ12.

Interpretation. In this case the likelihood ratio is compared directly with the ratio of misclassification costs.

Importance of Likelihood Ratio Test. The likelihood ratio test provides a practical way to implement Bayesian decision rules. Instead of computing posterior probabilities directly, the classifier compares the likelihood ratio with a threshold determined by prior probabilities and loss terms.

Applications. Likelihood ratio tests are widely used in statistical pattern recognition, signal detection theory, hypothesis testing, and machine learning classifiers.

pages.text: Example 2.1: Bayesian Decision Threshold for a Two-Class Gaussian Classification Problem. Consider a two-class classification problem where the feature vector consists of a single scalar feature x. Each class is modeled using a Gaussian probability distribution. For class ω1 the feature distribution is x ~ N(0, 1/2), meaning that the mean of the distribution is 0 and the variance is 1/2. For class ω2 the feature distribution is x ~ N(1, 1/2), meaning that the mean of the distribution is 1 and the variance is also 1/2. Assume that the prior probabilities of the two classes are equal, so P(ω1) = P(ω2) = 1/2. The objective is to determine the threshold value x0 that separates the two classes under different decision criteria. The first case considers minimizing the classification error probability Pe. In the minimum error probability framework the Bayesian classifier assigns a feature vector x to class ω1 if the posterior probability P(ω1 | x) is greater than P(ω2 | x). Conversely the classifier assigns x to class ω2 if P(ω2 | x) is greater than P(ω1 | x). Therefore the decision boundary or threshold occurs at the point where the two posterior probabilities are equal. This condition can be written as P(ω1 | x) = P(ω2 | x). Using Bayes theorem and the fact that the prior probabilities are equal the equality reduces to P(x | ω1) = P(x | ω2). This means the threshold x0 occurs at the point where the likelihood functions of the two Gaussian distributions intersect. Using the Gaussian probability density function p(x | ωi) = 1 / √π * exp(−(x − μ_i)^2) for the given variance formulation we substitute μ1 = 0 and μ2 = 1. Therefore the likelihood for class ω1 becomes p(x | ω1) = 1 / √π * exp(−x^2) and the likelihood for class ω2 becomes p(x | ω2) = 1 / √π * exp(−(x − 1)^2). The threshold value is obtained by equating these two likelihood expressions and solving for x. This intersection point represents the optimal decision boundary for minimum classification error. The second part of the example considers minimum average risk when a loss matrix is introduced. The loss matrix is defined as L = [[0, 0.5], [1.0, 0]]. This matrix specifies that different types of classification errors incur different penalties. In this situation the decision rule is no longer based purely on posterior probabilities but instead on minimizing the expected loss or risk. The Bayesian classifier compares the conditional risks associated with each possible decision and selects the class that results in the lower expected loss. The threshold value in this case shifts depending on the relative penalties defined in the loss matrix.

pages.text:
Example of Bayesian Decision Rule using Gaussian Class Conditional Densities. This page demonstrates how to determine the optimal decision boundary for two classes when the class conditional densities are Gaussian distributions.

Class Conditional Distribution. The probability density function for class ω2 is given by:

P(x | ω2) = (1 / √π) exp( −(x − 1)^2 ).

This represents a Gaussian distribution centered at x = 1.

Decision Boundary Calculation. Using equation (5) in equation (4), the equality condition for the decision boundary occurs when the two class conditional densities are equal.

Setting the densities equal gives:

exp(−x^2) = exp(−(x − 1)^2).

Solving the equation. Taking the exponents equal gives:

x^2 = (x − 1)^2.

Expanding the right side:

(x − 1)^2 = x^2 − 2x + 1.

Equating the expressions results in:

x^2 = x^2 − 2x + 1.

Solving for x gives:

2x = 1.

Therefore the decision boundary becomes:

x0 = 1 / 2.

Decision Rule using Likelihood Ratio. The Bayesian decision rule compares the likelihood ratio of the class conditional densities with a threshold determined by the priors and loss terms:

P(x | ω1) / P(x | ω2) > P(ω2)(λ21 − λ22) / [ P(ω1)(λ12 − λ11) ].

Threshold Determination. The threshold occurs at the value x0 where the likelihood ratio equals the threshold.

Using Given Information. Substituting the provided values gives:

P(x0 | ω1) / P(x0 | ω2) = 1.0 / 0.5.

Simplifying the Expression. Substituting the Gaussian expressions gives:

exp(−x^2) = 2 exp(−(x − 1)^2).

Taking Logarithm on Both Sides. Applying the natural logarithm gives:

−x^2 = ln(2) − (x − 1)^2.

Rearranging the equation leads to:

2x0 = 1 − ln(2).

Final Decision Boundary. Therefore the optimal decision boundary becomes:

x0 = (1 − ln 2) / 2.

Interpretation. This value represents the threshold point separating the two decision regions. If the observed feature value x is greater than this threshold, the classifier chooses one class; otherwise it chooses the other.

Significance. This example illustrates how Bayesian decision theory determines optimal decision boundaries using probability distributions, prior probabilities, and loss terms.

pages.text: Binary Classification with Gaussian Class-Conditional Densities and Minimum Average Risk Decision Rule. Consider a binary classification problem with a single scalar feature variable x. The two classes are denoted by ω1 and ω2. The feature distributions for each class are modeled using Gaussian probability density functions. For class ω1 the feature distribution is x ~ N(μ1, σ1²), meaning that the mean of the distribution is μ1 and the variance is σ1². For class ω2 the feature distribution is x ~ N(μ2, σ2²), meaning that the mean of the distribution is μ2 and the variance is σ2². A loss matrix is defined to represent the penalty associated with incorrect classification decisions. The loss matrix is written as L = [[0, λ12], [λ21, 0]]. In this matrix λ12 represents the loss incurred when a sample belonging to class ω1 is incorrectly classified as class ω2. Similarly λ21 represents the loss incurred when a sample belonging to class ω2 is incorrectly classified as class ω1. The diagonal elements are zero because there is no loss when the classification decision is correct. The prior probabilities of the classes are represented by P(ω1) and P(ω2). The goal is to determine the decision threshold x0 that minimizes the average risk. According to Bayesian decision theory the optimal decision boundary is obtained using the likelihood ratio condition derived from the minimum average risk rule. The threshold x0 satisfies the condition p(x0 | ω1) / p(x0 | ω2) = (P(ω2) λ21) / (P(ω1) λ12). This equation states that the ratio of the likelihood functions evaluated at the decision boundary equals a constant determined by the prior probabilities and the loss parameters. Using the Gaussian probability density function p(x | ωi) = 1 / √(2πσi²) * exp( −(x − μi)² / (2σi²) ), we substitute the likelihood expressions for the two classes into the likelihood ratio equation. Therefore p(x0 | ω1) becomes 1 / √(2πσ1²) * exp( −(x0 − μ1)² / (2σ1²) ), and p(x0 | ω2) becomes 1 / √(2πσ2²) * exp( −(x0 − μ2)² / (2σ2²) ). Substituting these expressions into the likelihood ratio equation produces an equation involving exponential functions and variance terms. Taking the logarithm of both sides simplifies the equation and allows solving for the threshold x0 explicitly. The resulting expression determines the optimal decision boundary that minimizes the expected classification risk while accounting for unequal error costs and different class prior probabilities.

pages.text:
Derivation of Decision Boundary for Gaussian Class Conditional Densities with Unequal Variances. This page derives the general form of the decision boundary when the class conditional distributions are Gaussian with different means and variances, including the effect of priors and loss terms.

Definition of Constant Term. Let

ρ = (σ1 / σ2) · [P(ω2) / P(ω1)] · (λ21 / λ12).

This constant combines the effect of class priors, variances, and loss terms into a single parameter used in the likelihood ratio decision rule.

Likelihood Equality for Decision Boundary. The decision boundary occurs where the likelihood ratio equals the threshold. This gives

exp( −(x − μ1)^2 / (2σ1^2) ) = ρ · exp( −(x − μ2)^2 / (2σ2^2) ).

Taking Logarithm. Taking the natural logarithm of both sides gives

−(x − μ1)^2 / (2σ1^2) = ln ρ − (x − μ2)^2 / (2σ2^2).

Expanding the Quadratic Terms. Expanding the squared expressions and rearranging terms leads to a quadratic equation in x:

a x^2 + b x + c = 0.

Decision Boundary Solution. The boundary points are obtained using the quadratic formula:

x0 = [ −b ± √(b^2 − 4ac) ] / (2a),   where a ≠ 0.

Coefficients of the Quadratic Equation. The coefficients are

a = σ2^2 − σ1^2

b = 2(σ1^2 μ2 − σ2^2 μ1)

c = 2σ1^2 σ2^2 ln ρ + σ2^2 μ1^2 − σ1^2 μ2^2.

These coefficients depend on the means, variances, and the combined parameter ρ that incorporates prior probabilities and misclassification losses.

Special Case: Equal Variances. If the two classes have equal variances and means μ1 = 0 and μ2 = 1, then

σ1^2 = σ2^2 = σ^2.

In this case the quadratic coefficient becomes

a = 0.

Thus the decision boundary equation reduces to a linear equation

b x + c = 0.

Solving for the threshold gives

x0 = −c / b.

Final Decision Boundary Expression. After simplification, the optimal threshold becomes

x0 = 1/2 − σ^2 ln [ (P(ω2) / P(ω1)) · (λ21 / λ12) ].

Interpretation. The decision boundary depends on the midpoint between the means (1/2 in this example) adjusted by a term involving variance, prior probabilities, and loss ratios. This shift reflects the influence of unequal priors or different costs of misclassification.

Significance. This derivation shows that when Gaussian distributions share equal variance, the optimal Bayesian classifier results in a linear decision boundary. When variances differ, the boundary becomes quadratic.

pages.text: Example Problem 2.3: Average Risk Calculation for Binary Classification with Loss Matrix. Consider a binary classification problem where two classes ω1 and ω2 are defined. A general loss matrix is provided to represent the cost associated with classification decisions. The loss matrix is defined as L = [[λ11, λ12], [λ21, λ22]]. In this matrix λ11 represents the loss incurred when a sample belonging to class ω1 is classified as ω1, λ12 represents the loss when a sample belonging to ω1 is misclassified as ω2, λ21 represents the loss when a sample belonging to ω2 is misclassified as ω1, and λ22 represents the loss when a sample belonging to ω2 is correctly classified as ω2. The prior probabilities of the classes are denoted as P(ω1) and P(ω2). The decision regions are defined as R1 and R2. Region R1 corresponds to the set of feature vectors that are assigned to class ω1 and region R2 corresponds to those assigned to class ω2. The probability of misclassifying a sample from class ω1 is defined as ε1 = ∫_{R2} p(x | ω1) dx. This represents the probability that a sample drawn from class ω1 falls into decision region R2 and is therefore incorrectly classified as class ω2. Similarly the probability of misclassifying a sample from class ω2 is defined as ε2 = ∫_{R1} p(x | ω2) dx. This represents the probability that a sample drawn from class ω2 falls into region R1 and is incorrectly classified as class ω1. The average risk r for the classifier is defined as the expected loss across all possible classes and decisions. Using the definition of risk in Bayesian decision theory the average risk is written as r = Σ_{i=1}^{2} ∫_{Ri} Σ_{k=1}^{2} λki p(x | ωk) P(ωk) dx. Expanding this expression leads to four terms corresponding to all combinations of true class and decision region. The expanded form becomes r = λ11 P(ω1) ∫_{R1} p(x | ω1) dx + λ21 P(ω2) ∫_{R1} p(x | ω2) dx + λ12 P(ω1) ∫_{R2} p(x | ω1) dx + λ22 P(ω2) ∫_{R2} p(x | ω2) dx. Using the definitions of the classification error probabilities we note that ∫_{R2} p(x | ω1) dx = ε1. From probability laws the complementary probability gives ∫_{R1} p(x | ω1) dx = 1 − ε1. Similarly ∫_{R1} p(x | ω2) dx = ε2 and ∫_{R2} p(x | ω2) dx = 1 − ε2. Substituting these relationships into the risk expression allows the average risk to be written entirely in terms of ε1 and ε2. This formulation clearly shows how the expected loss depends on the misclassification probabilities and the loss matrix parameters. It also highlights how Bayesian decision theory balances the probabilities of errors with the relative costs of those errors when designing an optimal classifier.

pages.text:
Expected Risk Expression for Binary Classification. This page derives the expression for the overall expected risk of a Bayesian classifier in terms of prior probabilities, loss values, and classification error probabilities.

Starting Expression for Risk. The total risk r of a decision rule is written as the weighted sum of losses for correct and incorrect decisions across the two classes:

r = λ11 P(ω1)(1 − ε1) + λ21 P(ω2) ε2 + λ12 P(ω1) ε1 + λ22 P(ω2)(1 − ε2).

Explanation of Terms.

P(ω1), P(ω2) are the prior probabilities of classes ω1 and ω2.

ε1 is the probability of misclassifying a sample from class ω1.

ε2 is the probability of misclassifying a sample from class ω2.

λij represents the loss incurred when the true class is ωi but the decision made is ωj.

Correct classification occurs with probabilities (1 − ε1) and (1 − ε2), while ε1 and ε2 represent classification errors.

Rearranging the Risk Expression. The equation can be simplified by grouping common terms.

The expected risk becomes

r = P(ω1)λ11 + P(ω1)(λ12 − λ11)ε1 + P(ω2)λ22 + P(ω2)(λ21 − λ22)ε2.

Interpretation of the Simplified Expression.

The first two terms correspond to the contribution of class ω1 to the expected risk.

The last two terms correspond to the contribution of class ω2.

The terms (λ12 − λ11) and (λ21 − λ22) show how the difference between misclassification loss and correct classification loss influences the total risk.

Key Insight. The expected risk depends on three factors: prior probabilities, loss values, and classification error probabilities.

Conclusion. This expression provides a compact form of the expected risk used in Bayesian decision theory and demonstrates how priors, losses, and errors jointly determine the optimal classifier.

pages.text: Example Problem 2.4: Upper Bound on Classification Error Probability for an M-Class Problem. The goal of this problem is to show that the classification error probability Pe for an optimal Bayesian classifier in an M-class classification problem is bounded by the expression Pe ≤ (M − 1) / M. To derive this result we begin with the relationship between the probability of error and the probability of correct classification. The probability of classification error is defined as Pe = 1 − Pc, where Pc represents the probability of making a correct classification decision. The probability of correct classification can be written as Pc = Σ_{i} P(x ∈ Ri, ωi), where Ri represents the decision region assigned to class ωi. This expression represents the probability that the feature vector x lies in the decision region Ri and the true class label is ωi, which corresponds to a correct decision. Using conditional probability relationships this expression can be written in integral form as Pc = Σ_{i} ∫_{Ri} P(ωi | x) p(x) dx. In this expression P(ωi | x) is the posterior probability that the sample belongs to class ωi given the observed feature vector x, and p(x) is the overall probability density of the feature vector. For an optimal Bayesian classifier the decision rule assigns each observation x to the class that has the largest posterior probability P(ωi | x). Therefore within each decision region Ri the posterior probability P(ωi | x) must be the maximum among all class posterior probabilities. The posterior probabilities satisfy the properties of a probability mass function. Specifically P(ωi | x) ≥ 0 for all i, P(ωi | x) ≤ 1, and the sum of all posterior probabilities across the M classes equals one, meaning Σ_{i=1}^{M} P(ωi | x) = 1. Consider the situation where the posterior probabilities are all equal. In that case P(ωi | x) = 1 / M for every class i. For any other probability distribution satisfying the normalization constraint, the maximum posterior probability must be at least 1 / M. Therefore max_i P(ωi | x) ≥ 1 / M. Since the optimal classifier chooses the class with the maximum posterior probability, the probability of correct classification Pc must be at least 1 / M. Using the relationship Pe = 1 − Pc we obtain Pe ≤ 1 − 1/M. This simplifies to Pe ≤ (M − 1) / M. This result shows that for an M-class classification problem the probability of error of the optimal classifier cannot exceed (M − 1) / M, which provides a theoretical upper bound on classification error.

pages.text:
Upper Bound on Classification Error in Multi-class Bayesian Decision Theory. This page derives a theoretical bound on the minimum classification error for an M-class problem.

Posterior Probability Visualization. The diagram shows posterior probabilities P(ω_k | x) for different classes k = 1, 2, ..., M. Different symbols such as '+', 'x', and 'o' represent different class probability mass functions or distributions across the feature space.

The horizontal axis represents the class index k, while the vertical axis represents the posterior probability P(ω_k | x).

Maximum Probability of Correct Classification. The maximum probability of correct classification can be written as

P_c^(max) ≥ Σ_i ∫_{R_i} (1/M) P(x) dx.

Here:

R_i represents the decision region assigned to class ω_i.

P(x) is the probability density of the feature vector x.

M is the number of classes.

Simplification of the Expression. Factoring out the constant term gives

P_c^(max) = (1/M) Σ_i ∫_{R_i} P(x) dx.

Since the decision regions R_i partition the entire feature space without overlap, the sum of integrals over all regions equals the total probability:

Σ_i ∫_{R_i} P(x) dx = ∫ P(x) dx = 1.

Therefore

P_c^(max) ≥ 1/M.

Minimum Probability of Error. The probability of error is related to the probability of correct classification by

P_e^(min) = 1 − P_c^(max).

Substituting the bound gives

1 − P_e^(min) ≥ 1/M.

Rearranging yields the inequality

P_e ≤ 1 − 1/M.

Interpretation. This result provides a theoretical upper bound on the classification error for an M-class classification problem. Even with optimal Bayesian decision rules, the error probability cannot exceed 1 − 1/M when considering the worst-case scenario.

Significance. The inequality highlights a fundamental property of multi-class classification systems: as the number of classes increases, the upper bound on classification error also increases. This emphasizes the increasing difficulty of classification problems with a larger number of classes.

pages.text: Discriminant Functions and Decision Surfaces in Pattern Classification. In statistical pattern recognition the goal of a classifier is to partition the feature space into decision regions corresponding to different classes. These decision regions are obtained by minimizing an objective function such as the probability of classification error or the expected risk. When the classifier assigns a feature vector to one of several possible classes the feature space becomes divided into multiple contiguous regions denoted by R1, R2, R3, and so on. Each region corresponds to one class label. If the regions Ri and Rj are contiguous then there is no reject option and every possible feature vector is assigned to one of the available classes. The boundaries between these regions are called decision surfaces. A decision surface is the geometric boundary that separates two neighboring decision regions in the multidimensional feature space. In a two-dimensional feature space the decision surface appears as a curve separating the regions, while in higher dimensions it becomes a hypersurface. For a minimum probability of error classifier the decision boundary between two classes ωi and ωj occurs where the posterior probabilities of the two classes are equal. This condition can be written as P(ωi | x) − P(ωj | x) = 0. In practical implementations it is often convenient to work with discriminant functions rather than directly comparing posterior probabilities. A discriminant function gi(x) is defined as a function of the posterior probability such that gi(x) = f(P(ωi | x)). Typically the function f is chosen to be a monotonically increasing function so that the ordering of the posterior probabilities is preserved. Using discriminant functions the classification rule becomes: assign the feature vector x to class ωi if gi(x) > gj(x) for all j ≠ i. The decision surface between two classes ωi and ωj is therefore defined by the condition gij(x) = gi(x) − gj(x) = 0. This equation describes the boundary in feature space where the classifier is indifferent between assigning the observation to class ωi or class ωj. For M classes there are multiple decision surfaces corresponding to each pair of classes. These discriminant functions provide a convenient mathematical framework for implementing classification rules and analyzing the geometry of decision boundaries in pattern recognition systems.

pages.text:
Bayesian Classifier for Normally Distributed Classes. This page derives the discriminant function used in Bayesian classification when the class conditional densities follow a multivariate normal distribution.

Class Conditional Density Assumption. Consider an M-class classification problem where the likelihood functions are given as

P(x | ω_i),   for i = 1, 2, ..., M.

These likelihood functions are assumed to follow multivariate normal (Gaussian) distributions.

Example Distribution. For each class ω_i, the feature vector x follows

P(x | ω_i) ~ N(μ_i, Σ_i).

Here

μ_i is the mean vector of class ω_i.

Σ_i is the covariance matrix of class ω_i.

Discriminant Function. In Bayesian classification, the decision rule is based on the posterior probability P(ω_i | x). Since the logarithm is a monotonic function, the discriminant function can be written as

g_i(x) = ln P(ω_i | x).

Using Bayes' theorem, this becomes

g_i(x) = ln P(x | ω_i) + ln P(ω_i).

Gaussian Likelihood Substitution. Substituting the probability density function of the multivariate normal distribution gives

g_i(x) = −1/2 (x − μ_i)^T Σ_i^{-1} (x − μ_i) + ln P(ω_i) + C_i.

Here C_i represents a constant term that does not depend on x.

Expansion of the Quadratic Form. Expanding the quadratic expression yields

g_i(x) = −1/2 x^T Σ_i^{-1} x
        + 1/2 x^T Σ_i^{-1} μ_i
        + 1/2 μ_i^T Σ_i^{-1} x
        − 1/2 μ_i^T Σ_i^{-1} μ_i
        + ln P(ω_i) + C_i.

Nature of the Discriminant Function. The resulting expression for g_i(x) contains quadratic terms of the feature vector x.

Therefore the discriminant function is a quadratic function of x.

Interpretation. Because the discriminant function is quadratic, the resulting decision boundaries between classes are quadratic surfaces in the feature space.

Significance. This formulation forms the basis of the Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) classifier, which is widely used in statistical pattern recognition when class covariance matrices differ.

pages.text: Quadratic Discriminant Function for Gaussian Class-Conditional Densities. Consider a special case of a Bayesian classifier where the feature vector has dimension l = 2 and the class conditional distributions are Gaussian. Assume that the covariance matrix for class ωi is diagonal and given by Σi = [[σi², 0], [0, σi²]]. This means the two feature components are uncorrelated and have identical variance σi². For Gaussian class conditional densities the discriminant function gi(x) used in Bayesian classification can be derived from the logarithm of the posterior probability. Substituting the Gaussian probability density function into the discriminant function expression leads to a quadratic form in the feature vector x. Let the feature vector be x = [x1, x2]^T and the class mean vector be μi = [μi1, μi2]^T. Using the quadratic form representation the discriminant function becomes gi(x) = −1/2 x^T Σi^{-1} x + μi^T Σi^{-1} x − 1/2 μi^T Σi^{-1} μi + Ci, where Ci includes constant terms such as the logarithm of the prior probability and normalization constants from the Gaussian density. Substituting the inverse covariance matrix Σi^{-1} = (1/σi²) I simplifies the expression. Expanding the quadratic form yields gi(x) = −(1/(2σi²))(x1² + x2²) + (1/σi²)(μi1 x1 + μi2 x2) − (1/(2σi²))(μi1² + μi2²) + Ci. This expression clearly contains quadratic terms in the feature variables, linear terms involving the mean parameters, and constant terms. Because the discriminant function contains quadratic components of the feature variables, the resulting decision boundaries between classes are quadratic surfaces. These boundaries may take the form of ellipses, parabolas, or hyperbolas depending on the parameters of the Gaussian distributions. Therefore the Bayesian classifier in this case is called a quadratic classifier or quadratic discriminant classifier. This result illustrates that when different classes have different covariance matrices the optimal Bayesian decision boundaries become nonlinear quadratic surfaces in the feature space.

Example: Decision Boundary for a Two-Class Bayesian Classification Problem. This example derives the decision boundary for a binary classification problem when the class conditional densities follow a specific exponential distribution form.

Problem Setup. Consider a two-class classification problem with prior probabilities

P(ω1) and P(ω2).

The feature variable x is one-dimensional.

Class Conditional Likelihood Functions. The likelihood functions for each class are defined as

P(x | ω_i) = (x / σ_i^2) exp( −x^2 / (2σ_i^2) ),   for x ≥ 0

and

P(x | ω_i) = 0,   for x < 0.

Thus the distributions are defined only for non-negative values of x.

Goal. The objective is to compute the decision boundary point. This boundary occurs where the discriminant function equals zero.

Decision Function. Define the discriminant difference function

g(x) = g1(x) − g2(x).

Here

g1(x) = ln P(ω1 | x)

g2(x) = ln P(ω2 | x).

Using Bayes rule and the monotonic property of logarithms, the function becomes

g(x) = ln P(ω1) + ln P(x | ω1) − ln P(ω2) − ln P(x | ω2).

Substituting the Likelihood Functions. For x ≥ 0

g(x) = ln P(ω1) + ln[(x / σ1^2) exp(−x^2 / (2σ1^2))]
      − ln P(ω2) − ln[(x / σ2^2) exp(−x^2 / (2σ2^2))].

Simplifying the Expression. Expanding the logarithmic terms gives

g(x) = ln[P(ω1) / P(ω2)] + ln(σ2^2 / σ1^2) + (x^2 / 2)(1/σ2^2 − 1/σ1^2).

Decision Boundary Condition. The decision boundary point occurs when

g(x) = 0.

Solving this equation determines the value of x at which the classifier is indifferent between the two classes.

Interpretation. The resulting decision boundary depends on the class prior probabilities and the variances σ1^2 and σ2^2 of the class conditional distributions.

Significance. This example illustrates how Bayesian decision theory determines the classification boundary by combining prior probabilities and likelihood functions using logarithmic discriminant functions.

pages.text: Derivation of Decision Boundary for Gaussian Classes with Unequal Variances. Consider the Bayesian decision rule for two Gaussian distributed classes where the class conditional densities have different variances. Let the prior probabilities of the classes be P(ω1) and P(ω2), and the variances of the Gaussian distributions be σ1² and σ2² respectively. Define a parameter ρ as ρ = ln[(P(ω1) / P(ω2)) (σ2² / σ1²)]. This parameter combines the effect of prior probabilities and the variance ratio of the two Gaussian distributions. When deriving the decision boundary using the likelihood ratio test, the resulting equation can be simplified into a quadratic form in the feature variable x. After algebraic manipulation the relationship becomes −ρ = (x² / 2) (1/σ2² − 1/σ1²). Solving this equation for the decision variable x gives the expression x = ± √[(2ρ σ1² σ2²) / (σ2² − σ1²)]. This result represents the possible decision boundary locations depending on the parameters of the Gaussian distributions and the prior probabilities. The existence and nature of the solution depend on the relationship between the variances σ1² and σ2². If σ2² − σ1² > 0 then ρ must be positive for the square root expression to produce a real solution. In this case the decision boundary corresponds to real positive values of x. If σ2² − σ1² < 0 then the parameter ρ becomes negative, but the resulting product inside the square root still produces a valid real solution for x. Therefore in both situations the decision boundary remains real and positive. This derivation illustrates how the position of the Bayesian decision boundary depends on the relative variances of the Gaussian distributions and the prior probabilities of the classes. When the variances differ the resulting decision rule produces nonlinear boundaries and the classifier behaves as a quadratic discriminant classifier rather than a linear classifier.

Problem: Bayesian Decision Boundary for Two Multivariate Normal Classes with Equal Covariance. This problem derives the optimal decision rule for two classes whose class conditional densities follow multivariate Gaussian distributions with identical covariance matrices.

Problem Setup. Consider a binary classification problem with the following class conditional densities:

P(x | ω1) = N(μ1, Σ)

P(x | ω2) = N(μ2, Σ)

Here

μ1 and μ2 are the mean vectors of the two classes.

Σ is the common covariance matrix shared by both classes.

The prior probabilities of the classes are

P(ω1) = η

P(ω2) = 1 − η.

Minimum Risk Criterion. According to Bayesian decision theory, the decision boundary occurs when the expected risk for both class decisions becomes equal. At the decision threshold we have

(λ21 − λ22) P(x | ω2) P(ω2) = (λ12 − λ11) P(x | ω1) P(ω1).

Assumption for Correct Classification Loss. If correct classifications have zero loss, then

λ11 = λ22 = 0.

Under this assumption the decision condition simplifies to

λ21 P(x | ω2) P(ω2) = λ12 P(x | ω1) P(ω1).

Substituting Gaussian Likelihoods. Substituting the multivariate Gaussian probability density expressions gives

λ21 (1 − η) exp[ −1/2 (x − μ2)^T Σ^{-1} (x − μ2) ]

= λ12 η exp[ −1/2 (x − μ1)^T Σ^{-1} (x − μ1) ].

Taking Logarithm. Taking the natural logarithm of both sides leads to

1/2 (x − μ1)^T Σ^{-1} (x − μ1) − 1/2 (x − μ2)^T Σ^{-1} (x − μ2) = ρ.

Here

ρ = ln( λ12 η / [ λ21 (1 − η) ] ).

Expanding the Quadratic Terms. Expanding the quadratic expressions results in

(μ2 − μ1)^T Σ^{-1} x + 1/2 μ1^T Σ^{-1} μ1 − 1/2 μ2^T Σ^{-1} μ2 = ρ.

Rearranging the Decision Boundary Equation. Rearranging the equation gives

(μ2 − μ1)^T Σ^{-1} x = ρ'.

where

ρ' = ρ + 1/2 μ2^T Σ^{-1} μ2 − 1/2 μ1^T Σ^{-1} μ1.

Nature of the Decision Boundary. The resulting equation is linear in the feature vector x. Therefore the decision boundary between the two Gaussian classes is a linear hyperplane in the feature space.

Interpretation. This result shows that when multiple classes have equal covariance matrices, the Bayesian classifier leads to a linear decision boundary. This forms the theoretical foundation of Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA).

Additional Definition. Define the vector

s = (μ2 − μ1)(μ2 − μ1)^T.

This vector relates to the direction separating the two class means and plays an important role in determining the orientation of the decision boundary.

pages.text: Derivation of a Point on the Linear Decision Boundary for Gaussian Classes with Equal Covariance. Consider a two-class classification problem where the class conditional distributions are Gaussian with mean vectors μ1 and μ2 and a common covariance matrix Σ. The Bayesian decision boundary separating the two classes is obtained from the discriminant functions and leads to a linear decision surface. Let x̄0 denote a point that lies on this decision boundary. Such a point must satisfy the equation (μ2 − μ1)^T Σ^{-1} x̄0 = ρ′. Here ρ′ is a scalar constant that incorporates the influence of prior probabilities of the classes and any constants arising from the Gaussian discriminant function formulation. This equation represents the linear decision boundary in the feature space. To determine a particular solution that lies on this boundary, we can construct a vector aligned with the direction Σ^{-1}(μ2 − μ1). One possible solution can therefore be expressed as x̄0 = ρ′ δ Σ^{-1}(μ2 − μ1), where δ is a scalar scaling factor chosen so that the boundary condition is satisfied. Substituting this candidate solution into the boundary equation gives (μ2 − μ1)^T Σ^{-1} x̄0 = (μ2 − μ1)^T Σ^{-1}[ρ′ δ Σ^{-1}(μ2 − μ1)]. Rearranging the expression results in δ (μ2 − μ1)^T Σ^{-1} x̄0 = ρ′ (μ2 − μ1). Solving this relationship yields the final form of the solution vector. Hence the point on the decision boundary can be written as x̄0 = Σ δ^{-1}(μ2 − μ1) ρ′. This derivation shows that the direction defining the boundary is determined by the difference between the class mean vectors transformed by the inverse covariance matrix. Therefore the separating surface depends on the Mahalanobis distance between the classes. The resulting classifier is linear because both classes share the same covariance matrix, which eliminates quadratic terms in the discriminant functions and produces a linear decision boundary.

Example: Linear Discriminant Function for Two Multivariate Gaussian Classes. This example derives the linear discriminant function for a two-class problem where both classes follow multivariate normal distributions with the same covariance matrix.

Problem Setup. Consider a classification problem with two classes whose distributions are defined as

P(x | ω1) = N(μ1, Σ)

P(x | ω2) = N(μ2, Σ).

The covariance matrix is given by

Σ = [ [0.3, 0.1, 0.1],
      [0.1, 0.3, -0.1],
      [0.1, -0.1, 0.3] ].

Mean Vectors. The class mean vectors are

μ1 = [0, 0, 0]^T

μ2 = [0.5, 0.5, 0.5]^T.

Objective. The goal is to derive the linear discriminant function for classification.

Prior Probabilities. Assume that the class prior probabilities are not necessarily equal, that is

P(ω1) ≠ P(ω2).

Discriminant Function Definition. The discriminant difference function between the two classes is defined as

g12(x) = ln P(ω1 | x) − ln P(ω2 | x).

Using Bayes' theorem this becomes

g12(x) = ln[P(ω1) / P(ω2)] + ln P(x | ω1) − ln P(x | ω2).

Multivariate Gaussian Density. The likelihood function for a multivariate normal distribution is

P(x | ω_i) = 1 / [ (2π)^{d/2} |Σ|^{1/2} ] · exp[ −1/2 (x − μ_i)^T Σ^{-1} (x − μ_i) ].

Substituting Likelihood Functions. Substituting the Gaussian density functions for both classes into the discriminant function yields

g12(x) = ln[P(ω1) / P(ω2)] − 1/2 (x − μ1)^T Σ^{-1} (x − μ1) + 1/2 (x − μ2)^T Σ^{-1} (x − μ2).

Simplification. Since both classes share the same covariance matrix Σ, the quadratic terms cancel during expansion, resulting in a linear discriminant function of the form

g12(x) = w^T x + w0.

Interpretation. The resulting discriminant function is linear in the feature vector x. Therefore the decision boundary between the two classes is a linear hyperplane in the feature space.

Significance. This example illustrates the principle behind Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), where Gaussian class distributions with equal covariance matrices lead to linear decision boundaries.

pages.text: Derivation of Linear Discriminant Function for Two Gaussian Classes with Equal Covariance Matrix. Consider a two–class classification problem where the feature vector x follows Gaussian distributions for each class. The class conditional densities are modeled as multivariate normal distributions with mean vectors μ1 and μ2 and a common covariance matrix Σ. The discriminant function difference between the two classes is denoted by g12(x) which is defined as g12(x) = ln P(ω1|x) − ln P(ω2|x). Using Bayes rule and substituting the Gaussian probability density functions, the expression becomes g12(x) = ln[P(ω1)/P(ω2)] + ln|Σ|^(1/2) − ln|Σ|^(1/2) − (1/2)(x − μ1)^T Σ^{-1} (x − μ1) + (1/2)(x − μ2)^T Σ^{-1} (x − μ2). Since both classes share the same covariance matrix, the determinant terms cancel each other. Expanding the quadratic forms and simplifying the equation results in g12(x) = ln[P(ω1)/P(ω2)] + (μ1 − μ2)^T Σ^{-1} x − (1/2) μ1^T Σ^{-1} μ1 + (1/2) μ2^T Σ^{-1} μ2. This expression can be written in a linear form with respect to the feature vector x. Therefore the discriminant function takes the form g12(x) = w^T x + w0, which represents a linear decision model. The weight vector w is given by w = (μ1 − μ2)^T Σ^{-1}, and the bias term w0 is given by w0 = ln[P(ω1)/P(ω2)] − (1/2) μ1^T Σ^{-1} μ1 + (1/2) μ2^T Σ^{-1} μ2. This formulation shows that when both classes have identical covariance matrices, the Bayesian classifier produces a linear decision boundary. The classification rule becomes: assign the feature vector x to class ω1 if g12(x) > 0 and assign it to class ω2 otherwise. This result forms the theoretical foundation of Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), where the separating surface between classes is a hyperplane in the feature space determined by the difference between the class means and the shared covariance structure.
