Likelihood Ratio Test for Gaussian Distributed Classes. Consider a two-class classification problem where the feature vector x follows different multivariate Gaussian distributions depending on the class.

Class Conditional Distributions. The class conditional densities are given as

x | ω1 ~ N(μ1, Σ1)

x | ω2 ~ N(μ2, Σ2).

This means that if the observation belongs to class ω1, it is generated from a multivariate normal distribution with mean μ1 and covariance matrix Σ1. Similarly, observations from class ω2 follow a Gaussian distribution with mean μ2 and covariance Σ2.

Likelihood Ratio Test. The optimal Bayesian decision rule can be expressed using the likelihood ratio test. A sample x is assigned to class ω1 or ω2 depending on the value of the likelihood ratio

Λ(x) = P(x | ω1) / P(x | ω2).

Decision Rule. The classification rule becomes

x ∈ ω1 if Λ(x) > θ

x ∈ ω2 if Λ(x) < θ.

Here θ represents the threshold determined by the prior probabilities of the classes.

Threshold Expression. The threshold can be written as

θ = P(ω2) / P(ω1).

Logarithmic Form of the Test. For computational convenience the likelihood ratio test is usually converted into logarithmic form

ln P(x | ω1) − ln P(x | ω2) + ln P(ω1) − ln P(ω2) > (<) 0.

Gaussian Likelihood Function. If the class conditional densities follow multivariate Gaussian distributions, then

P(x | ωi) ~ N(μi, Σi),   i = 1, 2.

The logarithm of the Gaussian density function becomes

ln P(x | ωi) = −(d/2) ln(2π) − (1/2) ln|Σi| − (1/2)(x − μi)^T Σi^{-1} (x − μi).

Substituting in the Decision Rule. Substituting these expressions into the logarithmic likelihood ratio test yields the discriminant inequality

−(1/2) ln|Σ1| − (1/2)(x − μ1)^T Σ1^{-1}(x − μ1)

+ (1/2) ln|Σ2| + (1/2)(x − μ2)^T Σ2^{-1}(x − μ2)

+ ln P(ω1) − ln P(ω2) > (<) 0.

Interpretation. This expression represents the general discriminant function for two Gaussian classes with possibly different covariance matrices. Because quadratic terms in x remain, the resulting decision boundary is generally quadratic in the feature space.

Significance. This result forms the basis of the Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) classifier. When the covariance matrices of the classes differ, the optimal Bayesian decision boundary becomes a quadratic surface separating the classes.

Expectation of Maximum Likelihood Variance Estimate. Consider a set of N independent samples drawn from a distribution with true mean μ and true variance σ². The maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) of variance is defined using the sample mean.

Sample Mean. The maximum likelihood estimate of the mean is

μ_ML = (1/N) Σ x_n.

Expectation of Squared Sample Mean. The expectation of the square of the estimated mean is

E[μ_ML²] = μ² + (1/N)σ².

Expectation of Product Term. Consider the expectation of the product between the sample mean and a sample value

E[μ_ML x_n] = E[(1/N) Σ x_m x_n].

Taking expectation,

E[μ_ML x_n] = (1/N) Σ E[x_m x_n].

Using the statistical property of independent samples,

E[x_m x_n] = μ² + δ_{mn} σ²,

where δ_{mn} is the Kronecker delta.

Substituting and simplifying gives

E[μ_ML x_n] = μ² + (σ² / N).

Maximum Likelihood Estimate of Variance. The MLE of variance is

σ_ML² = (1/N) Σ (x_n − μ_ML)².

Expectation of the Variance Estimator. Expanding the expectation gives

E[σ_ML²] = (1/N) Σ [ μ² + σ² + μ² + (σ² / N) − 2(μ² + σ² / N) ].

Simplifying the expression leads to

E[σ_ML²] = (σ² / N) Σ (1 − 1/N).

Since the summation runs over N samples,

E[σ_ML²] = ((N − 1)/N) σ².

Result. Therefore the expectation of the maximum likelihood variance estimator is

E[σ_ML²] = ((N − 1)/N) σ².

Interpretation. This shows that the maximum likelihood estimator of variance is biased. It systematically underestimates the true variance by the factor (N−1)/N.

Implication. To obtain an unbiased estimator of variance, the denominator N in the variance formula is replaced by (N−1), leading to the commonly used sample variance estimator in statistics.

pages.text: Expectation of the Maximum Likelihood Variance Estimator. Consider a random sample x1, x2, ..., xN drawn independently from a distribution with true mean μ and variance σ². The maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) of the variance is defined as σ_ML² = (1/N) Σ_{n=1}^N (x_n − μ_ML)², where μ_ML is the maximum likelihood estimate of the mean, given by μ_ML = (1/N) Σ_{n=1}^N x_n. To analyze the bias of the variance estimator, we examine the expected value of the estimator. Using algebraic expansion, the variance estimator can be written as σ_ML² = (1/N) Σ x_n² − μ_ML². Taking expectations of both terms allows us to evaluate the expected value of the estimator. First, consider the expectation of the squared observations. Since each sample comes from a distribution with mean μ and variance σ², we know that E[x_n²] = μ² + σ². Therefore the expectation of the first term becomes E[(1/N) Σ x_n²] = (1/N) Σ E[x_n²] = μ² + σ². Next consider the expectation of μ_ML². Since μ_ML is the sample mean, we compute its squared expectation using the joint expectation of sample products. The result is E[μ_ML²] = μ² + (σ² / N). Substituting these results into the variance estimator expression gives E[σ_ML²] = (μ² + σ²) − (μ² + σ²/N). Simplifying this expression yields E[σ_ML²] = σ² − σ²/N. Therefore the expected value of the maximum likelihood variance estimator becomes E[σ_ML²] = ((N − 1) / N) σ². This result shows that the MLE estimator for variance is biased because its expected value is slightly smaller than the true variance. The bias decreases as the sample size increases, and in the limit as N approaches infinity the estimator becomes unbiased. This derivation explains why in classical statistics the unbiased estimator of variance uses the factor 1/(N − 1) instead of 1/N.

pages.text:
Expectation of Maximum Likelihood Variance Estimator – Detailed Derivation. Consider a set of N independent samples drawn from a distribution with true mean μ and true variance σ². The maximum likelihood estimators (MLE) for the mean and variance are derived using the sample data.

Sample Mean Estimator. The maximum likelihood estimate of the mean is

μ_ML = (1/N) Σ x_n.

Property of Second Moment. For a random variable x drawn from a distribution with mean μ and variance σ²,

E[x_n²] = μ² + σ².

Using this property, the expected value of the average of squared samples becomes

(1/N) Σ E[x_n²] = μ² + σ².

Expectation of Squared Mean Estimate. Consider the expectation of the squared sample mean

E[μ_ML²] = E[(1/N Σ x_n)²].

Expanding the square,

E[μ_ML²] = (1/N²) Σ Σ E[x_n x_m].

Using the property of independent samples,

E[x_n x_m] = μ² + δ_nm σ²,

where δ_nm is the Kronecker delta which equals 1 when n = m and 0 otherwise.

Substituting and simplifying gives

E[μ_ML²] = μ² + (σ² / N).

Maximum Likelihood Variance Estimator. The MLE of variance is defined as

σ_ML² = (1/N) Σ (x_n − μ_ML)².

Taking expectation,

E[σ_ML²] = E[(1/N) Σ x_n² − μ_ML²].

Substituting the expectations derived earlier,

E[σ_ML²] = (μ² + σ²) − (μ² + σ²/N).

Simplifying the expression,

E[σ_ML²] = σ² − σ²/N.

Final Result. Therefore the expectation of the maximum likelihood variance estimator is

E[σ_ML²] = ((N − 1) / N) σ².

Conclusion. This result shows that the maximum likelihood estimate of variance is biased because its expected value is slightly smaller than the true variance. The bias decreases as the sample size N increases.

Statistical Insight. To remove this bias, the unbiased variance estimator divides the squared deviations by (N − 1) instead of N, which leads to the standard sample variance formula used in statistics.

pages.text: Linear Models and Discriminant Functions for Two-Class Classification. In pattern recognition, linear models are commonly used to perform classification tasks by separating classes using linear decision boundaries. For the two-class case, the objective is to determine the class label of a feature vector x using a discriminant function. The classification process can be viewed as a sequence of operations where the input feature vector x is first passed into a discriminant function y(x). The output of this function is then evaluated using a sign function which determines the class label. The final output corresponds to assigning the input sample to one of the two classes, typically denoted as C1 or C2. The discriminant function computes a scalar value that represents how strongly the feature vector belongs to one class relative to the other. In the linear case, the discriminant function takes the form y(x) = x^T w + w0 = w^T x + w0. Here w represents the weight vector that determines the orientation of the decision boundary, and w0 represents the bias or threshold term that shifts the boundary in the feature space. The decision rule is defined as follows: if y(x) ≥ 0 then the sample x is assigned to class C1, otherwise it is assigned to class C2. The set of points satisfying y(x) = 0 defines the decision boundary. In a D-dimensional feature space this boundary forms a hyperplane of dimension D−1. The hyperplane separates the feature space into two regions corresponding to the two classes. Points for which y(x) > 0 lie on one side of the boundary and are assigned to class C1, while points for which y(x) < 0 lie on the other side and are assigned to class C2. Geometrically, the weight vector w is perpendicular to the decision boundary and therefore determines the orientation of the separating hyperplane. The bias term w0 determines the offset of the hyperplane from the origin and acts as a threshold in the classification decision. Thus the linear discriminant function defines a simple yet powerful classification model in which the decision boundary is a straight line in two-dimensional space or a hyperplane in higher-dimensional feature spaces.

pages.text:
Geometric Interpretation of Linear Decision Boundary. Consider a linear discriminant function defined as

y(x) = w^T x + w0.

The decision boundary is defined by the set of points for which the discriminant function equals zero.

Decision Boundary Condition.

y(x) = 0.

Thus any point lying on the decision boundary satisfies

w^T x + w0 = 0.

Points on the Boundary. Suppose two points x_A and x_B lie on the decision boundary. Then

w^T x_A + w0 = 0

w^T x_B + w0 = 0.

Subtracting the two equations gives

w^T (x_A − x_B) = 0.

Interpretation. The vector (x_A − x_B) lies along the decision boundary. Since its dot product with w is zero, the vector w is orthogonal to (x_A − x_B).

Therefore, w is perpendicular to every vector lying on the decision boundary.

Geometric Meaning. This implies that

w is the normal vector to the decision boundary.

Thus the decision boundary y(x) = 0 represents a hyperplane in the feature space whose orientation is determined by the vector w.

Role of the Weight Vector.

The vector w determines the orientation of the hyperplane.

The bias term w0 determines the offset of the hyperplane from the origin.

Distance from the Origin. For any point x on the decision boundary,

w^T x + w0 = 0.

This can be written as

w^T x = −w0.

The perpendicular distance from the origin to the hyperplane is obtained by projecting x onto the direction of w.

Distance Formula.

Distance = (x^T w) / ||w||.

Since w^T x = −w0 for points on the boundary, the distance from the origin to the hyperplane becomes

Distance = −w0 / ||w||.

Here

||w|| = sqrt(w^T w)

represents the Euclidean (L2) norm of the weight vector.

Unit Direction Vector. The normalized vector

w / ||w||

represents a unit vector in the direction normal to the decision boundary.

Conclusion. Therefore, the linear discriminant function defines a hyperplane decision boundary where w controls the orientation and w0 controls the distance of the boundary from the origin.

pages.text: Distance of a Point from the Linear Decision Surface. In linear classification models, the decision boundary is defined by the discriminant function y(x) = w^T x + w0. The set of points satisfying y(x) = 0 forms the decision surface that separates the feature space into two regions corresponding to two classes. To understand the geometric interpretation of the classifier, it is useful to compute the perpendicular distance of an arbitrary point x from this decision surface. Consider a point x located anywhere in the feature space. Let x⊥ denote the orthogonal projection of the point x onto the decision boundary defined by y(x) = 0. The vector connecting x⊥ to x lies along the direction of the weight vector w, since w is perpendicular (normal) to the decision boundary. The unit vector in the direction of w is given by w / ||w||. Using vector algebra, the point x can therefore be written as x = x⊥ + r (w / ||w||), where r represents the perpendicular distance from the decision boundary to the point x. Since x⊥ lies on the decision boundary, it must satisfy the boundary equation y(x⊥) = 0. Substituting x = x⊥ + r (w / ||w||) into the discriminant function gives y(x) = w^T x + w0 = w^T (x⊥ + r (w / ||w||)) + w0. Because x⊥ lies on the boundary, the term w^T x⊥ + w0 equals zero. This simplifies the expression to y(x) = r (w^T w) / ||w||. Noting that w^T w = ||w||², we obtain y(x) = r ||w||. Solving for r yields the final result r = y(x) / ||w||. This equation shows that the signed distance from the point x to the decision boundary is equal to the discriminant function value divided by the magnitude of the weight vector. A positive value of r indicates that the point lies on the side of the hyperplane corresponding to class C1, while a negative value indicates that the point lies on the side corresponding to class C2. This result provides an important geometric interpretation of linear classifiers: the discriminant function not only determines the class label but also measures how far a sample lies from the decision boundary in the direction of the normal vector.

pages.text:
Distance of a Point from a Linear Decision Surface. Consider a linear discriminant function defined as

y(x) = w^T x + w0.

The decision surface or decision boundary is the set of all points satisfying

y(x) = 0.

This represents a hyperplane in the feature space.

Geometric Setup. Let x be any point in the coordinate space. Let x⊥ denote the orthogonal projection of x onto the decision boundary y(x) = 0. The vector w is normal (perpendicular) to the decision surface.

Let the distance from the decision boundary to the point x along the direction of the normal vector be denoted by r.

Vector Representation of the Point. From vector geometry, the point x can be expressed as

x = x⊥ + r (w / ||w||).

Here

w / ||w||

is the unit normal vector to the decision boundary.

Property of Projection Point. Since x⊥ lies on the decision boundary,

y(x⊥) = 0.

Substituting into the discriminant equation gives

w^T x⊥ + w0 = 0.

Substituting x into the Discriminant Function.

Using

x = x⊥ + r (w / ||w||)

in the discriminant function

y(x) = w^T x + w0

we obtain

y(x) = w^T ( x⊥ + r (w / ||w||) ) + w0.

Expanding the expression,

y(x) = w^T x⊥ + r (w^T w / ||w||) + w0.

Since

w^T x⊥ + w0 = 0,

the expression simplifies to

y(x) = r (w^T w / ||w||).

Because

w^T w = ||w||²,

we obtain

y(x) = r ||w||.

Distance Formula. Solving for r gives the perpendicular distance from point x to the decision surface

r = y(x) / ||w||.

Final Result.

Distance from point x to the linear decision boundary is

r = ( w^T x + w0 ) / ||w||.

Interpretation.

The sign of y(x) indicates which side of the decision boundary the point lies on.

The magnitude |r| represents the perpendicular distance of the point from the decision surface.

||w|| represents the Euclidean norm of the weight vector and determines the scaling of the distance.

Conclusion. This geometric interpretation shows that the discriminant function value y(x) is proportional to the distance of the point from the decision boundary along the normal direction defined by the weight vector.

pages.text: Least Squares Method for Multi-Class Classification using Linear Models. In pattern recognition, least squares techniques can be used to determine the parameters of linear discriminant functions for classification problems. Consider a K-class discrimination problem where the classifier uses linear models for each class. For each class k, the discriminant function is defined as y_k(x) = w_k^T x + w_{k0}. Here w_k represents the weight vector associated with class k and w_{k0} is the bias term. The index k ranges from 1 to K, meaning that the classifier uses K different linear discriminant functions corresponding to the K classes. The classification decision is typically made by selecting the class whose discriminant function value is the largest. The objective is therefore to determine the optimal parameters w_k for each class such that the classifier correctly separates the data points belonging to different classes. To simplify the representation, the set of discriminant functions can be written explicitly for all classes as y_1(x) = w_1^T x + w_{10}, y_2(x) = w_2^T x + w_{20}, and continuing up to y_K(x) = w_K^T x + w_{K0}. These equations can be combined into a compact matrix formulation. Define the vector of discriminant outputs as y(x) = [y_1(x), y_2(x), ..., y_K(x)]^T, which is a K×1 vector containing the output of each discriminant function. The parameters of all classifiers can be combined into a single matrix denoted as W̃. This matrix contains the bias terms in its first row and the weight vectors in the remaining rows. The matrix has the structure W̃ = [ w_{10}  w_{20} ... w_{K0} ; w_1  w_2 ... w_K ], where each column corresponds to the parameters of a particular class. If the input vector is augmented by adding a constant component (usually 1) to incorporate the bias term, the discriminant functions can be expressed compactly as y(x) = W̃^T x̃, where x̃ represents the augmented feature vector. In this representation the dimensions of W̃ become (d+1) × K, where d is the dimensionality of the original feature vector. This matrix formulation provides a convenient way to compute all discriminant outputs simultaneously and forms the basis for applying least squares optimization techniques to estimate the optimal weight parameters for multi-class linear classifiers.

pages.text:
Linear Model Representation for Multi-Class Classification. Consider an augmented input vector used in linear classification.

Augmented Input Vector.

x̃ = [1 ; x]

This vector has dimension (D+1) × 1, where the extra element 1 accounts for the bias term in the linear model.

Training Requirement. To determine the weight matrix W̃, a training dataset is required.

For each training sample x̃_n, the output of the linear model is defined as

y(x_n) = W̃^T x̃_n = t_n

for n = 1, 2, ..., N.

Here

t_n is a K × 1 target vector representing the desired output for the n-th training example.

Target Vector Structure. The target vector t_n follows a one-of-K (one-hot) encoding scheme. If the input sample x̃_n belongs to class C_k, then

t_n = [0, ..., 0, 1, 0, ..., 0]^T

where the value 1 appears at the k-th position and all other elements are 0.

Thus t_n is a binary indicator vector identifying the correct class.

Dataset Representation. The entire training dataset can be expressed in matrix form.

Input Matrix.

X̃ = [ x̃_1^T
      x̃_2^T
      ...
      x̃_N^T ]

This matrix has dimension

N × (D + 1).

Target Matrix.

T = [ t_1^T
      t_2^T
      ...
      t_N^T ]

This matrix has dimension

N × K.

Weight Matrix. The weight matrix W̃ contains the parameters of the classifier and has dimension

(D + 1) × K.

Model Objective. The goal is to determine W̃ such that the linear model outputs match the target vectors. In matrix form the model becomes

X̃ W̃ = T.

Dimensions of the Matrices.

X̃ : N × (D + 1)

W̃ : (D + 1) × K

T : N × K.

Interpretation. Each column of W̃ corresponds to the parameters of a linear discriminant function for one class. The model simultaneously produces K outputs for each input sample, representing the responses of K linear classifiers.

This formulation forms the foundation for multi-class linear classification models such as linear regression classifiers and softmax classifiers.

pages.text: Least Squares Error Function for Multi-Class Linear Classification. In the least squares approach to classification, the goal is to determine the parameter matrix that minimizes the squared error between the predicted outputs of the linear discriminant functions and the desired target outputs. Suppose we have N training samples where each sample is represented by an augmented feature vector x̃_n and a corresponding target vector t_n. The linear model predicts the output as y(x_n) = W̃^T x̃_n. To estimate the parameters, we define a squared error function that measures the difference between the predicted outputs and the target outputs for all training samples. The total error function is written in matrix form as E(W̃) = (1/2) Tr[(X̃ W̃ − T)^T (X̃ W̃ − T)]. Here X̃ is the design matrix containing the augmented feature vectors of all training samples arranged as rows, W̃ is the parameter matrix containing the weights and bias parameters for each class, and T is the matrix containing the target vectors for each sample. The trace operator Tr(.) represents the sum of diagonal elements of the matrix and ensures that the error function sums the squared differences across all training samples and classes. This expression can also be written in an equivalent summation form. Specifically, the error function becomes E(W̃) = (1/2) Σ_{n=1}^N || W̃^T x̃_n − t_n ||². This formulation shows that the least squares objective is simply the sum of squared differences between predicted output vectors and the desired target vectors for each training example. Expanding the expression explicitly gives E(W̃) = (1/2)[||W̃^T x̃_1 − t_1||² + ||W̃^T x̃_2 − t_2||² + ... + ||W̃^T x̃_N − t_N||²]. In matrix notation, the predictions for all samples can be written as X̃ W̃, which produces an N × K matrix where each row corresponds to the predicted output vector for a training sample. The matrix T is also an N × K matrix containing the corresponding target vectors. The difference (X̃ W̃ − T) therefore represents the error matrix for all samples and classes. Minimizing this squared error function with respect to the parameter matrix W̃ yields the least squares solution for multi-class linear classification. This formulation provides a convenient framework for deriving the optimal weight matrix using matrix calculus and forms the basis for many linear classification algorithms in machine learning.

pages.text:
Least Squares Error Function for Multi-Class Linear Models. Consider the linear model formulation where the predicted outputs are given by

Y = X̃ W̃

where

X̃ : N × (D+1) augmented input matrix,
W̃ : (D+1) × K weight matrix,
T : N × K target matrix.

The objective of training is to determine W̃ such that the predicted outputs approximate the target values.

Error Function Definition. The least squares error function is defined using the squared difference between the predicted outputs and target values:

E(W̃) = (1/2) Tr[(X̃W̃ − T)^T (X̃W̃ − T)].

Here Tr(·) denotes the trace of a matrix.

Equivalent Summation Form. The trace form of the error function is equivalent to the sum of squared errors over all training samples:

E(W̃) = (1/2) Σ_{n=1}^{N} || W̃^T x̃_n − t_n ||^2.

Expanded Representation. Writing the expression explicitly,

E(W̃) = (1/2) [ ||W̃^T x̃_1 − t_1||^2
               + ||W̃^T x̃_2 − t_2||^2
               + ...
               + ||W̃^T x̃_N − t_N||^2 ].

Dimensions of Quantities.

x̃_n : (D+1) × 1

W̃^T x̃_n : K × 1

t_n : K × 1

Thus each squared term measures the discrepancy between predicted and desired K-dimensional output vectors.

Matrix Representation of Predictions. For the entire dataset,

X̃ = [ x̃_1^T
      x̃_2^T
      ...
      x̃_N^T ]

and

T = [ t_1^T
      t_2^T
      ...
      t_N^T ].

Therefore

X̃W̃ − T

produces an N × K matrix whose rows represent the prediction error for each training sample.

Interpretation of the Error Matrix.

X̃W̃ − T = [ x̃_1^T W̃ − t_1^T
             x̃_2^T W̃ − t_2^T
             ...
             x̃_N^T W̃ − t_N^T ].

Each row corresponds to the error vector for one training example.

Purpose of the Error Function. Minimizing the least squares error function determines the weight matrix W̃ that best fits the training data in the least-squares sense.

This formulation is widely used in linear regression based classification models and provides a closed-form solution for the optimal weight parameters.

pages.text: Fisher Linear Discriminant for Two-Class Classification. The Fisher Linear Discriminant is a classical method in pattern recognition used to find a linear projection that maximizes the separation between two classes. The basic idea is to project a high-dimensional feature vector x onto a one-dimensional space using a projection direction vector w. The projection is defined as y = w^T x. After projection, classification is performed in the one-dimensional space. For a two-class problem, the decision rule becomes: classify a sample into class C1 if y ≥ −w0, otherwise classify it into class C2. The main challenge is to determine the optimal projection vector w that provides the best separation between the two classes after projection. Since the data is reduced from multiple dimensions to a single dimension, some information may be lost. Therefore the projection direction must be carefully chosen so that the projected class distributions remain well separated. Consider a two-class dataset where samples belonging to class C1 are denoted by x_n for n = 1, ..., N1 and samples belonging to class C2 are denoted by x_n for n = 1, ..., N2. The mean vectors of the two classes are computed as m1 = (1/N1) Σ_{n∈C1} x_n and m2 = (1/N2) Σ_{n∈C2} x_n. When the samples are projected onto the direction w, the projected class means become w^T m1 and w^T m2. A natural measure of class separation in the projected space is the distance between these projected means. Therefore one objective is to maximize the difference between the projected class means, which can be written as w^T(m2 − m1). However, if the magnitude of w is allowed to grow without restriction, this difference can increase indefinitely. To prevent this trivial solution, a constraint must be introduced on the magnitude of w. A common constraint is to normalize the weight vector so that ||w|| = 1. Under this constraint, the optimization problem becomes finding the direction w that maximizes the separation between the projected class means while maintaining a bounded weight vector. This idea forms the foundation of the Fisher Linear Discriminant method, which ultimately derives the optimal projection direction that maximizes class separability.

pages.text:
Fisher Linear Discriminant Criterion. Consider a two-class classification problem where the goal is to project high dimensional data onto a line such that the projected classes are well separated.

Objective. Let m1 and m2 be the mean vectors of classes C1 and C2 respectively. The projection direction w is chosen such that the separation between the projected class means is maximized.

The optimization problem can be written as

arg max_w  w^T (m2 − m1)

subject to

w^T w = 1.

Lagrangian Formulation. Introducing a Lagrange multiplier λ to enforce the constraint,

L(w) = w^T (m2 − m1) + λ (w^T w − 1).

Taking derivative with respect to w and setting it to zero,

∇_w L = (m2 − m1) + λ w = 0.

Solving for w,

w = −(1/λ)(m2 − m1).

Thus the optimal projection direction is proportional to the difference between the class means,

w ∝ (m2 − m1).

Interpretation. This result indicates that the projection direction aligns with the vector connecting the two class means. When projected onto this direction, the distance between class centers becomes maximum.

Limitation. However, maximizing only the separation between means is not sufficient because the classes may have large within-class variance. Large spreads in each class can cause overlap even if the means are far apart.

Improved Criterion. Fisher proposed maximizing the ratio of between-class variance to within-class variance.

Fisher Criterion.

J(w) = (w^T S_B w) / (w^T S_W w).

Between-Class Scatter Matrix.

S_B = (m2 − m1)(m2 − m1)^T.

This matrix measures the separation between class means.

Within-Class Scatter Matrix.

S_W = Σ_{x_n ∈ C1} (x_n − m1)(x_n − m1)^T

      + Σ_{x_n ∈ C2} (x_n − m2)(x_n − m2)^T.

This matrix measures the spread of data within each class.

Interpretation of the Criterion. Maximizing J(w) ensures that

• The projected class means are far apart (large between-class variance).
• The projected samples within each class remain tightly clustered (small within-class variance).

Thus Fisher’s criterion provides an optimal projection direction that balances class separation and compactness of class distributions.

Geometric Insight. After projection onto the optimal direction w, the two classes become maximally separated along a one-dimensional axis, which improves classification performance.

pages.text: Derivation of the Optimal Projection Direction in Fisher Linear Discriminant. The Fisher Linear Discriminant determines the optimal projection vector w by maximizing a criterion function that measures class separability. The Fisher criterion is defined as J(w) = (w^T S_B w) / (w^T S_W w), where S_B is the between-class scatter matrix and S_W is the within-class scatter matrix. The objective is to find the vector w that maximizes this ratio, which represents maximizing the separation between class means while minimizing the spread of samples within each class after projection. The optimization problem is written as argmax_w J(w). To solve this, we compute the gradient of the criterion with respect to w and set it equal to zero. This leads to the condition ∇_w J(w) = 0. Applying differentiation to the ratio form of the criterion produces the equation [(w^T S_B w)(2 S_W w) − (w^T S_W w)(2 S_B w)] / (w^T S_W w)^2 = 0. Simplifying the numerator gives (w^T S_B w) S_W w = (w^T S_W w) S_B w. The between-class scatter matrix for the two-class case can be written as S_B = (m2 − m1)(m2 − m1)^T, where m1 and m2 are the mean vectors of class 1 and class 2 respectively. Substituting this expression into the equation shows that S_B w = (m2 − m1)(m2 − m1)^T w. This means S_B w is a vector in the direction of (m2 − m1). Substituting this result into the previous equation leads to a proportionality relationship between S_W w and the vector (m2 − m1). Rearranging terms gives w proportional to S_W^{-1}(m2 − m1). Therefore the optimal projection direction for Fisher Linear Discriminant is ŵ = S_W^{-1}(m2 − m1). This result shows that the optimal projection vector is obtained by scaling the difference between the class means by the inverse of the within-class scatter matrix. Intuitively, this transformation accounts for the covariance structure of the data and ensures that the projection maximizes class separation while minimizing the effect of within-class variance.

pages.text:
Decision Rule for Linear Discriminant Classifier. After determining the optimal projection vector w using Fisher’s Linear Discriminant Analysis, classification of a new input vector x is performed using a simple decision rule based on projection.

Projection of Input. The input vector x is projected onto the direction defined by w. The projected value is

y = w^T x.

This scalar value represents the coordinate of x along the discriminant direction.

Decision Threshold. A threshold value y0 is defined to separate the two classes. The classification decision is based on comparing the projected value y with this threshold.

Decision Rule.

If y ≥ y0, then x ∈ C1.

Else, x ∈ C2.

Here

y0 is the threshold that determines the separation boundary between the classes in the projected one-dimensional space.

Interpretation. After projecting the data onto the discriminant direction, the multidimensional classification problem reduces to a one-dimensional problem. The classes are separated by a threshold along the projection axis.

Role of the Threshold. The threshold y0 is typically chosen based on the projected class means or prior probabilities so that classification error is minimized.

Geometric Meaning. In the original feature space, the rule corresponds to a linear decision boundary perpendicular to the vector w. The sign and magnitude of w^T x determine on which side of the boundary the sample lies.

Conclusion. Thus the Fisher Linear Discriminant ultimately performs classification by projecting data onto an optimal direction and applying a threshold decision rule in the projected space.

pages.text: Probabilistic Generative Models for Two-Class Classification. In probabilistic generative models, the classification task is approached by modeling the probability distributions of the data for each class and then using Bayes’ theorem to compute the posterior probabilities of the classes given an observed feature vector x. Consider a two-class classification problem with classes C1 and C2. The posterior probability that a sample x belongs to class C1 can be written using Bayes’ rule as P(C1|x) = (P(x|C1)P(C1)) / (P(x|C1)P(C1) + P(x|C2)P(C2)). Here P(x|Ci) represents the class-conditional likelihood and P(Ci) represents the prior probability of class Ci. This expression computes the probability that the observation x belongs to class C1 based on both the likelihood of the data under the class distribution and the prior belief about that class. To simplify the expression, we define a quantity a as the logarithm of the ratio of the class likelihoods weighted by their priors. Specifically, a = ln[(P(x|C1)P(C1)) / (P(x|C2)P(C2))]. Rearranging this expression gives (P(x|C1)P(C1)) / (P(x|C2)P(C2)) = e^a. Substituting this result back into the posterior probability expression leads to P(C1|x) = 1 / (1 + e^{-a}). This function is known as the sigmoid or logistic function and is typically denoted by σ(a). Therefore the posterior probability can be written compactly as P(C1|x) = σ(a), where σ(a) = 1 / (1 + e^{-a}). The sigmoid function maps any real-valued input a into the interval between 0 and 1, making it suitable for representing probabilities. Graphically, the sigmoid function has an S-shaped curve where the output approaches 0 for large negative values of a and approaches 1 for large positive values of a, with σ(0) = 0.5 representing equal class probability. This formulation shows how probabilistic generative models naturally lead to the logistic sigmoid function when expressing posterior probabilities for binary classification problems.

pages.text:
Properties of the Sigmoid (Logistic) Function and its Inverse.

The sigmoid function is widely used in probabilistic classification models such as logistic regression and neural networks. It maps any real-valued input into the interval (0,1), allowing the output to be interpreted as a probability.

Definition of Sigmoid Function.

The sigmoid function is defined as

σ(a) = 1 / (1 + e^{-a}).

This function is monotonic and bounded between 0 and 1.

Property 1: Symmetry Property.

The sigmoid function satisfies an important symmetry relationship:

σ(-a) = 1 - σ(a).

Proof.

σ(-a) = 1 / (1 + e^{a})

Multiply numerator and denominator appropriately:

σ(-a) = (1 + e^{a} - e^{a}) / (1 + e^{a})

= 1 - e^{a} / (1 + e^{a})

But

e^{a} / (1 + e^{a}) = 1 / (1 + e^{-a})

Therefore

σ(-a) = 1 - σ(a).

This shows that the sigmoid function is symmetric around the point (0, 0.5).

Property 2: Inverse of the Sigmoid Function.

Let

σ(a) = σ.

From the definition

σ = 1 / (1 + e^{-a}).

Rearranging,

1 + e^{-a} = 1 / σ.

Thus

e^{-a} = (1 / σ) - 1.

Taking reciprocal,

e^{a} = σ / (1 - σ).

Taking the natural logarithm on both sides gives

a = ln( σ / (1 - σ) ).

This expression is known as the logit function.

Logit Function.

logit(σ) = ln( σ / (1 - σ) ).

The logit function is the inverse of the sigmoid function and converts probabilities back into real-valued scores.

Application in Probabilistic Classification.

In binary classification, if

σ = P(C1 | x),

then

1 - σ = P(C2 | x).

Substituting into the logit expression gives

a = ln( P(C1 | x) / P(C2 | x) ).

Thus the logit corresponds to the logarithm of the posterior odds between the two classes.

Interpretation.

This shows that logistic regression models the log-odds of class membership as a linear function of the input features. The sigmoid function then converts this log-odds value back into a probability.

Conclusion.

The sigmoid function provides a smooth probabilistic mapping, while its inverse (logit) reveals that classification decisions are fundamentally based on log-odds ratios between competing classes.

pages.text: Probabilistic Generative Models for Multi-Class Classification. In the multi-class case, the probabilistic generative approach extends the Bayesian framework to K classes. Suppose the classes are denoted as C1, C2, ..., CK. The posterior probability that a sample x belongs to class Ck is obtained using Bayes’ theorem. It is expressed as P(Ck|x) = [P(x|Ck)P(Ck)] / [Σ_j P(x|Cj)P(Cj)]. In this expression, P(x|Ck) represents the class-conditional probability density of the feature vector x for class Ck, and P(Ck) represents the prior probability of class Ck. The denominator ensures that the posterior probabilities across all classes sum to one. To simplify the expression, we define a quantity ak as ak = ln[P(x|Ck)P(Ck)]. Substituting this definition into the posterior probability expression and exponentiating both sides gives P(Ck|x) = e^{ak} / Σ_j e^{aj}. This formulation is known as the normalized exponential function or the softmax function. The softmax function converts arbitrary real-valued scores into probabilities that sum to one across all classes. Therefore, the posterior probability for each class can be interpreted as the softmax of the corresponding log-likelihood score. As an example, consider the Gaussian generative model where the class-conditional densities are assumed to follow multivariate normal distributions. In this case we assume P(x|Ck) follows a Gaussian distribution with mean vector μk and covariance matrix Σ, written as P(x|Ck) ~ N(x | μk, Σ). The probability density function of the multivariate Gaussian distribution is given by P(x|Ck) = 1 / [(2π)^{D/2} |Σ|^{1/2}] exp[ −1/2 (x − μk)^T Σ^{-1} (x − μk) ]. If the covariance matrix Σ is assumed to be the same for all classes, this leads to a simplified discriminant function that depends primarily on the class means and shared covariance structure. A special case occurs when the number of classes K equals 2. In this binary case, the softmax function reduces to the logistic sigmoid function, and the posterior probability becomes P(C1|x) = σ(a), where σ(a) = 1 / (1 + e^{−a}). Thus the binary classification case can be viewed as a special instance of the more general multi-class softmax formulation.

pages.text:
Derivation of Logistic Regression from Gaussian Class-Conditional Densities.

Consider a two-class classification problem with classes C1 and C2. The posterior probability of class membership can be expressed in terms of the log-odds ratio between the two classes.

Log-Odds Function.

Define the discriminant function as

a(x) = ln [ P(x|C1) P(C1) / P(x|C2) P(C2) ].

This represents the logarithm of the ratio of the joint probabilities of the two classes.

Separating the terms gives

a(x) = ln [ P(C1) / P(C2) ] + ln [ P(x|C1) / P(x|C2) ].

Assume that the class-conditional densities follow multivariate Gaussian distributions with a shared covariance matrix Σ:

P(x|Ci) = 1 / ((2π)^{d/2} |Σ|^{1/2}) * exp[ -1/2 (x − μi)^T Σ^{-1} (x − μi) ].

Substituting these expressions into the log-odds function, the constant normalization terms cancel out, resulting in

a(x) = ln [ P(C1) / P(C2) ] - 1/2 (x − μ1)^T Σ^{-1} (x − μ1) + 1/2 (x − μ2)^T Σ^{-1} (x − μ2).

Expanding the quadratic forms leads to a linear function of x:

a(x) = w^T x + w0.

Thus the discriminant function becomes linear in the feature vector.

Weight Vector.

The weight vector is

w = Σ^{-1} (μ1 − μ2).

Bias Term.

The bias term is

w0 = 1/2 μ2^T Σ^{-1} μ2 - 1/2 μ1^T Σ^{-1} μ1 + ln [ P(C1) / P(C2) ].

Posterior Probability Using Sigmoid.

The posterior probability of class C1 given x can be written using the sigmoid function:

P(C1 | x) = σ(a) = σ(w^T x + w0).

Here

σ(a) = 1 / (1 + e^{-a}).

Interpretation.

This derivation shows that when class-conditional densities are Gaussian with equal covariance matrices, the posterior probability takes the form of a logistic sigmoid applied to a linear function of x.

Conclusion.

Therefore logistic regression can be interpreted as a probabilistic discriminative model derived from generative Gaussian assumptions, where the decision boundary is linear and the class probability is obtained through the sigmoid transformation.

pages.text: Linear Discriminant Functions for the General K-Class Case with Gaussian Generative Models. Consider the general case of classification with K classes where the class-conditional densities follow multivariate Gaussian distributions with a shared covariance matrix. The discriminant function for each class Ck can be expressed in linear form as a_k(x) = w_k^T x + w_{k0}. In this formulation, w_k represents the weight vector associated with class Ck and w_{k0} represents the bias term. These parameters are derived from the Gaussian generative model assumptions. Specifically, the weight vector is given by w_k = Σ^{-1} μ_k, where μ_k is the mean vector of class Ck and Σ is the shared covariance matrix. The bias term is defined as w_{k0} = −(1/2) μ_k^T Σ^{-1} μ_k + ln P(C_k), where P(C_k) denotes the prior probability of class Ck. To derive this result, we begin by defining a_k as the logarithm of the joint probability of the data and the class. That is, a_k = ln[P(x|C_k) P(C_k)]. This can be expanded as a_k = ln P(C_k) + ln P(x|C_k). Assuming the class-conditional densities follow a multivariate Gaussian distribution, we write P(x|C_k) = 1 / [(2π)^{D/2} |Σ|^{1/2}] exp[−1/2 (x − μ_k)^T Σ^{-1} (x − μ_k)]. Taking the logarithm of this expression yields ln P(x|C_k) = −(D/2) ln(2π) − (1/2) ln |Σ| − (1/2) (x − μ_k)^T Σ^{-1} (x − μ_k). Expanding the quadratic term results in −(1/2) x^T Σ^{-1} x + μ_k^T Σ^{-1} x − (1/2) μ_k^T Σ^{-1} μ_k. The first three terms −(D/2) ln(2π), −(1/2) ln |Σ|, and −(1/2) x^T Σ^{-1} x are identical for all classes and therefore do not affect the comparison between classes during classification. These common terms can therefore be ignored when constructing discriminant functions. The remaining terms lead to the linear discriminant expression a_k(x) = (Σ^{-1} μ_k)^T x − (1/2) μ_k^T Σ^{-1} μ_k + ln P(C_k). Hence the discriminant function takes the linear form a_k(x) = w_k^T x + w_{k0}, where the parameters depend on the class means, shared covariance matrix, and prior probabilities. This result demonstrates that when Gaussian class-conditional distributions share the same covariance matrix, the resulting decision boundaries between classes become linear hyperplanes.

pages.text:
Maximum Likelihood Solution for a Two-Class Gaussian Classification Problem.

Consider a binary classification problem with two classes C1 and C2. The class prior probabilities are defined as

P(C1) = p,
P(C2) = 1 − p.

Each data point xn belongs to one of the two classes and is associated with a target label tn. The target encoding is defined as

If xn ∈ C1, then tn = 1,
If xn ∈ C2, then tn = 0.

Assume that the class-conditional distributions follow multivariate Gaussian distributions with a shared covariance matrix Σ.

Thus the joint distributions become

P(xn, C1) = P(C1) P(xn | C1) = p N(xn | μ1, Σ),

P(xn, C2) = P(C2) P(xn | C2) = (1 − p) N(xn | μ2, Σ).

Overall Likelihood.

For a dataset consisting of N independent samples {xn , tn}, the likelihood function is written as

P(T, X | p, μ1, μ2, Σ) = ∏_{n=1}^{N} [P(xn , C1)]^{tn} [P(xn , C2)]^{1−tn}.

Substituting the Gaussian class-conditional densities gives

P(T, X | p, μ1, μ2, Σ) = ∏_{n=1}^{N} [p N(xn | μ1, Σ)]^{tn} [(1 − p) N(xn | μ2, Σ)]^{1−tn}.

Log-Likelihood.

To simplify optimization, we take the logarithm of the likelihood function

ln L = Σ_{n=1}^{N} [ tn ln p + (1 − tn) ln (1 − p) ]

− Σ_{n=1}^{N} [ tn ( d/2 ln(2π) + 1/2 ln |Σ| + 1/2 (xn − μ1)^T Σ^{-1} (xn − μ1) )

+ (1 − tn) ( d/2 ln(2π) + 1/2 ln |Σ| + 1/2 (xn − μ2)^T Σ^{-1} (xn − μ2) ) ].

Interpretation.

The first term represents the contribution from the class prior probabilities, while the remaining terms correspond to the Gaussian likelihood contributions from each class.

This log-likelihood formulation forms the basis for estimating the parameters p, μ1, μ2, and Σ using the maximum likelihood principle.

Conclusion.

By maximizing the log-likelihood with respect to these parameters, we obtain the optimal estimates of the class priors, class means, and shared covariance matrix for the Gaussian generative classifier.

pages.text: Maximum Likelihood Estimation of Parameters in Gaussian Generative Classification. In probabilistic generative models, the parameters of the model are typically estimated using the maximum likelihood principle. The goal is to determine the parameter vector θ that maximizes the likelihood function of the observed training data. Formally, this can be written as argmax_θ L(θ), where L represents the likelihood of the observed data given the parameters. The maximum likelihood estimate is obtained by taking the derivative of the likelihood (or log-likelihood) with respect to each parameter and setting it equal to zero. First consider the estimation of the prior probability parameter p for class C1. Suppose we have N total training samples where N1 samples belong to class C1 and N2 samples belong to class C2, such that N = N1 + N2. Let t_n denote the class indicator variable where t_n = 1 if the sample belongs to class C1 and t_n = 0 otherwise. Taking the derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to p and setting it equal to zero leads to the equation Σ_n [ t_n / p − (1 − t_n) / (1 − p) ] = 0. Simplifying this equation using the fact that Σ_n t_n = N1 and Σ_n (1 − t_n) = N2 gives the solution p = N1 / N. Thus the maximum likelihood estimate of the prior probability for class C1 is simply the fraction of training samples belonging to that class. Next consider the estimation of the class mean parameter μ1. The derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to μ1 is set to zero, leading to a condition involving the training samples belonging to class C1. After simplifying the expression, the result shows that the maximum likelihood estimate of μ1 is the average of all samples assigned to class C1. That is, μ1 = (1 / N1) Σ_{n∈C1} x_n. This result matches the intuitive estimate of the mean of the data points belonging to that class. Similar derivations can be performed for the mean of class C2 and the shared covariance matrix. Therefore the maximum likelihood estimates for the parameters of a Gaussian generative model correspond to the empirical statistics of the training data: the class priors equal the relative frequencies of the classes, and the class means equal the sample averages of the corresponding data points.

pages.text:
Maximum Likelihood Estimation of Class Means and Covariance Matrix for a Two-Class Gaussian Model.

Continuing from the log-likelihood formulation of the Gaussian generative model, the next step is to estimate the parameters μ1, μ2, and Σ using maximum likelihood.

Estimation of Class Mean μ1.

Taking the derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to μ1 and setting it to zero gives

μ1 Σ_n tn = Σ_n tn xn.

Let

N1 = Σ_n tn

be the number of samples belonging to class C1. Then the estimate of the mean for class C1 becomes

μ̂1 = (1 / N1) Σ_{n=1}^{N} tn xn.

Thus μ1 is simply the average of all samples that belong to class C1.

Estimation of Class Mean μ2.

Similarly, differentiating the log-likelihood with respect to μ2 and setting the result to zero yields

Σ_n (1 − tn) (Σ^{-1} xn − Σ^{-1} μ2) = 0.

Rearranging gives

μ2 Σ_n (1 − tn) = Σ_n (1 − tn) xn.

Let

N2 = Σ_n (1 − tn)

be the number of samples belonging to class C2. Therefore the maximum likelihood estimate of μ2 is

μ̂2 = (1 / N2) Σ_{n=1}^{N} (1 − tn) xn.

This corresponds to the average of all samples in class C2.

Estimation of Covariance Matrix Σ.

To estimate the shared covariance matrix, we take the derivative of the log-likelihood with respect to Σ and set it equal to zero

∇Σ L = 0.

This leads to the covariance estimate based on contributions from both classes:

Σ = (1 / N) [ Σ_{n ∈ C1} (xn − μ1)(xn − μ1)^T + Σ_{n ∈ C2} (xn − μ2)(xn − μ2)^T ].

Interpretation.

The estimated covariance matrix represents the pooled within-class covariance, combining the scatter of samples around their respective class means.

Conclusion.

Thus the maximum likelihood estimates for the parameters of the Gaussian generative classifier are

μ̂1 = (1 / N1) Σ tn xn,
μ̂2 = (1 / N2) Σ (1 − tn) xn,
Σ̂ = pooled covariance of both classes.

These parameter estimates are then used to construct the linear discriminant function and posterior class probabilities.

pages.text: Maximum Likelihood Estimation of the Shared Covariance Matrix in Gaussian Generative Models. In Gaussian generative classification models where all classes share the same covariance matrix, the covariance parameter must also be estimated from the training data using maximum likelihood estimation. Suppose we have N training samples with class indicator variables t_n such that t_n = 1 if the sample belongs to class C1 and t_n = 0 if it belongs to class C2. Let μ1 and μ2 denote the mean vectors of class C1 and class C2 respectively. First we define the sample covariance matrices for each class separately. For class C1 the covariance estimate is S1 = (1/N1) Σ_{n=1}^{N} t_n (x_n − μ1)(x_n − μ1)^T, where N1 is the number of samples belonging to class C1. Similarly for class C2 the covariance estimate is S2 = (1/N2) Σ_{n=1}^{N} (1 − t_n)(x_n − μ2)(x_n − μ2)^T, where N2 is the number of samples belonging to class C2. Since the model assumes a common covariance matrix across classes, the overall covariance estimate must combine the covariance contributions from both classes. The pooled covariance matrix is therefore defined as S = (N1/N) S1 + (N2/N) S2. To find the maximum likelihood estimate of the shared covariance matrix Σ, we differentiate the log-likelihood function with respect to Σ and set the derivative equal to zero. This leads to the expression ∇_Σ { −(N/2) ln |Σ| − (N/2) Tr(Σ^{-1} S) } = 0. To solve this expression, we use standard matrix derivative identities. The derivative of the log determinant with respect to Σ is ∇_Σ ln|Σ| = Σ^{-1}. The derivative of the trace term is ∇_Σ Tr(Σ^{-1} A) = −Σ^{-1} A Σ^{-1}. Applying these results and simplifying yields the equation −(N/2) Σ^{-1} + (N/2) Σ^{-1} S Σ^{-1} = 0. Solving this equation leads directly to the result that the maximum likelihood estimate of the shared covariance matrix is Σ̂ = S. Thus the optimal covariance estimate for the Gaussian generative model is simply the pooled covariance matrix computed from all training samples across the classes. This estimate captures the overall spread of the data while respecting the assumption that all classes share the same covariance structure.

pages.text:
Binary Classification Using Linear Logistic Regression.

Logistic regression is a probabilistic model used for binary classification problems. In this setting, the target variable takes values from the set {0,1}.

Target Representation.

For each data point xn, the corresponding target label is defined as

tn ∈ {0,1}.

If tn = 1, the sample belongs to class C1.
If tn = 0, the sample belongs to class C2.

Goal of Logistic Regression.

The objective is to construct a model that predicts the probability that a data point belongs to class C1. The output of the model must lie in the interval

hw(x) ∈ [0,1].

Model Definition.

Logistic regression uses the sigmoid function applied to a linear combination of the input features:

hw(x) = σ(w^T x).

The sigmoid function is defined as

σ(a) = 1 / (1 + e^{-a}).

This transformation ensures that the model output is a valid probability.

Probabilistic Interpretation.

The logistic regression model defines the probability of the class label as

P(tn = 1 | xn, w) = hw(xn).

Since there are only two classes,

P(tn = 0 | xn, w) = 1 − hw(xn).

Combined Probability Model.

Both cases can be written compactly using the target label tn:

P(tn | xn, w) = [hw(xn)]^{tn} [1 − hw(xn)]^{1−tn}.

This expression automatically selects the correct probability depending on the value of tn.

Likelihood Function.

Given a dataset of N independent observations, the likelihood of the parameter vector w is

L(w) = P(t | X, w) = ∏_{n=1}^{N} P(tn | xn, w).

Substituting the probability model gives

L(w) = ∏_{n=1}^{N} [hw(xn)]^{tn} [1 − hw(xn)]^{1−tn}.

Log-Likelihood.

To simplify optimization, the logarithm of the likelihood is taken:

L(w) = ln L = Σ_{n=1}^{N} ln P(tn | xn, w).

Substituting the probability expression results in

L(w) = Σ_{n=1}^{N} { tn ln hw(xn) + (1 − tn) ln [1 − hw(xn)] }.

Interpretation.

This function represents the log-likelihood of the logistic regression model. Maximizing this expression with respect to w yields the optimal parameters that best fit the training data.

Conclusion.

Thus logistic regression models class probabilities using the sigmoid transformation of a linear function and estimates the parameters by maximizing the likelihood of the observed binary targets.

pages.text: Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Logistic Regression Parameters. In logistic regression, the model parameters are estimated using maximum likelihood estimation. The objective is to find the weight vector w that maximizes the likelihood function of the observed data. This optimization problem can be written as argmax_w L(w). To find the optimal parameters, we take the gradient of the log-likelihood with respect to the weight vector w and set it equal to zero. That is, ∇_w L(w) = 0. Suppose we have N training samples where each sample is represented by a feature vector x_n and a corresponding target label t_n ∈ {0,1}. The logistic regression model predicts the probability of class C1 using the sigmoid function. Specifically, the hypothesis function is defined as h(x) = σ(w^T x), where σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^{−z}) is the sigmoid function. To compute the gradient of the log-likelihood, we first evaluate the derivative of the sigmoid function with respect to the weight vector. The derivative of h(x) with respect to w is given by ∇_w h(x) = σ(w^T x)(1 − σ(w^T x)) x. This follows from the derivative property of the sigmoid function, which states that σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)). Substituting this derivative into the gradient of the log-likelihood expression leads to the equation Σ_n [ t_n / h(x_n) ∇_w h(x_n) − (1 − t_n) / (1 − h(x_n)) ∇_w h(x_n) ] = 0. After simplifying the terms and canceling common factors, the resulting condition becomes Σ_n σ(w^T x_n) x_n = Σ_n t_n x_n. This equation defines the optimality condition for the logistic regression parameters. However, the equation is nonlinear in w because the sigmoid function depends on w through the term σ(w^T x_n). As a result, there is no closed-form analytical solution for the parameter vector. Therefore the optimal weights must be obtained using iterative numerical optimization techniques such as gradient ascent, gradient descent, or Newton-Raphson methods. These iterative algorithms progressively update the parameter vector until convergence is achieved.

pages.text:
Gradient Ascent Algorithm for Training Logistic Regression.

To estimate the parameters of the logistic regression model, the log-likelihood function derived earlier must be maximized. This is typically done using an iterative optimization method known as gradient ascent.

Gradient Ascent Update Rule.

At iteration i, the weight vector is updated using

w_{i+1} = w_i + α ∇_w L(w).

Here

w_i : current parameter vector
α : learning rate (step size)
∇_w L(w) : gradient of the log-likelihood function with respect to w.

Gradient Vector.

The gradient of the log-likelihood with respect to the weight vector is

∇_w L(w) = [ ∂L/∂w1 , ∂L/∂w2 , ... , ∂L/∂wd ]^T.

Derivative of Log-Likelihood.

Using the logistic regression probability model, the derivative with respect to the j-th weight component becomes

∂L(w)/∂w_j = Σ_{n=1}^{N} ( t_n − σ(w^T x_n) ) x_n^{(j)}.

Here

σ(w^T x_n) = h_w(x_n)

is the predicted probability given by the sigmoid function.

Thus the gradient can be written compactly as

∇_w L(w) = Σ_{n=1}^{N} ( t_n − h_w(x_n) ) x_n.

Weight Update Rule.

Substituting the gradient into the update equation gives the iterative learning rule

w_j ← w_j + α Σ_{n=1}^{N} ( t_n − h_w(x_n) ) x_n^{(j)}.

Interpretation.

The term

(t_n − h_w(x_n))

represents the prediction error between the true label and the predicted probability. The weights are adjusted proportionally to this error and the corresponding input feature value.

Learning Mechanism.

If the predicted probability is smaller than the actual label, the weights are increased in the direction of the input vector. If the predicted probability is larger than the target value, the weights are decreased.

Conclusion.

This iterative gradient ascent procedure updates the model parameters so that the log-likelihood of the observed training data increases at each step, eventually converging to the optimal logistic regression parameters.

pages.text: Convex Hulls and Linear Separability in Classification. In pattern recognition and machine learning, the concepts of convex hulls and linear separability help us understand whether two sets of data points can be separated by a linear decision boundary. Consider a dataset consisting of points {x_n}. The convex hull of this dataset is defined as the set of all points that can be written as a convex combination of the data points. Mathematically, a point x belongs to the convex hull if it can be expressed as x = Σ_n α_n x_n, where the coefficients α_n satisfy α_n ≥ 0 and Σ_n α_n = 1. This definition means that the convex hull represents all possible weighted averages of the points in the dataset. Geometrically, the convex hull can be visualized as the smallest convex region that contains all the points of the dataset. Now consider two sets of points, denoted by {x_n} and {y_n}. Each of these sets has its own convex hull. The relationship between these convex hulls determines whether the two classes are linearly separable. Two sets of points are said to be linearly separable if there exists a vector w and a scalar bias term w0 such that the following conditions hold: w^T x_n + w0 > 0 for all points x_n in the first set, and w^T y_n + w0 < 0 for all points y_n in the second set. In this case the linear function y(x) = w^T x + w0 defines a decision boundary that separates the two classes. The geometric interpretation is that a hyperplane exists that divides the feature space into two regions, with each region containing points from only one class. An important result related to convex hulls states that if the convex hulls of the two classes intersect, then the classes cannot be linearly separated by any hyperplane. Conversely, if the two classes are linearly separable, then their convex hulls must not intersect. Therefore linear separability is equivalent to the condition that the convex hulls of the two sets of points are disjoint. This geometric interpretation provides an intuitive understanding of classification boundaries and is particularly important in the theory of support vector machines and other linear classifiers.

pages.text:
Convex Hull Interpretation of Linear Separability.

Consider two sets of data points belonging to two different classes. Let the points from class C1 be denoted by {x_n} and the points from class C2 be denoted by {y_n}. Any point inside the convex hull of class C1 can be expressed as a convex combination of its samples:

x = Σ α_n x_n

where

α_n ≥ 0 and Σ α_n = 1.

Similarly, any point inside the convex hull of class C2 can be written as

y = Σ β_n y_n

where

β_n ≥ 0 and Σ β_n = 1.

Part I: Convex Hull Intersection.

If the convex hulls of the two classes intersect, then there exist points x and y such that

x = y.

This means a point can simultaneously be expressed as a convex combination of points from both classes.

Suppose the linear classifier is defined as

w^T z + w0 = 0.

For linearly separable data, the classifier must satisfy

w^T x_n + w0 > 0 for all x_n ∈ C1,

w^T y_n + w0 < 0 for all y_n ∈ C2.

However, if the convex hulls intersect, then at an intersection point

w^T x + w0 = w^T y + w0.

Thus a point cannot simultaneously satisfy both class inequalities, violating the condition for linear separability.

Therefore, if the convex hulls intersect, the dataset is not linearly separable.

Part II: Linear Separability Implies Disjoint Convex Hulls.

Assume the dataset is linearly separable. Then there exists a separating hyperplane such that

w^T x_n + w0 > 0 for all points in class C1,

w^T y_n + w0 < 0 for all points in class C2.

Consider any point inside the convex hull of class C1:

x = Σ α_n x_n.

Substituting into the discriminant function gives

w^T x + w0 = w^T (Σ α_n x_n) + w0.

Using linearity,

w^T x + w0 = Σ α_n (w^T x_n + w0).

Since each term (w^T x_n + w0) > 0 and α_n ≥ 0, their weighted sum is also positive. Therefore

w^T x + w0 > 0

for every point in the convex hull of class C1.

Similarly, for any point inside the convex hull of class C2:

w^T y + w0 < 0.

Conclusion.

Thus all points in the convex hull of class C1 lie on one side of the separating hyperplane and all points in the convex hull of class C2 lie on the other side. Hence the convex hulls cannot intersect.

Final Result.

A dataset is linearly separable if and only if the convex hulls of the two classes do not intersect.

pages.text: Recall the classification problem in supervised learning where we are given a training dataset consisting of input feature vectors and their corresponding target labels. Let the training data be represented by the matrix X, where each row corresponds to a feature vector x_n^T for n = 1,...,N. Thus X is an N × D matrix containing N samples each of dimensionality D. The corresponding class label matrix is denoted by T, where each row t_n^T represents the target vector for the nth sample. Typically T is an N × K matrix where K is the number of classes and the targets are encoded using one-hot representation. Assume that bias terms are not included in the input matrix X. The quadratic error function used for learning the model parameters can be written as E_D(W̃) = (1/2) Tr{(XW + 1w_0^T − T)^T (XW + 1w_0^T − T)}, where Tr(.) denotes the trace of a matrix. In this formulation, X is an N × D data matrix, W is a D × K weight matrix, T is an N × K target matrix, w_0 is a K × 1 bias vector, and 1 denotes an N × 1 vector of ones used to add the bias term to every data point. The augmented parameter set can be represented as W̃ = [W, w_0], which combines both the weight matrix and bias parameters into a single parameter structure. The goal is to find the optimal values of W and w_0 that minimize the quadratic error function over the training dataset. Now consider that the target vectors satisfy a linear constraint of the form a^T t_n + b = 0, where a is a vector and b is a scalar constant. This constraint expresses a linear relationship among the components of the target vectors. The objective is to show that the same linear constraint also holds for the model outputs y(x), that is, a^T y(x) + b = 0. To prove this property, we determine the optimal parameters W and w_0 by minimizing the quadratic error function E_D(W̃). The solution is obtained by solving the optimization problem arg min_{W,w_0} E_D(W̃), which leads to the least-squares solution for the classifier parameters. This formulation provides a matrix-based representation of the least squares classification model and establishes how constraints on the targets propagate to constraints on the predicted outputs of the model.

pages.text:
Derivation of Bias Term in Linear Least Squares Classification.

Consider a linear model used for classification or regression of the form

y(x) = w^T x + w0.

To determine the optimal parameters, the squared error function is minimized. The derivative of the error function with respect to the bias term w0 is computed and set equal to zero.

Gradient with Respect to w0.

Taking the derivative of the error function ED(w) with respect to w0 gives

∇_{w0} ED(w) = 0.

Using matrix trace identities and differentiating the quadratic error expression results in

w^T X^T 1 − T^T 1 + 1^T 1 w0 = 0.

Here

1 is a vector of ones of length N,
X is the data matrix,
T is the target vector.

Since

1^T 1 = N,

the equation simplifies to

w0 = (1/N) (T^T − w^T X^T) 1.

Mean Representation.

Define the average target value and the average input vector as


t̄ = (1/N) T^T 1,

x̄ = (1/N) X^T 1.

Substituting these expressions into the equation for the bias term yields

w0 = t̄ − w^T x̄.

Interpretation.

This result shows that the optimal bias term aligns the linear model so that the predicted outputs match the mean of the target values when evaluated at the mean of the input data.

Thus the bias adjusts the position of the decision boundary without changing its orientation.

Conclusion.

For the optimal weight vector w obtained by minimizing the squared error function, the corresponding optimal bias is

w0 = t̄ − w^T x̄.

This expression is commonly used in linear regression and linear classification models when solving the least squares optimization problem.

pages.text: Substitute the linear constraint derived earlier into the quadratic error formulation of the least squares classifier. Starting from the original error expression, substitute the relation obtained from the constraint a^T t_n + b = 0 into the objective function. The quadratic error becomes E_D(w̃) = (1/2) Tr{(XW + 1(t − W̄^T t)^T − T)^T (XW + 1(t − W̄^T t)^T − T)}. To simplify the notation, define transformed matrices. Let T̄ = 1 t^T and X̃ = 1 x̄^T, where the overbar quantities represent mean vectors across the dataset. Using these substitutions, the quadratic error can be rewritten as E_D(w̃) = (1/2) Tr{(XW − X̃W + T̄ − T)^T (XW − X̃W + T̄ − T)}. Now define new centered variables to simplify the expression. Let X̂ = X − X̃ represent the centered data matrix and T̂ = T̄ − T represent the centered target matrix. The quadratic error function becomes E_D(W) = (1/2) Tr{(X̂W + T̂)^T (X̂W + T̂)}. To obtain the optimal parameters, differentiate the error with respect to W and set the gradient equal to zero. This gives the least squares normal equation ∇_W E_D(W) = 0, which leads to the solution Ŵ = (X̂^T X̂)^{-1} X̂^T T̂. This expression is the closed-form least squares estimate of the weight matrix using centered input data and targets. Recall that the model output is given by y(x) = W^T x + w_0. Substituting the obtained solution into the model and using the centered representation leads to the final expression for the predicted output y(x) = t̄ − T̂^T (X̂^T X̂)^{-1} (x − x̄). This result shows that the predicted output depends on the deviation of the input vector from the mean of the training inputs. The derivation demonstrates that the least squares classifier solution can be expressed entirely in terms of centered data matrices and provides insight into how the prediction function depends on the geometry of the training dataset.

pages.text:
Derivation of Linear Constraint on the Model Output.

Starting from the expression for the model output y(x), we multiply both sides by the vector a^T in order to analyze the projection of the output along direction a.

Multiplying the Model Equation.

a^T y(x) = a^T t̄ − a^T T̂^T (X^T X)^{-1} (x − x̄)

where

x̄ = mean of input vectors

t̄ = mean of target values

T̂ represents the centered target vector.

Mean Target Term.

The term involving the mean target is

a^T t̄ = (1/N) a^T T^T 1

where

T = [t1, t2, ..., tN]^T

and 1 is a vector of ones.

Expanding the expression

a^T T^T = a^T (t1, t2, ..., tN).

From the relations derived earlier in the analysis, this simplifies to

a^T T^T = −b 1^T.

Therefore

a^T t̄ = (1/N)(−b 1^T 1).

Since

1^T 1 = N,

we obtain

a^T t̄ = −b.

Centered Target Contribution.

Using the decomposition

T̂ = T − t̄

we obtain

a^T T̂^T = a^T (T − t̄)^T.

Expanding

a^T T^T = −b 1^T

a^T t̄^T = −b 1^T.

Therefore

a^T T̂^T = −b 1^T − (−b 1^T) = 0.

Thus the second term of the original equation becomes zero.

Final Result.

Substituting these results into the original expression gives

a^T y(x) = −b.

Rearranging

a^T y(x) + b = 0.

Interpretation.

This equation represents a linear constraint satisfied by the output of the model. It corresponds to a hyperplane in the transformed output space. The vector a defines the orientation of the hyperplane, while the scalar b controls its offset from the origin.

Hence the model output lies on the hyperplane defined by

a^T y(x) + b = 0.

This form frequently appears in linear classification theory and geometric interpretations of decision boundaries.

pages.text: Support Vector Machine (SVM) Theory introduces the concept of finding an optimal separating boundary between two classes in a feature space. Consider a classification problem in which we are given two sets of labeled training patterns. The dataset consists of positive examples and negative examples. Let the positive class be represented by the set S+ containing all positive (+ve) samples and the negative class be represented by the set S− containing all negative (−ve) samples. Each data point lies in a feature space defined by its feature coordinates, for example (f1, f2) in a two-dimensional representation. The goal of the classification problem is to find a hyperplane that separates the positive and negative examples. A hyperplane is a linear decision boundary defined by an equation of the form w^T x + b = 0, where w is the weight vector and b is the bias term. In the SVM framework the objective is not only to separate the classes but to do so in a way that maximizes the margin between the two classes. The margin refers to the distance between the decision boundary and the closest data points from each class. These closest points are known as support vectors. In geometric terms, SVM attempts to construct the widest possible separating region between the two classes. This region is often described as the "widest street" that separates the positive and negative data points. The decision boundary lies at the center of this region. The two parallel boundaries on either side correspond to the maximum margin constraints that pass through the support vectors. Thus the optimal separating hyperplane is the center line of the maximum width separating region between the two classes. This maximum margin property improves the generalization ability of the classifier because it chooses the boundary that is most robust to small perturbations in the training data. Therefore the fundamental idea of SVM is to identify the hyperplane that maximizes the separation margin between the positive and negative classes in the feature space.

pages.text:
Geometric Interpretation of Linear Decision Boundary and Optimal Hyperplane.

Consider a linear classifier defined by the decision function

y(x) = w^T x + b.

The vector w represents the normal vector to the decision boundary (hyperplane). It determines the orientation of the separating line or plane in the feature space.

Geometric Meaning of w.

The vector w points in the direction perpendicular to the decision boundary. Therefore, the projection of any input vector x onto w determines on which side of the boundary the point lies.

For a test pattern u, the projection onto the vector w is given by

u · w.

Decision Rule.

The classification decision is made by comparing this projection with a threshold value C.

u · w ≥ C

If this condition holds, the sample belongs to the positive class; otherwise it belongs to the negative class.

Let the threshold constant be represented as

C = −b.

Then the decision rule becomes

u · w + b ≥ 0.

Thus

If w^T u + b ≥ 0 → u belongs to class C1 (positive class)

If w^T u + b < 0 → u belongs to class C2 (negative class).

Here, the values w and b jointly define the decision function.

Geometric Visualization.

The hyperplane defined by

w^T x + b = 0

separates the feature space into two regions. Points on one side produce positive values of the decision function, while points on the other side produce negative values.

The shaded region around the separating line illustrates the possible locations of different separating hyperplanes. Among these, the goal is to find the optimal hyperplane that best separates the two classes.

Optimal Hyperplane Concept.

When multiple separating hyperplanes are possible, the optimal one is the hyperplane that maximizes the margin between the two classes. The margin is the distance between the hyperplane and the closest points from each class.

The optimal hyperplane therefore:

1. Separates the classes correctly.
2. Maximizes the distance from the nearest data points of both classes.

This geometric interpretation forms the foundation for maximum margin classifiers such as Support Vector Machines (SVM).

Thus, the parameters w and b determine both the orientation and position of the decision boundary that separates the classes in feature space.

pages.text: Consider a binary classification problem in the Support Vector Machine framework where we have two sets of training data. Let the set S+ contain the positive training examples denoted by x_i^+ and the set S− contain the negative training examples denoted by x_i^−. The objective is to find a separating hyperplane that maximizes the margin between these two classes. A separating hyperplane can be expressed in the form w^T x + b = 0, where w is the weight vector and b is the bias term. For the widest separating hyperplane, constraints are imposed on the training examples such that positive examples lie on one side of the margin and negative examples lie on the other side. These constraints are written as w^T x_i^+ + b ≥ 1 for all positive examples and w^T x_i^− + b ≤ −1 for all negative examples. To express these constraints in a unified form, class labels are introduced. Let y_i = +1 for positive examples and y_i = −1 for negative examples. Using these labels, both constraints can be combined into a single inequality given by y_i (w^T x_i + b) ≥ 1 for all training samples. This formulation ensures that all training points lie outside or on the margin boundaries. The data points that satisfy the equality condition y_i (w^T x_i + b) = 1 are known as support vectors. These support vectors lie exactly on the margin boundaries and play a critical role in defining the optimal hyperplane. Geometrically, they can be thought of as points located on the edges or curbs of the widest separating street between the two classes. The central line of this street corresponds to the decision boundary. The learning objective of the Support Vector Machine is therefore to determine the parameters w and b that maximize the separation margin between the two classes. This can be expressed as an optimization problem in which we search for the parameters that maximize the separation measure S(w,b). The resulting hyperplane is called the maximum margin hyperplane because it provides the largest possible distance between the two classes while still correctly classifying the training examples.

pages.text:
Derivation of Margin and Optimal Hyperplane in Maximum Margin Classification.

Consider a linear classifier defined by the decision boundary

w^T x + b = 0.

The vector w is normal to the decision boundary and determines the orientation of the separating hyperplane.

Margin Concept.

For two linearly separable classes, there exist support vectors from each class that lie closest to the decision boundary. Let

x_{s+} = closest point from the positive class
x_{s−} = closest point from the negative class.

The margin is defined as the perpendicular distance between the two supporting hyperplanes passing through these closest points.

Unit Direction Vector.

Define a unit vector along the direction of w as

i = w / ||w||.

This unit vector represents the direction normal to the separating hyperplane.

Projection Interpretation.

The margin can be computed using projections of the support vectors onto the unit vector i.

Margin μ_s = (x_{s+} · i) − (x_{s−} · i).

Substituting i = w / ||w|| gives

μ_s = (x_{s+} · w − x_{s−} · w) / ||w||.

Support Vector Constraints.

For support vectors, the classifier is scaled such that

w^T x_{s+} + b = 1

and

w^T x_{s−} + b = −1.

From these equations

w^T x_{s+} = 1 − b

w^T x_{s−} = −1 − b.

Margin Computation.

Substituting into the margin expression gives

μ_s = [(1 − b) − (−1 − b)] / ||w||.

Simplifying

μ_s = (2) / ||w||.

Thus the geometric margin between the two classes is

μ_s = 2 / ||w||.

Optimization Objective.

To obtain the optimal separating hyperplane, the margin must be maximized. Therefore the optimization problem becomes

maximize 2 / ||w|| with respect to w and b.

Since the constant 2 does not affect the optimization, the equivalent formulation is

maximize 1 / ||w||

or equivalently

minimize ||w||.

Interpretation.

Minimizing the magnitude of w while satisfying the classification constraints results in the hyperplane that maximizes the separation between the classes.

This formulation forms the foundation of the maximum margin classifier and leads to the Support Vector Machine (SVM) optimization problem.
